The Central Competent Authority responsible for animal health is the Subdirectorate-General for Animal Health (Subdirección General de Sanidad Veterinaria, SGSV), which belongs to the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food. The SGSV is in charge of the preparation, planning and co-ordination of national eradication programmes. However, the supervision, implementation and development of the eradication programmes are the responsibility of the animal health section of the official veterinary services in each of the 17 ACs. These services must report to the SGSV on their plans for the implementation of the programme and the results achieved. The SGSV forwards the results obtained in eradication programmes co-financed by Community funds to the Commission services. The National Co-operation and Monitoring Committee for the National Animal Diseases Eradication Programmes, CDEP, already described in report nº XXIV/1028/99 is also active as a discussion and co-ordination body in the BBEP. The representatives of the 17 ACs, together with the SGSV, have regular meetings to discuss the results of the programmes between ACs. The official veterinary services of the ACs are organised from local (&RPDUFD) to central level in comarcal units, a provincial office (if the AC is constituted by more than one province) and a central office. Their legal base is established by `Normas Autonómicas' or 'Resoluciones Autonómicas' (Autonomous legislation), which are published every year. Generally, these are direct transpositions of national law, which must be taken as the minimum standard. The costs of the eradication programmes are financed by the budgets of the ACs and the General State Administration through periodic transfers of funds Farm owners incur no costs. Most activities related to animal identification, herd registration, movement permits and eradication programmes are carried out by staff of the official services of the ACs. Blood sampling for eradication programmes is normally undertaken by temporarily contracted sanitary teams, constituted by authorised veterinarians. In areas where membership to $VRFLDFLRQHV GH 9 'HIHQVD 6DQLWDULD Associations of Sanitary Defence, $'6V)1 is high, those tasks are normally carried out by the veterinarian associated with the ADS. $QLPDO LGHQWLILFDWLRQ IDUP UHJLVWUDWLRQ Farm registration and animal identification is compulsory for cattle. The requirements are laid down in Royal Decree 1980/1998, which is based on Council Regulation 97/820. The Royal Decree is in line with the Regulation and was intended as a supporting and clarifying document to the Regulation. Council Directive 92/102/EEC is no longer applied since Council Regulation 97/820 came into force. The system includes the granting of a unique registration number, double ear-tagging of the animal, identification of calves within 30 days of birth, inclusion of the data on a computerised system and granting of a passport which accompanies the animal wherever it goes. The passport contains information of a veterinary nature such as results of Tuberculosis (TB), Brucellosis, Bovine Pleuro-pneumonia (BPP) and Enzootic Bovine Leucosis (EBL) tests as well as all vaccinations and the disease status of the herd. Since the 1st January 1998, no bovine movements are permitted which do not respect of the above system. The competent authority declares that all existing herds are registered and that the number of registered herds has dropped in recent years because a lot of small farms have ceased their activity. At present, beef production is becoming increasingly important. Beef as well as milk production is largely concentrated in the north of the country, which has a mild climate and high average yearly rainfall. Grazing practises vary from region to region. In the ACs visited, most dairy herds do not mix as they graze in individually fenced, clearly separated, 3 Transhumance is the practice of moving flocks between different areas according to the seasonal availability of pasture 11 areas. The communal pastures in the mountains are generally used by beef cattle, which often remain in these pastures from April to October. For dairy cattle, breeding is not linked to season. Beef cattle are generally born in early spring when the animals are in the stables. The most problematic areas regarding BA infection in Asturias and Galicia are concentrated in remote mountainous areas. The mission team was told that cattle grazing in communal pasture are treated as one epidemiological unit. This practice is respected when all animals present in the communal pasture are registered in one AC. A high number of communal pastures, however, are located in bordering areas between ACs and frequent contacts may exist between herds registered in different ACs. No interactive data exchange regarding results of the eradication programmes existed between the visited ACs and their adjacent ACs. In the winter months a number of herds are sent for transhumance to Extremadura, 500 km further to the south. Authorisation for movement is required by sending an official request by fax from the veterinary services of origin to the veterinary services of destination, 48 hours prior to departure. Only sanitarily qualified cattle are allowed to move. No sanitary checks are carried out at their destination, prior to the return of the animals, although a high number of cows are in late pregnancy and BA prevalence here is much higher than in the originating AC.4 Due to the lack of knowledge on the bio-types of Brucella sp. involved, the importance of cross-infection between different species (bovines/small ruminants) grazing on the same pastures is not clear. recommendations.text: To the Spanish Authorities The supervision of all the relevant companies within the feed and food sector should be reinforced in the light of the experience acquired during the current dioxin problem. Particular attention should be paid to the documentary systems in order to improve the traceability of potentially suspect products. The Spanish authorities should urgently inform the Commission services about any relevant information on this matter, particularly as regards the results of the analyses carried out on the samples of suspect oils, the outcome of the investigation conducted in Company A and the decisions taken in regard of the blockaded consignments of suspect oils. In addition, detailed written information on the implementation of the corrective measures and further actions taken in the light of this report, should be made available to the Commission services within one month after the receipt of the final version of the report. A general reflection on the strategy for handling emergency situations should be carried out, particularly by MAPA, in order to make sure that more co-ordinated, better defined and properly documented decisions and mechanisms can be put in place in an efficient manner in the future.

To the Commission Services The Commission services should consider reviewing and reinforcing the EU legal framework related to the production and use of feed materials, particularly as to their traceability. The Commission services should consider reviewing the legal framework concerning the use of recycled frying oils as raw materials in the feed chain. 20

recommendations.text: Competent authorities Legislation transposing Council Directives 91/493/EEC and 91/492/EEC should be fully implemented and enforced in the CCAA visited and in all the other CCAA in similar situation. In order to achieve this goal, the supervision of the inspection services should be improved and the number of qualified inspectors should be increased. On the basis of the potential risk for public health (e.g. marine biotoxins and viral contamination in bivalve molluscs), the Spanish authorities should consider putting in place all the necessary measures to guarantee a uniform 24 implementation of the EU relevant legislation in all the CCAA in a similar situation.

Laboratories All laboratories performing official analyses should be accredited. All private laboratories performing own-checks analyses should be approved by the CA taking into account the requirements of EN 45001 standards or equivalent requirements. The CA should also approve establishments' internal laboratories. The CA should recognise laboratories performing analyses for checking the efficiency of purification of bivalve molluscs. Co-ordination should be established between the NRLs and all the regional laboratories performing official analyses sited on the CCAA where the production areas of bivalve molluscs are declared. Spain should inform the Commission services of the actual date of designation of the NRL for monitoring bacteriological and viral contamination of bivalve molluscs. Furthermore, this should establish a network of contacts and a programme of work to meet its commitments under Council Decision 1999/313/EC. The competent authority should ensure that the NRL is adequately funded to undertake these tasks.

Official control 8.1.3.1.Fishery products The Spanish authorities should take all the necessary measures in cases where the relevant requirements of approval of establishments and factory vessels cease to be met. The guides produced by the central and regional services visited for the approval and assessment of HACCP systems should be put into force. Pending adoption of Community provisions, those issued by the central authorities for controls over Listeria monocytogenes in smoked fishery products should at least be respected. The Real Decreto 202/2000, for the supervision of staff handling foodstuffs, should be implemented. In order to avoid any risk of possible fraudulent imports of fishery products from TCs, the system of bilateral agreements in place should take into consideration the information produced by the TC authorities and by FVO missions. 8.1.3.2.Bivalve molluscs The relevant Spanish authorities should take all the necessary measures to guarantee that bivalve molluscs are put on the market only if they are harvested in officially declared production areas where the respective 25 classification and monitoring of phytoplankton, microbiological and marine biotoxins contamination are put in place. The registration documents should be amended, in accordance with the relevant requirements, in all the purification/dispatch centres visited. All the relevant marine biotoxins (PSP, DSP and ASP) should be checked in all bivalve molluscs, gastropods, echinoderms and tunicates harvested. The Spanish authorities should take all the necessary measures in cases where the relevant requirements of approval purification/dispatch centres cease to be met.

Written guarantees Within one month of receipt of the draft report, the competent authorities of Spain should inform the Commission Services of the progress and result of the measures taken including a timetable for completion of measures and actions still outstanding at that time. The competent authorities of Spain should also inform the Commission Services every six months on the progress made for the execution of the measures mentioned in the above mentioned action plan until all those measures have been put in place completely. 8.2. Recommendations to the Commission Services The linguistic discrepancy between the English and the Spanish text of Directive 91/492/EEC (and other linguistic versions, if applicable), noticed by the inspection team should be rectified.

Efforts should be maintained to improve the operational efficiency of the national database (SIMOGAN) and to ensure that all establishments/animal have been entered and data validated.
Animal movement control should be re-inforced, to prevent the movement of animals out of infected herds (other than direct to slaughter) and to avoid movement between non-qualified herds.
Introduce bi-annual serological testing for the maintenance of OBF status in line with national legislation and the provisions of Council Directive 97/12/EC.

More effort should be made to isolate Brucella in the serologically positive herds. Follow-up should be undertaken to confirm the disease status of farms screened by the 3 laboratories with erroneous RBT results.

Infected dairy farms should be issued with specific instructions on the treatment/disposal of milk. An action plan for the implementation of the above recommendations and conclusions, including deadlines for action, should be sent to the Commission Services within two months of receipt of the final report. 9.2. To the Commission Services 9.2.1. Review future proposals for the BBEP from Spain in the light of this report. 9.2.2. Consider updating the "Guide for the achievement of eradication and control programmes in the veterinary field34" to give specific guidance on the interpretation of laboratory results for farms/regions with high levels of disease prevalence. 34 SANCO/1775/2001 20 ADDENDUM Competent authority's response to the draft report In a letter dated 24 May 2002 responding to the draft report, the competent authority offered comprehensive comments which have where possible been included in the text of the report. audits.title: Follow-up on Plant Health in the Potato Sector

recommendations.text: Ensure that all staff dealing with outbreaks of ring rot and brown rot are adequately trained in the requirements of the two control directives. Particular attention should be given to the investigation of outbreaks along clonal links and the consequent designation of contamination and probable contamination.
Correct the contingency plan for ring rot to include measures for all fields on a contaminated place of production.
Consider updating or supplementing the two contingency plans with additional, practical information for the inspectors carrying out the investigations and controls.
Increase the survey efforts in potatoes for both diseases.
Where relevant, systematically include the initial clonal selections in the surveys as required in Article 8 of Council Directive 93/85/EEC and Article 7 of Council Directive 98/57/EC.

Implement correctly all the control measures of Council Directive 93/85/EEC and Council Directive 98/57/EC, in particular: a. Prohibit movement, except under official control, of potato lots with a "suspected occurrence" until the suspicion has been verified/refuted as required in Article 4 (2) (a) of both directives. b. Prescribe measures on all fields of a contaminated place of production as required by Article 5 of the two directives (and specified in detail in Annexes III and IV of the ring rot directive and Annex V and VI of the R. solanacearum directive). c. Carry out thorough investigation along clonal links for each case as required in Article 6 of the ring rot directive and Article 5 of the R. solanacearum directive and take the necessary consequences in the form of designating contamination and probable contamination. Where a clonal link is the most likely cause of the contamination (i.e. separate outbreaks have been found without any other identifiable cause than their common source of seed), at least all sister lots should be designated as "probably contaminated" ­ or, of course, if test results are positive, "contaminated". The farms where this designation has been done - regardless of test results ­ should be included in the "demarcated zone" with the corresponding requirements for surveys, renewal of seed etc.. d. Where the investigations point at "imported" material as the most likely source, notify the "exporting" Member State (and the Commission) in a timely manner and with the necessary detail, so that this Member State 14 can follow up. ­ Articles 5 (2) and 5 (3) of both directives. For R. solanacearum, such notification is even obligatory already before the "suspected occurrence" has been confirmed (Article 4 (3)). These clauses apply similarly if "probably contaminated" lots have been identified in Spain after they have been "exported". e. Designate as "probably contaminated" all potato lots that have been irrigated with R. solanacearum contaminated water, at least under circumstances where such irrigation has proven to cause outbreaks in some crops. This is required under Article 5 (1) (c) (iii) of Council Directive 98/57/EC. The competent authorities in Spain are requested to submit to the Commission, within two months of the receipt of the translated final report, an action plan addressing the above recommendations and giving deadlines for their implementation. 9. ADDENDUM At the time of finalisation of the report, the Spanish Authorities had not yet provided any response to the recommendations. 15

ADDENDUM TO MISSION REPORT DG(SANCO)/7660/2005 In response to the recommendations in Annex 4 to the draft report, the CCA provided an action plan indicating the following corrective actio 3 In relation to cooperation between the various authorities coordination meetings have taken place after the mission between the MAPA/MISACO with the MAP (one meeting), two meetings with the Customs Department and three meetings with the Puertos del Estado (the national ports management board). Puertos del Estado is also following up the mission's conclusions and coordinating appropriate corrective measures with the port authorities. Moreover, an effort is being made to remedy the lack of cooperation at local level mentioned in the report. AENA is placing central-level cooperation on a formal basis and has scheduled a meeting for 21 November to discuss this matter. Recommendation 5 The CCAs continued the programme for supervising inspection post infrastructure in 2005. Some of which were to follow up Community inspections or view facilities and study plans for conversion or replacement of existing facilities. The representatives of the various central authorities and of Puertos del Estado and AENA took part as the competent bodies for infrastructure management. The following inspections were carried out after the mission and copies of the reports were provided: ­ Port of Castellon BIP (MAPA-MISACO) 14 July 2005. ­ Port of Tarragona BIP (MAPA-MISACO-MAP) 13 October 2005. ­ Palma de Mallorca Airport BIP (MAPA-MISACO-MAP) 2 November 2005. Recommendation 8 The CCAs inform that, in order to ensure that supervision of rejected consignments and kitchen waste from international means of transport meets the requirements laid down in Regulation (EC) No 1774/2002, in the National Subproducts Committee's Working Party on Subproducts Derived from International Goods Trade, meetings have been held with representatives of the various authorities involved to draw up a protocol enabling the rejection procedure to comply with the transport, labelling and documentation requirements under Regulation (EC) 1774/2002 for transfer from border inspection points to Category 2 plants. The problems stemming from disposal of kitchen waste from international means of transport have also been studied, taking into account the fact that the protocol to be adopted must tally with what is laid down for goods rejected at BIPs. The compromise arrived at by the group is for several proposals for a protocol to be drawn up for presentation at the National Subproducts Committee's meeting in December 2005. Recommendation 10 The CCAS provided updated figures in relation to staffing of the BIPs. These appear to indicate that some vacancies have been filled and some new posts created. Revised figures for percentage of time of officials devoted to BIP tasks were also given. 14 Recommendation 11 and 12 Puertos del Estado and AENA have undertaken to rectify the shortcomings in terms of scarcity of certain facilities, the lack of certain equipment or inadequate hygiene conditions determined during the mission within the periods indicated by sending out notices, copies of which were provided. Recommendation 13 As regards BIP veterinary service access to cargo manifests in order to enable them to have an overall picture of the consignments being imported, the computer connection between the TRACES and SISAEX systems and the PORTEL application is being reviewed with Puertos del Estado to make it possible to present documents affecting the various inspection services in electronic form in order to enable them to have an overall picture of the consignments being imported. Recommendation 14 As regards the procedure for veterinary checks of goods which do not comply with veterinary legislation and are destined for establishments authorised in accordance with Articles 12(4) and 13 of Directive 97/78/EC, the Subdirectorate-General of Health Controls at Borders has contacted DG SANCO to ask it to give a course or a talk to BIP inspectors. Likewise, during the meeting of the Working Party on Veterinary Checks held in Brussels on 14 October, the Spanish representatives asked the Commission to set up a working party or hold a meeting specifically to clarify these procedural matters which have given rise to discrepancies and application problems in various Member States visited by the FVO. Finally, we would point out that proposals have been made to MAP for it to hold a course on this subject for BIP inspectors in 2006. Recommendation 15 The SE use the SISAEX IV developed by Subdirectorate-General for Health Controls at Borders which is based upon and adapted to the TRACES system. This national system operates in connection with TRACES (through a system-to-system connection) and CCA is awaiting a reply from the Commission to enable both Part 1 (declaration) and Part 2 (decision) of CVEDs to be sent.

recommendations.text: To fully implement the requirements of Art 4, 6 and 8 of Council Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

To bring the testing regime for maintaining the animal health status in relation to bovine tuberculosis and brucellosis (officially free/free), into compliance with the requirements of Council Directive 64/432/EEC.

To cease the discriminatory checks on pigs arriving in Spain from other Member States and to ensure that checks carried out on live 23 animals at their destination are in accordance with the requirements of Art 5 (1) of Council Directive 90/425/EEC.

To ensure that official veterinarians at slaughterhouses apply the provisions of Art 5, (1) (b) (ii), of Council Directive 90/425/EEC, to verify that only animals that meet the requirements of Art 3(1) of that Directive are slaughtered.

To ensure that Community rules in relation to standstill, residency and imports from third countries are respected and controlled by the CA before certificates are issued as specified in Council Directive 64/432/EEC Art 6 for cattle for breeding and production and in Council Directive 91/68/EEC Article 4 (a) or 4 (c) for sheep.

To ensure that the time limits for clinical inspection of swine and equidae before dispatch, laid down in Council Directive 64/432/EEC Art 3 (2) (a) and Council Directive 90/426/EEC, Art 4, respectively, are respected.

To ensure that private veterinary practitioners involved in pre- certification are free of possible conflicts of interests to meet the requirements of Art 4 (2) (1) of Council Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.
To ensure that further, continuous training on TRACES and certification is organised for staff designated to use TRACES to guarantee correct use of the certification system.
To ensure that the principles of certification, as laid down in Council Directive 96/93/EC are respected and that TRACES is implemented correctly.

To ensure that official controls on holdings, dealers premises and assembly centres verify that stockfarmers and veterinarians record and retain information on veterinary treatments as required by Article 10 of Council Directive 96/23/EC. 10. COMPETENT AUTHORITY RESPONSE TO RECOMMENDATIONS

The competent authorities should ensure that amendments to Council Directives 86/362/EEC, 86/363/EEC and 90/642/EEC as regards maximum residue levels are transposed and national legislation providing for coordination of control measures under Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 is introduced without undue delay.

The competent authorities should ensure that efficient and effective co- ordination takes place between all competent authorities carrying out official controls for pesticide residues, in accordance with Article 4 (3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

The competent authorities should ensure that all monitoring results, including follow-up, are routinely reported to the Commission as required by Articles 4(3) and 7(3) of Council Directives 90/642/EEC and 86/362/EEC respectively.

The competent authorities should consider taking into account the draft "Guidance document on notification criteria for pesticide residues findings to the Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed (RASFF)" (SANCO/3346/2001, rev 7), including systematic consumer risk assessments for adults and children.

The competent authorities should ensure that (i) all laboratories involved in the official control of pesticide residues are designated in accordance with Article 12 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, and (ii) all designated laboratories comply with Article 12 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, or are availing of the derogation foreseen in Article 18 of Commission Regulation (EC) No 2076/2005. The quality control system in the laboratories availing of Article 18 should be based on the SANCO guidelines for 'Quality Control Procedures for Pesticide Residue Analysis' (Document No SANCO/10232/2006).

In cases where monitoring shows non-compliance, the competent authorities should ensure that appropriate enforcement actions are taken in accordance with Article 54 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and should consider taking into account the analytical uncertainty, established in accordance with the SANCO guidelines for 'Quality Control Procedures for Pesticide Residue Analysis' (Document No SANCO/10232/2006).

In accordance with Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, the competent authorities should ensure that staff receive appropriate training so that samples are taken in accordance with Commission Directive 2002/63/EC.

The competent authorities should consider substantially increasing the range of validated analytical methods for detection of pesticide residues and metabolites being sought, so as to better reflect those substances being marketed and used. 23

The competent authorities should ensure the introduction of co-ordinated and comprehensive inspection and enforcement procedures for controlling the marketing of plant protection products, including follow-up, in accordance with Article 17 of Council Directive 91/414/EEC and clarify the competencies and procedures for importation of plant protection products.

The competent authorities should ensure the introduction of co-ordinated and comprehensive inspection and enforcement procedures for controlling the use of plant protection products, including the use of illegal products and follow-up, in accordance with Article 17 of Council Directive 91/414/EEC.

The competent authorities should ensure that the annual report to the Commission in the framework of Article 17 of Council Directive 91/414/EEC includes results from all Autonomous Communities. The CA of Spain is invited to send to the Commission, within 25 working days of receipt of the report, an action plan in response to the recommendations. This action plan should clearly set out the manner and deadline by which the competent authorities will address each recommendation. 9. COMPETENT AUTHORITY RESPONSE TO RECOMMENDATIONS

recommendations.text: Ensure that the results of the survey carried out for B. xylophilus on the basis of the survey plan are notified to the Commission and the other Member States as soon as they are available in accordance with Article 4, Point 2 of Decision 2006/133/EC.

Ensure that the official system provides sufficient guarantees that susceptible material is continuously undergoing an appropriate heat treatment to achieve a minimum core temperature of 56 °C for 30 minutes in order to ensure freedom from live B. xylophilus where required by Annex to Decision 2006/133/EC, including the verification of the measuring equipment and the placing of wood probes at appropriate places in the wood and taking the temperature gradient in the HT chamber into consideration.

Ensure that official inspections of the authorised processing plants for wood and wood packaging material are carried out on a continuous basis to verify the effectiveness of the treatment as well as the traceability of the wood in accordance with point 1 (d) of the Annex to Decision 2006/133/EC.

Ensure that the requirements on the control of movements provided for by the Annex to Decision 2006/133/EC are fully met. In particular the movements of untreated material shall not be permitted and assemblers of wood packaging material in the demarcated area shall not be authorised to apply the ISPM 15 mark.

Ensure that adequate surveys for the presence of R. ferrugineus are carried out in all territories where plants of Palmae are present, as laid down in Article 5(1) of Commission Decision 2007/365/EC, so that the true distribution of the pest is fully recognised; in particular palms grown in private properties should be included.

Ensure that any suspected or actual appearance of R. ferrugineus in the country is immediately notified to the responsible official bodies of Spain, as laid down in Article 5(2) of Commission Decision 2007/365/EC; in particular co-operation with the stakeholders should be improved.

Ensure that in cases where R. ferrugineus is found, demarcated areas are defined in each case, as required by Article 6(1)(a) of Commission Decision 2007/365/EC and, when they are defined, that they comply with provisions of Point 1 of Annex II to the same Decision; in particular isolated focal points in areas where R. ferrugineus is not known to occur should be included.

Ensure that in cases where R. ferrugineus is found, the control measures are imposed in each case, as required by Article 6(1)(b) of Commission Decision 2007/365/EC and, when they are imposed, that they comply with provisions of Point 2 of Annex II to the same Decision; in particular palms grown in private properties should be included and further spread of the pest during final disposal actions should be prevented.

Ensure that susceptible plants, listed in Article 1(b) of Commission Decision 2007/365/EC, may only be moved within the Community if the conditions specified in Point 2 of Annex I to the same Decision are met; in particular, time restrictions and inspection requirements applied prior to movement of the plants, should be respected.

recommendations.text: To develop tools for efficient and effective co-ordination and co-operation between all Competent Authorities involved in the import controls as required by Article 4(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, and specifically in relation to follow-up controls, between MARM, MSPSI and local authorities, in order to comply with requirements laid down in Directive 97/78/EC, 91/496/EEC and other relevant implementing legislation.

To ensure that staff receive appropriate training in the areas referred to in Annex II, Chapter I of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and keep up to date in their area of competence as laid down in Article 6 of the same Regulation, in order to comply with requirements laid down in Directive 97/78/EC, 91/496/EEC and other relevant implementing legislation, and more specifically in view of the changes foreseen with the implementation of the 2010 Resolution.

To ensure that the administrative procedure for sourcing equipment and consumables for the BIPs ensures their availability, as required in Article 4.2(d) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, in order to comply with requirements laid down in Directives 91/496/EEC and 97/78/EC, and Decision 2001/812/EC.

To ensure that appropriate actions are taken in order to ensure that, when a non- compliance is identified, the operator remedies the situation as required in Article 54 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, in order to fulfil the requirements laid down in Council Directives 97/78/EC, 91/496/EEC, and relevant implementing legislation.

To review the verification process, in order to ensure that, when deficiencies are reported, corrective actions are effectively implemented as required in Article 8 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, in order to fulfil the requirements laid down in Council Directives 97/78/EC, 91/496/EEC, and relevant implementing legislation.

To verify the effective implementation of the Protocol between Customs and the veterinary services in ensuring that all animal products and live animals undergo veterinary checks, as required in Articles 5 and 6 of Regulation 136/2004 and Articles 4 and 5 of Regulation 202/2004.

To ensure that the audit system in relation to import/transit controls is implemented as planned, covers all levels of the official controls and ensures effectiveness of the official controls at BIPs, in line with Decision 2006/677/EC, in order to achieve the objectives of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, as laid down in Article 4.6 of the same Regulation.
To ensure that, in BIPs approved for animal products, the registers and records are maintained as laid down in points 4 and 5 of the Annex to Decision 2001/812/EC.

To ensure that TRACES is correctly and effectively used, also for consignments channelled, rejected, reimported, and for non-EU-complying consignments for transit, warehousing or ship supplying, in line with requirements laid down in Article 3 (2) of Commission Decision 2004/292/EC.

To ensure that (i) categorisation of any BIP reflects the categories of products for which facilities, equipment and procedures are in place and in line with requirements laid down in Directive 91/496/EEC, Directive 97/78/EC and Decision 2001/812/EC and (ii) enforcement measures are effectively implemented, including suspension or withdrawal of a category, where the BIP is found, during the checks carried out by the competent authority, not to be complying with the above requirements.

To ensure that deficiencies in facilities, equipment and hygienical standards in the BIPs visited are rectified, in order to comply with requirements of Decision 2001/812/EC and Directives 97/78/EC and 91/496/EC.
To implement procedures for verifying the effectiveness of official controls on imports of feed of non-animal origin as required by Art. 8(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.
To carry out regular official controls in all feed establishments, taking into account the risk criteria referred to in Art. 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

To finalise the registration of all feed establishments as required by Art. 9 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005 and to ensure that feed establishments for which approval is required by Art. 10 of the said Regulation do not operate without such approval.
To ensure that all registered and approved feed establishments are recorded on the national lists referred to in Art. 19 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005.

To ensure that feed establishments falling under the scope of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005 monitor the presence of undesirable substances and that those using coccidiostats demonstrate that they implement measures which are sufficient to minimise cross-contamination of non-target feed.
To ensure that feed establishments falling under the scope of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005 implement procedures based on HACCP principles.

To make further progress towards the implementation of the risk-based approach required by Art. 16 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 when implementing official controls, in particular physical checks, on imports of feed of non-animal origin.

To ensure, as required by Art. 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, that official controls, in particular official sampling, take account of the identified risks linked to feed, including those referred to in Directive 2002/32/EC.
To take the actions required by Art. 54 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 in order to ensure that, when non-compliance is identified, the feed operators concerned remedy the situation

recommendations.text: The CA should ensure that procedures are in place to verify the effectiveness of official controls in order to comply with the requirements of the EU legislation (Article 8(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004).
The CA should ensure that audits are carried out in line with Article 4(6) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 to ensure achieving the objectives of this Regulation.

The CA should ensure that an establishment is approved or maintains its approval only if the FBO has demonstrated that it complies with the relevant requirements of food law, in particular Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, in accordance with paragraph 2(c) of Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.
The CA should ensure that audits of HACCP-based procedures are performed in the establishments in line with the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004.

The CA should ensure that post-mortem inspection in slaughterhouses is carried out in conformity with EU requirements. In particular, all birds (including their viscera) shall undergo post-mortem inspection (see Part D, Chapter II, Section I and Part B, Chapter V, Section IV of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 854/2004).

In order to comply with EU requirements, the CA should ensure that deficiencies found are corrected in the establishments visited and are not present in other approved ones (see Article 54 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004).
The CA should ensure that procedures based on HACCP principles maintained by FBOs are fully in compliance with EU requirements (see Article 5 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004).
The CA should ensure that when FBO own-check sampling programmes are implemented, the sampling plans are in compliance with EU requirements (see
Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005). The CA should ensure that FCI contains all the information required by EU legislation (see Regulation (EC) No 853/2004).

recommendations.text: To ensure that regional public health authorities have access to TRACES and are trained, and that the official controls in abattoirs of consignments of live animals for slaughter and the follow-up of re-imported consignments of products of animal origin are recorded in TRACES, as laid down in Decision 2004/292/EC and Article 6 (a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. Associated with findings: 2, 11, 36, 42 and 54.

citations.text: Designation of authorities (e.g. regional animal health and public health authorities and BIPs) are well defined. BIPs and regional animal health authorities have proper access to TRACES and use it with regards to imports and intra-Union trade of live animals and animal by-products. However, not all regional public health authorities have access to TRACES, thus they can not exchange information with other Member States in relation to animals sent for slaughter and re-imports.

The competent authorities have experienced staff with the exception of the regional public health authorities, who have not been using the system, do not have access to it and have not received training. Therefore, the minimum prerequisites for the use of TRACES by the regional public health authorities are not in place.

recommendations.text: To ensure that official samples to check for the presence of ruminant DNA in compound feed are analysed using a validated method in a laboratory that fulfils the requirements of Article 12 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

citations.text: According to representatives of the National Reference Laboratory met, they have not been able to complete the validation of the PCR method for detecting the presence of ruminant DNA in feed put in place by the European Reference Laboratory owing to a number of technical difficulties. However, the laboratory achieved satisfactory results in the proficiency tests conducted by the European Reference Laboratory in 2013 and 2014. The official regional laboratories have experienced similar difficulties and so the method is not included in the scope of accreditation of any of the official laboratories conducting this PCR analysis in Spain. As a result, representatives from the Autonomous Community where the compound feed producers visited are located stated that it was decided not to take official samples from these establishments. The audit team noted that no other laboratory has been designated by the Spanish competent authorities to perform these tests in the meantime. The lack of appropriate laboratory facilities does not satisfy the requirements of Article 12 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and has resulted in no routine 4 official samples being taken in any of the producers of compound feed for aquaculture in 2013 and 2014. Conclusions on official control systems

There are largely adequate arrangements in place to enable the organisation and planning of regular official controls to monitor and verify that operators comply with the requirements related to the use of eligible PAP for the production of compound feed for aquaculture animals. However, the effectiveness of these measures is currently undermined by the lack of appropriate means to analyse official samples to verify the absence of ruminant DNA in such feed.

responses.response: El Laboratorio Arbitral Agroalimentario (LAA) está acreditado bajo la Norma UNE-EN ISO/IEC 17025, para el análisis de ) alimentos y piensos y está designado como Laboratorio Nacional de Referencia (LNR) para el control de la presencia de restos o productos de animales, incluidas harinas de carne y huesos, en sustancias destinadas a la alimentación de animales de producción (PAT´s). recommendations.text: To carry out official sampling on the production and use of compound feed containing derogated PAP, as required by Article 7 and Section F, Chapter V of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001.

citations.text: According to representatives of the National Reference Laboratory met, they have not been able to complete the validation of the PCR method for detecting the presence of ruminant DNA in feed put in place by the European Reference Laboratory owing to a number of technical difficulties. However, the laboratory achieved satisfactory results in the proficiency tests conducted by the European Reference Laboratory in 2013 and 2014. The official regional laboratories have experienced similar difficulties and so the method is not included in the scope of accreditation of any of the official laboratories conducting this PCR analysis in Spain. As a result, representatives from the Autonomous Community where the compound feed producers visited are located stated that it was decided not to take official samples from these establishments. The audit team noted that no other laboratory has been designated by the Spanish competent authorities to perform these tests in the meantime. The lack of appropriate laboratory facilities does not satisfy the requirements of Article 12 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and has resulted in no routine 4 official samples being taken in any of the producers of compound feed for aquaculture in 2013 and 2014. Conclusions on official control systems

The compound feed producers visited had comprehensive own controls systems in place; the risk that the PAP received could be contaminated with ruminant material had been identified and a number of measures taken to prevent this from happening. These included a specific procedure to approve suppliers, laboratory certificates from suppliers showing an absence of ruminant DNA in the PAP (the frequency depended on each supplier) and incompatibility charts for road hauliers showing that ruminant material could not be transported before non-ruminant PAP. In addition, one of the feed producers periodically tested the final product for the absence of ruminant DNA. The results of the tests checked by the audit team were negative for ruminant DNA. Official controls in both plants were extensive and included checks on the operators' measures put in place to ensure the absence of ruminant material. However, no routine official samples for the detection of PAP of ruminant origin were taken in any of these establishments during 2013 and 2014 (see point 7). This is not in line with Article 7 and Section F, Chapter V of Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001.

Although there is no routine sampling at compound feed producers and aquaculture farms, competent authorities perform adequate documentary and other verification checks along the chain and this, coupled with the robust measures put in place by the operators, allows them to largely ensure that only eligible PAP is used for the production of aquaculture feed.

citations.text: The CA identified eight samples as compliant with the labelling requirements. The non- compliances identified by the CA were mainly related to ingredients (not corresponding to the actual use), and missing or wrong information on the use of allergens. For one sample, the CA considered their findings on labelling as inconclusive. The FVO audit team made some additional observations: The label of a sample of burger meat did not mention the name of the species used. The label indicated only "lean" (magro) and "fat" (tocino). One sample of rabbit meat contained voluntary labelling information on feeding and the animal welfare conditions of the rabbits. This information was not verified by the CA. Following the provision of additional information by the CA, it was possible to trace the rabbit meat cuts to the slaughterhouse of origin. This was also the case for another sample of cut lamb meat.

The results of the traceability exercises conducted indicate that the official controls are partially effective, with the results that some serious and/or systemic deficiencies are not detected and acted upon.

recommendations.text: In line with Art. 5 (1) of Decision 2012/697/EU, ensure that all measures and sanctions necessary to effectively address and eliminate illegal intentional introductions of Pomacea sp. are fully implemented and enforced from a legal perspective. This can be aided by the application of a specific and designated action plan.

citations.text: The CA stated that the right delta is considered free of Pomacea sp., despite on-going reports of small, isolated incidences (approximately 10 per annum) which the CA considers as intentional introductions. The CA qualified this view based on both the 8 isolated sporadic pattern of incidences and physiological age of individual snails found (which tend to be mature adults (commonly estimated at 3-4 years old minimum)).

During the course of the current audit; The audit team received technical information and an explanation of survey approaches, including river surveys as conducted from boats (normally out-sourced contractors with training) as co-ordinated by the DALFF, as well as those conducted by the DGNEB. The audit team observed the presence of snails and egg clutches across various sites and locations in the left delta area, both in fields and irrigation/drainage channels, as well as clutches, and remnants of clutches, in lower parts of the Ebro river (downstream from the town of Amposta at the location of the river mooring facility as mentioned in Finding 16). The CA stated that incidences of random, sporadic intentional introductions to various rice fields in the right delta have each been eradicated following the application of intense measures (with the audit team taking the opportunity to visit several such locations as part of the audit). The CA stated that some 520 rural agents, under the control of DGNEB are responsible for surveillance, law enforcement and control activities of the natural environment. In addition to regular, on-going field inspections, the CA stated that 600 Km of irrigation/drainage channels were surveyed in 2014 with the aim of inspecting the entire irrigation/drainage network of the right delta by the end of 2015. 9 The CA stated that the distribution of the pest in the Ebro delta has not extended beyond that as reported during the previous audit in 2013. The demarcated area remains much larger than required under the Implementing Decision 2012/697/EC. 5.3.2.2 Pals municipality

Following this recommendation as a general guide throughout this follow-up audit, the audit team noted; A high technical understanding of the organism and management/eradication solution(s), with a well-developed range of technical measures for control and eradication purposes e.g. salination (via an integrated water management approach), drying and phytosanitary approaches (saponins, cyanamides, lime), as well physical containment measures. All measures are well documented under the eradication action plan. 14 Overall strengthened involvement of stakeholders towards successful application of the eradication action plan (e.g. via the ''Technical commission for Island apple snail'', including a similar committee at Pals). Persistent and on-going illegal intentional introductions in the right delta buffer zone and possibly Pals. However, the audit team found that, despite routine patrols and spot checks, as evidenced through documentation provided to the auditors, the authorities have been unable to deal effectively with this intentional element of spread in the right delta. Furthermore, the CA stated that no sanctions had been made to date. With regards to the Pals outbreak site, irrigation to the site, via two irrigation pipes (with the source quoted as the river Ter some 7-8 Km distant) was immediately closed (and officially sealed) with open ditch drainage channels plugged with compacted earth (approximately 2 m long, and to a height equal to that of the field) at various strategic locations to effectively seal off any drainage from and to the site. The site, as well as drainage channels, was treated with saponins (evidence of which was apparent from the presence of numerous dead crayfish carcasses). 5.4.2.2 Containment measures

Furthermore, with regards to illegal intentional introductions, although routine patrols and spot checks are carried out, given the frequency of such outbreaks in the right delta, there is an absence of legal enforcement to effectively tackle this worrisome situation. No sanctions have been established to date. This is not consistent with Article 5 (1) of Decision 2012/697/EC, and represents a further impediment to fully satisfying Recommendation 1.

recommendations.text: Ensure that appropriate biosecurity measures, in line with Art. 5 (1) of Decision 2012/697/EU, are implemented in places where agriculture machinery is cleaned, with particular emphasis on upgrading the physical infrastructure of the recently constructed cleaning platform and the introduction of standard operating procedures to minimise risk of spread.

citations.text: However, although the location of the designated place where agricultural machinery is cleaned has improved significantly, the modifications made in response to Recommendation 2 from the previous audit cannot exclude all risks of spreading the organism, and as such remains not in line with the Section 2 (c) of Annex II of Commission Decision 2012/697/EU. Ensuring physical containment as well as introduction of standard operating procedures for general site management of the facility and process(es) were considered necessary. Based on this assessment, it was concluded that Recommendation 2 remained partially addressed.

recommendations.text: Ensure that all the measures necessary for the eradication of Pomacea sp. in line with Art. 5 (1) of Decision 2012/697/EU are taken, and they are implemented in such a way that further risks of spreading to new areas is prevented, in particular with respect to the appropriate and effective installation of physical barriers to prevent movement of Pomacea sp. from the river to fields, and between fields, and that these installations are correctly enforced and that sanctions are actively established in cases of non-compliance.

citations.text: On visits to various rice production field sites during the audit, particularly within the left delta, the audit team noted/observed; Presence of incorrect, as well as absence of maintenance and official control, of mesh screen installations (physical barriers), especially in the left delta fields, to prevent snail movement via infested irrigation river water between fields. Despite 15 effectively undermining eradication efforts, and being subject to legal controls, no sanctions have been made. Limited progress with the installation of physical barriers/traps to prevent physical movement of snails direct from the river into fields. Use of sluice gates to prevent the access of infested waters to the river or to other channels. Issues with regards to machinery and boat cleaning. Conclusions

However, issues regarding the effectiveness of physical containment installations (which lacks official enforcement and controls despite regional legislation requiring mandatory compliance with official measures at farm level) are not consistent with Article 5 (1) of Decision 2012/697/EC. Furthermore, no sanctions have been established for cases of non- compliance with regards physical containment. In view of this, Recommendation 1 remains only partially addressed.

Subsequently, based on Recommendation 3 as a guide, the audit team noted that; Of the 280 drainage outlets to the river which were considered a pathway for the physical movement of Pomacea sp. directly from the river to fields, only 40 had been repaired (including 13 of the most important breaches), or amended in such a way to prevent such movement (elevated in relation to the river waterline to prevent snail movement direct for the river) The installation of mesh netting in open ditches and field level channels, to prevent the movement of Pomacea sp. in and around fields is often substandard, or inappropriately installed. Furthermore, control and quality checks on the installations and maintenance of such mesh barriers, despite a legal requirement, are not enforced. 17 Conclusions

recommendations.text: In line with Art. 5 (1) of Decision 2012/697/EU, ensure that measures are taken with regards to eradication in the river, in particular with respect to reducing the risk of spread from movement of boats, especially upstream from Tortosa and beyond the demarcated area. That a designated biosecure hull washing facility is established, and that a procedure for certification is developed (as is the case for machinery) and is equally applied and enforced to boats as it is to machinery.

citations.text: During the audit, the auditors noted that: To date, no successful measures have been found to eradicate the pest in the river which is seen as a critical element in the overall eradication and maintenance of pest free status across the delta. 16 Until now, the eradication treatments implemented are manual collection of adults and egg clutches and elimination of the vegetation in the river banks for egg clutches destruction. The aim of such actions is to maintain levels of the snail in the river below the threshold of population explosion. Tracts of river bank vegetation had been removed the previous year, and periodic surveys continue. The audit team visited one such site on the right part of the Ebro river, below Amposta.

Although measures have been taken to reduce the level of infestation, no overall successful measures have been found to effectively eradicate the pest from the river. This is inconsistent with Decision 2012/697/EU which requires that all measures to eradicate Pomacea sp. should be taken and an integrated eradication approach for rice fields, channel network and river, should be in place.

Subsequently, the audit team noted; Evidence of clutches along the edges of the Ebro river, particularly around the mooring facility as mentioned in Finding 15. Based on discussions with some leisure boat owners, Pomacea sp. egg clutches have been known from boat hulls that navigate the Ebro river course. A prohibition exists on the movement of boats from saltwater to freshwater in the absence of a specific authorisation, in particular beyond Tortosa. It was unclear to the audit team who issued this authorisation or how it was controlled. The Harbour Master Authority has, since 2013, incorporated Pomacea sp. inspections as part of, and in parallel to, their hull checks, but do not issue any documentation or certification for this. 20 An absence of restrictions to transfer boats from the Ebro river or delta complex to outside the demarcated area (e.g. to other parts of Spain, especially where rice may be grown). Although unable to witness on this follow-up audit, the CA stated that the boat hull cleaning facility is a mobile service that operates very much as the machinery cleaning service did as reported in the previous audit, i.e. as a mobile call out service, operating on unsealed ground (with no general fixed location) and without any controlled waste water/soil management, etc. Conclusions

A designated biosecure hull washing facility is not available and no certification procedure for the movement of boats exists (as is now the case for machinery). No biosecurity controls exist for the movement of boats outside the demarcated area

With respect to boats, although now recognized as a potential source of spread, given the level of uncertainty and concern over the biosecurity issues and level of risk management of further spread of Pomacea sp. in and along the river Ebro water course, and potentially beyond the demarcated area, it was concluded that Recommendation 4 remained partially addressed. 5.4.5 Follow-up The table below summarizes the follow-up to the relevant recommendation(s) made in report DG(SANCO)2013-6803-MR Final. citations.text: There is a good awareness of the pest amongst central competent and regional official staff with the message of the risks and impacts reaching the general public and those directly involved in rice production. recommendations.text: To ensure that the survey for Epitrix sp. is adequate to fully determine the presence and spread in Spain, in line with the requirements of Article 4(1) of Decision 2012/270/EU. In particular, the survey should be representative of the ware and seed potato production, the total number of field inspections and samples taken should be increased and survey should include other host plants as appropriate.

citations.text: Data in Tables 2 and 3 indicate that for the vast majority of the ACs, there was practically the same overall level of implementation of the surveillance in 2013 and 2014. However, there was a significant increase in the area inspected and the number of inspections carried out in Galicia in 2014. In addition to potatoes, 40 ha of tomato crops were also inspected in 2013 and 20 ha in 2014. The average inspected area of the total ware potato production in 2013 represented 4.8 % and in 2014 3.8 %, which is in accordance with the required 3 % in the National Contingency Plan. However, there was very significant variance between the ACs from 0.5 % to 100 % of fields inspected. In Andalucía the proportion of potato production inspected in 2013 and 2014 was similar to the national average with 3.2 % and 4.1 % respectively. In Asturias the proportion of potato production inspected was significantly lower (0.7 % and 0.5 % respectively) than the national average and in Galicia the proportion was very low with 0.7% in 2013, increased to 2.0 % in 2014. Concerning other regions in Spain, the area inspected in the main ware potato producing AC Castilla y Leon was significantly lower than the national average and targeted level from the National Contingency Plan with 0.6 % of the area inspected in 2013 and 0.5 % in 2014.

Another way of evaluating the inspection data is looking at the number of fields inspected compared with the total production area which gives an indication of the 8 inspection density. As shown in the last column of Tables 2 and 3 above, the average inspection density in Spain was 96 ha and 48 ha of potato production per inspection in 2013 and 2014 respectively and varies very much between the ACs. In Andalucía there were 311 ha of potatoes per one inspection in 2013 and 339 ha in 2014 which is significantly below the national density average. It indicates that large but few potato plots were inspected there and consequently a very low density of inspection. The inspection density in Asturias and in Galicia was in both years similar or higher than the national average. However, taking into account the fragmented potato production with very small plots in Asturias, the proportion of fields inspected there was very low as well.

Seed production in Spain is concentrated in three ACs, namely in Castilla y Leon with the largest share of production of around 68 %, followed by Basque Country and Navarra. In 2013 and 2014 on average some 30 % plots of seed potatoes were surveyed for PFB with some 1,300 visual inspections of seed potato fields per year. However, in the largest seed producing, AC Castilla y Leon, there were only 56 visual inspections carried out and 7 plots inspected each year covering an area of 12 ha in in 2013 and 13 ha in 2014. Furthermore, in the same AC there were no lot inspections carried out in 2014, although in total 515 lot inspections were carried for domestic seed produced in Spain. The intensity of survey for PFB in seed potatoes in AC Castilla y Leon is significantly lower compared to other ACs and does not reflect the potential risk related to the neighbouring affected ACs Galicia and Asturias.

Taking into account the high proportion of inspected fields found infested in Asturias and Andalucía, the high proportion of unregistered producers of potatoes, the lack of systematic surveys of other cultivated host plants and vegetable hobby growers, the intensity of survey is not considered sufficient to determine the actual distribution and spread of the pest. Furthermore there is a very low intensity of surveys for PFB carried out in some other key potato producing ACs in Spain which does not provide sufficient information of the presence of the organism. This is not in line with Article 4 of Commission Decision 2012/270/EU. Conclusions on Epitrix sp. surveillance strategy and results

A detailed surveillance protocol and good inspection guidelines have been elaborated in Spain for the detection and identification of PFB. However, the percentage of ware and seed potato producing areas inspected and sampled in annual official surveys varies widely between the ACs and is, in many cases, significantly lower than required in the National Contingency Plan and is insufficient to reliably identify or rule out the actual presence of PFB.

The suspected occurrence of PFBs triggered increased surveying activities in both recently affected ACs. However, the implemented intensity of surveillance does not provide sufficient information about the actual distribution of the harmful organism in these ACs.

recommendations.text: To ensure that where the presence of Epitrix sp. is confirmed, a demarcated area is established in line with Article 5(1) of Decision 2012/270/EU and the requirements laid down of Annex II, Section 1 of the same Decision. In particular, that geographically close buffer zones are merged and sound scientific principles are taken into account when establishing demarcated area as referred to in points 2 and 3 of the said section.

citations.text: The representative of Asturias also stated that they establish a demarcated area and designate an infested zone and a buffer zone around each infested plot according to the minimum required by Decision 2012/270/EU of a 100 m width from the infested plot. The geographically close demarcated areas were merged. However, where the 100 m radius intersects plots, the entire plot is not added to the demarcated area, which is not in line with Decision 2012/270/EU, Annex II, Section 1, point 1.

When delimiting the size of the buffer zone, the minimum required by Decision 2012/270/EU was always applied in Andalucía and Asturias. There was a very high proportion of inspected fields found infested in Asturias (some 50 %) with a high level of infestation, fragmented cultivation of host plants and presence of host weeds. Due to the recency of the outbreaks in Andalucía and insufficient intensity of surveillance, there was uncertainty about the actual spread of the pest. Thus the plant health services in both ACs did not take into consideration other elements for delimitation, such as, the presence of other cultivated or wild PFB hosts in the area and the capacity of the pest to spread naturally, the distribution of other potato crops or other host plants between two or more demarcated areas that have not been selected for sampling during the official surveillance. Consequently the establishment of infested zones and buffer zones was not carried out taking into consideration the sound scientific principles required by Decision 2012/270/EU, Annex II, Section 1, point 3.

The establishment of demarcated areas in Asturias and Andalucía were notified immediately in line with EU requirements. However, due to uncertainty regarding the actual spread of PFB, the establishment of infested zones and buffer zones was not carried out taking into consideration the sound scientific principles required by Decision 2012/270/EU. In particular, geographically close demarcated areas were not merged. This is not in line with Decision 2012/270/EU, Annex II, Section 1, points 2 and 3.

recommendations.text: To ensure that measures taken in a demarcated area are in line with Article 5(1) of Decision 2012/270/EU and compliant with the requirements laid down in Annex II, Section 2 of the same Decision. In particular, that prohibition of planting of host plants, intensive monitoring in the entire demarcated area and surveillance of movement of potatoes out of demarcated areas are carried out as referred to in points 1, 2 and 3 of the said section.

citations.text: The FVO team visited five demarcated areas in Andalucía and met plant health inspectors, owners of the infested fields and of fields in the buffer zone and noted that: All the fields visited were tilled and without any potato debris left and clean of weeds, including along the field's borders. Owners of the infested fields and of the fields in the buffer zone confirmed the receipt of the official demarcation notice and were aware of the harmful organism and imposed control measures. They intended to plant other crops in the next growing season. Professional farmers have their own technical staff responsible for the management of the crop production and protection. They confirmed regular and intensive insecticide treatments (clorpyrifos and pyrethroid) during the growing season for other potato harmful organisms like potato tuber moth and Colorado beetle. The insecticides used for these organisms are also effective against PFBs. Inspectors were knowledgeable about the harmful organism and inspection techniques. However, when they inspected suspected potato fields they generally had not inspected neighbouring potato plots, plots of other cultivated PFB hosts or wild host plants in the vicinity of the potato fields. Inspectors stated that they performed follow-up visits to the infested fields in demarcated areas to verify the implementation of control measures like destruction of the crop debris and weeds in the field and along the field border. However, during the follow-up monitoring they were not inspecting other plots in the buffer zone with cultivated host plants or in the vicinity of the demarcated area. In one demarcated area there was an urban area included in the buffer zone with many home gardens producing potatoes and vegetables. Monitoring was not carried out there and the residents had not been informed about the pest. 14 5.3.3 Movement of potato tubers, decontamination and issuance of plant passports Legal requirements Article 3 of Decision 2012/270/EU. Findings

The representative of Galicia stated that five warehouses in the demarcated areas comply with the requirements for the marketing of potatoes outside demarcated area, including the management of waste. Potatoes are inspected in the warehouses after washing. In Asturias all infested plots identified by the regional authorities so far were intended for own-consumption or at most for local market and surveillance of the movement of potato tubers out of the demarcated areas was not carried out. Thus, the control activities in Asturias do not ensure that all potatoes produced in the demarcated areas comply with the requirements for movement laid down in Annex I to Decision 2012/270/EU.

Official control measures put in place in demarcated areas were generally in line with Decision 2012/270/EU, however, confirmation of the outbreak did not trigger intensive monitoring or additional investigation in the demarcated area or its vicinity. Not all necessary measures were put in place like prohibition of planting of host plants and alternative measures are not equally effective to achieve eradication. This is not in line with Article 5 of Decision 2012/270/EU and the requirements for official measures to be taken within demarcated areas as laid down in Section 2 of Annex II to the same Decision.
Control measures in place for commercial scale movement of potato tubers outside demarcated areas are adequate, however, surveillance is not carried out for non- commercial movement of potatoes.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the staff collecting samples in the framework of Decision 2013/652/EU are provided with access to the necessary slaughterhouses to ensure that sampling is performed in slaughterhouses processing at least 60% of the broiler domestic population, in order to fulfil the requirements of point 2.3 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU.

citations.text: During the audit, the audit team confirmed that under the Spanish legal framework the competent authorities have adequate powers to take the necessary samples for AMR monitoring. However, the personnel from the designated laboratory are not considered part of the competent authority and therefore can only access slaughterhouses if the operators voluntarily agree to grant this access. In 2014, staff from this laboratory were not allowed to enter a significant number of broiler slaughterhouses initially included in the work plan. In one particular case, this problem was overcome through the intervention of MAGRAMA, which resulted in the operator of the largest turkey slaughterhouse in the country finally granting access to staff members of the concerned laboratory. Although the situation has improved in 2016, some large broiler slaughterhouses are still denying access to these staff to perform the sampling.

The competent authorities responsible for the monitoring of AMR in food producing animals and food are clearly designated, well-structured and organised, and have the necessary powers and resources, which is a prerequisite for the adequate implementation of the harmonised monitoring of AMR. The lack of powers of the designated laboratory staff for accessing slaughterhouses and perform sampling has an impact on fulfilling the Decision requirements regarding the poultry population to be covered by the sampling design.

Regarding the broiler slaughterhouses the following was noted by the audit team: In 2014 the broiler slaughterhouses included in the sampling plan, contrary to point 2.3.1 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU, processed only 40% of the domestic production while for 2016 the figure improved and has reached 54% (see point 6). The figures on slaughter production used for the sample allocation corresponded to two years before the sampling year and not to the previous year as recommended in EFSA 2014 guidance document. These data were obtained from an industry publication that does not include all the national slaughterhouses. As a consequence, in the case of slaughtered broilers the designated laboratory calculations of the population covered by the sampling plan were overestimated. The audit team noted that in the autonomous communities visited the slaughter volumes per slaughterhouse were readily available while at central level this information was not compiled.

recommendations.text: To ensure that sampling at slaughterhouses and retail is representative, as set out by Article 2(1) and points 2.3 and 2.3.1 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU, namely by allocating samples to the minimum population targets, recovering the minimum required C. jejuni isolates and distributing samples evenly over each month of the year.

citations.text: In 2014, the minimum required 170 Campylobacter jejuni isolates were not achieved for broilers and turkeys. Only 80 and 37 isolates were tested for AST and reported to EFSA for these populations respectively. According to the data provided by the competent authority in Spain C. coli is more prevalent than C. jejuni. The competent authority stated that for this reason they have difficulties to achieve the minimum required 170 isolates for the latter, especially in the turkey population. However, the amount of caecal samples to be taken for both populations of broilers and turkeys in the 2016 sampling plan (500 each), has been unchanged from 2014 despite the minimum number of isolates not being achieved. EFSA 2014 guidance document recommends that the number of samples to be taken should be established depending on the prevalence. MAGRAMA stated that it would be very cumbersome to increase significantly the number of samples to be taken.

The requirement set out in point 2.3.1 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU that caecal samples collected at slaughterhouses shall be distributed evenly over each month of the year was not adhered to in 2014, 2015 and 2016. The designated laboratory stated that this was due to delays in the public tender approval and to the fact that submission of the AST results to MAGRAMA has to take place by December. In 2014 caecal samples were gathered from May to November while in 2015 sampling took place from March to October and in 2016 it started in April.

AECOSAN has designed the collection of samples at retail outlets distributing the samples to be taken proportionally in the 13 provinces (NUTS-3 areas) more populated representing 60% of the total population. This approach to ensure the representativeness of sampling at this level is detailed in EFSA 2014 guidance document, where it is highlighted that NUTS-3 areas selected should cover at least 80% of the population (see section on Closing Meeting). In Catalonia, the authorities allocate the requested number of samples proportionally to the population to the three administrative areas of the province of Barcelona, which is the only Catalan province included in the sampling plan. In Murcia the authorities allocate the samples to the metropolitan area which is the most populated and also logistically allows the samples to be submitted to the laboratory within the required timeframes. In both autonomous communities, and to ensure the representativeness of the samples taken, the authorities took samples mainly obtained in the supermarket chains that have the biggest market share and are widely represented in the region. 7 Isolates from samples collected at poultry primary production

The overall bovine slaughter data were used for the sampling design of caeca from bovine under one year of age. As a consequence, the sampling allocations were not proportional to the slaughter of eligible animals as required by point 2.3.1 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU and detailed in EFSA 2014 guidance document.

Regarding the broiler slaughterhouses the following was noted by the audit team: In 2014 the broiler slaughterhouses included in the sampling plan, contrary to point 2.3.1 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU, processed only 40% of the domestic production while for 2016 the figure improved and has reached 54% (see point 6). The figures on slaughter production used for the sample allocation corresponded to two years before the sampling year and not to the previous year as recommended in EFSA 2014 guidance document. These data were obtained from an industry publication that does not include all the national slaughterhouses. As a consequence, in the case of slaughtered broilers the designated laboratory calculations of the population covered by the sampling plan were overestimated. The audit team noted that in the autonomous communities visited the slaughter volumes per slaughterhouse were readily available while at central level this information was not compiled.

The documented procedures and instructions in place could ensure adequate implementation of most of the provisions laid down in the legislation. However, there are deficiencies in the design and implementation of the sampling plan that call into question the representativeness of sampling. These concern notably the information available to exclude the sampling of repeated epidemiological units, the amount of samples taken for C. jejuni in relation to the prevalence, the exclusion of some months of the year, the type of samples taken at retail and, notably, the sample allocation to slaughterhouses and retail, These issues could lead to the gathering of AMR monitoring data not fully comparable with those obtained by other Member States.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the information available allows for the exclusion of repeated epidemiological units to comply with point 3 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU and the samples taken at retail comply with point 2.3.3 of the said Part A. 17

The instructions given by this autonomous community to the samplers requested that samples should be taken from bovine meat from bovines under 1 year of age, which is contrary to point 2.3.3 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU that specifies that samples should be taken from bovine meat. However, there are deficiencies in the design and implementation of the sampling plan that call into question the representativeness of sampling. These concern notably the information available to exclude the sampling of repeated epidemiological units, the amount of samples taken for C. jejuni in relation to the prevalence, the exclusion of some months of the year, the type of samples taken at retail and, notably, the sample allocation to slaughterhouses and retail, These issues could lead to the gathering of AMR monitoring data not fully comparable with those obtained by other Member States.

The selection of the isolates to be tested for susceptibility and reported on is done by the laboratories performing these tests. In the case of the isolates reported by AECOSAN the information available did not allow officials to ascertain if repeated epidemiological units were reported (see points 33 and 46).
