recommendations.text: To ensure that, when the minimum number of Salmonella isolates from different epidemiological units required by point 2.2 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU to be subject to antimicrobial susceptibility testing are not achieved, all available Salmonella isolates are subject to antimicrobial susceptibility testing, in order to comply with Article 2(2)(a) of the said Decisio

citations.text: In 2014, the number of isolates tested and reported for Salmonella for testing and verification of compliance with Chapter 2 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 at slaughterhouse level was 130 for broilers and 1 for turkeys. For the year 2015, 128 isolates were tested and reported under the same category for pigs and 9 for bovines under 1 year of age. The audit team noted that, even though the minimum 170 isolates had not been achieved for 2014 and 2015, isolates available from official samples at autonomous community level were not always gathered and tested for AST by the CNA. In Catalonia this issue has been solved and for the year 2016 all relevant isolates have been submitted so far. At the time of the audit and for the year 2016, 68 and 35 Salmonella isolates obtained from official samples from broiler and turkey carcasses respectively were gathered by the CNA. This represents an improvement from the 2014 data. 5

Despite the minimum required number of Salmonella isolates at slaughterhouses not being achieved, the competent authority did not systematically make use of the food business operators' isolates for AST, as set out by Article 3 of Decision 2013/652/EU (see point 31). AECOSAN and Catalonia presented evidence that, in 2015, the slaughterhouse industry representatives were encouraged to submit Salmonella carcass isolates with only four isolates provided altogether. In addition, and in relation to this point, the audit team noted that relevant Salmonella isolates originating from samples collected by food business operators in the context of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 were obtained in two out of the three private laboratories performing laboratory tests for the food business operators visited. These isolates were not used for AST testing in the context of Decision 2013/652/EU.
Despite the minimum 170 isolates for each species not being achieved the gathering of food business operators' isolates amounted only to 4. 8

As a consequence of the competent authority not gathering a sufficient number of Salmonella isolates (for the purpose of antimicrobial susceptibility testing), obtained by food business operators from carcass samples taken in the context of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005, the minimum 170 Salmonella isolates had not been achieved for the relevant species since the introduction of Decision 2013/652/EU.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the coordination role of the National Reference Laboratory for antimicrobial resistance, the laboratory documented procedures and the storage of the isolates are in line with points 3, 4 and 5 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU, in order to comply with Article 4 of Decision 2013/652/EU and Article 33 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

citations.text: The audit team noted that the CVL did not carry out any oversight, as NRL, over the designated laboratory and was not aware of the performance in the relevant proficiency tests to ensure that adequate follow up of such tests as required by point 2(c) of Article 33 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

Laboratory procedures were available on the spot and generally followed the relevant international standards. However, the following was noted by the audit team: In the designated laboratory the procedures and records for sample acceptance and ESBL testing did not include verification of the temperature and time requirements set in the EURL Laboratory protocol for isolation of ESBL-, AmpC- and carbapenemases-producing E. coli for ceacal samples. In the NRLs, adequate quality controls with reference strains were run for each batch of plates tested and adequate records were kept. In the designated laboratory the reference strain was run weekly and not for every batch. The laboratory was able to present ample information regarding past satisfactory results using this reference strain. Nevertheless, there was no documented procedure in place, in line with Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) standard M07-A10, as required by point 3 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU, in order to describe the rationale behind the reduced frequency of the use of the reference strain and describing in which cases the laboratory must revert to use the strain for every AST batch. In all three laboratories, the procedures as explained dealt generally with out of range or unusual results and prevented the exposition to light of microdilution trays. Nevertheless, these procedures were not documented and for some unusual combinations of resistance no investigation was performed. Likewise, the procedures as explained dealt correctly with skips but the procedure was not documented. The laboratory procedures for Campylobacter minimum inhibitory concentration determination in the CVL and the designated laboratory were not based on the M45 13 CLSI standard as required by point 3 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU. In particular, the time defined for incubation was not in line with the relevant standard and included deviations of up to eight hours. With regard to the detection of ESBL- or AmpC-producing E. coli, the audit team noted that reference strains were regularly used to validate the preparation of the McConkey agar when the media was prepared in the laboratory and the positive and negative controls were used weekly as recommended. Nevertheless, this was not described in the documented procedures. In the three laboratories when performing the second panel for AST (Table 4 of Decision 2013/652/EU) the reference strain E. coli ATCC 25922 was used. CLSI protocol M100S latest edition recommends using both reference E. coli ATCC 25922 and Klebsiella pneumonia ATCC 700603 strains. The latter is more suitable for ESBL profiles in order to verify more effectively that the test performance is satisfactory. 5.2.2.4 Storage of the isolates

Both NRLs have the necessary equipment to freeze isolates at temperatures below -80°C and to store them for at least 5 years. Nevertheless, the audit team noted that in the designated laboratory only Campylobacter isolates were stored at -80°C while other isolates were stored at -40°C without any validation to ensure viability and absence of changes in strain properties as required by point 5 of Part A of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU. The designated laboratory stated that relevant isolates will be moved to -80°C storage. Back-up equipment and emergency plans in case of equipment malfunction were available. Conclusions on official laboratories

An appropriate laboratory network for official monitoring of AMR is in place. Laboratories are properly designated and operate in accordance with the EU requirements. Some weaknesses have been identified during this audit mainly in relation to documented procedures and the use of reference strains. Further weaknesses in the coordination role of the NRL for AMR over the designated laboratory were noted. These weaknesses could affect the ability of the laboratories to obtain harmonised and comparable results. 14

recommendations.text: To ensure that the information included in the overall description of the implementation of antimicrobial resistance monitoring provided to the European Food Safety Authority is complete and accurate, as required by points 2 and 2.1 of Part B of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU, in order to comply with Article 5 of the said Decisio

citations.text: The collection form used for reporting the "generic description of the implementation of the AMR monitoring" was also submitted to EFSA as required in Part B (2) of the Annex to Decision 2013/652/EU. The description of the sampling designs, stratification and randomisation per animal population and food was not complete enough and mainly included the following text "according to EFSA technical specifications and Commission implementing Decisions 2013/652/EU and 2013/653/EU". The competent authorities stated that the information provided was incomplete due to the difficulties they encounter when introducing text in the reporting excel text forms.

The annual report includes all the mandatory information for each individual isolate reported under harmonised monitoring, and some information reported on a voluntary basis exceeds the current mandatory monitoring under EU legislation. audits.title: pesticide residue controls in organic production

recommendations.text: Ensure that the CA when delegating tasks includes clear instructions regarding (a) the sampling procedures for pesticide residue analysis in organic production, and (b) the methodology and scope of laboratory analysis, to facilitate the reliable detection and quantification of the presence of substances not authorised for organic production, in line with Article 27 of Regulation 834/2007 read in conjunction with Article 65.2 of Regulation 889/2008.

citations.text: Spain complies with the EU legal requirement for the number of samples taken and analysed on an annual basis (the number must correspond to at least 5% of the number of organic operators). In 2015, a total of 1 220 samples were taken by the designated CBs in Andalusia, compared to 13 296 organic operators (9.2 %). This is fully compliant with Article 65 of Regulation (EC) No 889/2008. Both CBs visited complied with this requirement. The authorities in Andalusia stated that 118 of the samples taken in 2015 contained pesticide residues. At the two CBs, samples were taken across the production and processing chain, based on the identified risks. In addition to food and feed, a substantial number of samples were taken from leaves and soil. The audit team considered this sampling approach as good practice.

Both CBs visited had included a Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) in their Manual of Procedures regarding the risk assessment for prioritising samples for pesticide residue analyses. There were also sampling instructions in place. They were very detailed at one CB, but the other CB only referred to the Royal Decrees stated above. A sample of leaves with a weight of 290 grams had been taken at one of the CBs, but it was unclear whether the amount was sufficient to qualify as a representative sample, and where in the field the sample was taken. At one of the laboratories visited, a sampling record for a grape sample 5 of 500 grams was accepted, whereas Royal Decree 291 of 2003 and Directive 63/2002/EC require a weight of at least one kilogram for the laboratory sample.

At the two CBs visited, multi-residue analyses combining both liquid chromatography (LC) and gas chromatography (GC) techniques were not requested from the laboratory, except in particular cases of higher risk. One of the CBs requested only GC analyses for samples of lower risk. The other CB requested, for such samples, analyses alternating between LC and GC techniques, so that individual samples were not analysed with both techniques. One laboratory confirmed, in respect of six examples chosen by the laboratory, that requests for analysis by a third CB related to GC only. In this context it should be noted that analysis by GC techniques is not suitable to detect modern polar (watersoluble) pesticides, which are widely used by conventional farmers. Neither is an LC technique alone suitable to detect many of the relevant pesticides.

The lack of clear official criteria on sampling procedures for products other than those of plant and animal origin covered by Royal Decree No 290/2003 poses a risk that the interpretation of laboratory results is affected by a sampling procedure which is not representative for its purpose.

The lack of clear official CA criteria for the scope of analyses to be carried out (in particular, as to gas and liquid chromatographic techniques) impacts negatively on the control system: as gas chromatography is used as the only laboratory detection technique in many cases, the data on pesticide detections is likely to represent an underestimation of the true presence of pesticide residues in organic produce.

recommendations.text: Ensure that laboratories for pesticides residues in organic products are designated as required by Article 12(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

citations.text: The Spanish multi-annual National Control Plan for the Food Chain (2016 ­ 2020) specifies that the CAs may refer to the lists of laboratories that have already been previously designated by other competent authorities in order to select a laboratory to carry out analyses for pesticide residues in organic production. The SGCDAE stated that a representative of the ministry unit, with competence in the corresponding laboratories or agri-food laboratories, will be invited to the next Organic Production Coordination Group meeting, and the implementation of this provision would be discussed, as would the scope of pesticide residue analyses in Organic Production.

The two laboratories visited by the audit team are listed by the Andalusian CA for Organic Production, the CAPDR, however they had not been formally designated by the CA to carry out official analyses (the CAPDR informed the audit team that the process for designation has started). The laboratories conduct analyses for pesticide residues in different plant products. The laboratories had an adequate level of qualified staff. The equipment in the laboratories was state of the art. 7

The process for official designation of laboratories for pesticide residue analysis in organic production is being developed. The official designation is expected to facilitate co-ordination and supervision of these laboratories.

recommendations.text: Verify that the data on organic control reported by CBs in Andalusia are accurate, in order to ensure that Annual Reports submitted under Article 44 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 contain correct informatio

citations.text: The organic section of the Spanish 2014 Annual Report submitted under Article 44 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 shows that both CBs visited met the minimum requirements in terms of the number of samples taken. One CB was reported to have detected one sample that indicated a breach of Regulation (EC) No 834/2007. However, the audit team found that in 2014 at least 8 samples taken by this CB actually tested positive, often showing residues of non-authorised substances, leading to measures and sanctions issued by the CB against the organic operators. The CAPDR investigated this anomaly at the CB and confirmed the discrepancy of communicated results after the audit. The CAPDR have informed the audit team that administrative sanctions have been imposed on the CB in question for inaccurate reporting to the CA. Conclusions on measures in cases of pesticide residue detections
A discrepancy in reported data for non-compliant results raises questions as to the accuracy of the organic control data reported by Andalusia in the 2014 Annual Report.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the presence, or actual appearance, of a harmful organism, as referred to in Articles 16(1) and (2) of Directive 2000/29/EC is notified no later than eight working days following the date of confirmation, in line with Article 2(1) of Decision 2014/917/EU. and

citations.text: The notifications provided the information required by Decision 2014/917/EU, however the long delay, between confirmation of the presence of the pest and its notification to the Commission and other Member States in both cases, is not in line with Article 2 of Decision 2014/917/EU, which provides for a maximum of eight working days for the provision of at least a preliminary notification. 5.2.2 Surveys for Trioza erytreae and Ca. Liberibacter spp

The outbreaks of T. erytreae have been notified to the European Commission and other Member States, but after a significant delay. That is not in line with Article 16(1) of Directive 2000/29/EC nor Article 2 of Decision 2014/917/EU; it also hinders the response of other Member States, in particular in adapting their official controls as necessary.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the control measures for Trioza erytreae are systematically implemented, at least in those areas bordering free areas, in order to inhibit the spread of the pest as required by Article 16(1) of Directive 2000/29/EC. and ­ 74.

citations.text: The audit team observed the application of a pesticide treatment to a recently identified infested tree, on the boundary of the infested zone close to Santiago de Compestela, within the area targeted by the official pesticide treatment programme. It was noted that the treatments were applied by specially trained staff from TRAGSA using appropriate equipment. The active ingredient applied was chlorpyriphos, which was chosen primarily on the basis of cost.

However, the application of authorised plant protection products, which is the only measure aimed at inhibiting the further natural spread of the pest, is not carried out systematically, particular in those areas bordering the remaining free areas of the AC of Galicia. The further spread of T. erytreae is therefore inevitable. It cannot therefore be concluded that all necessary measures have been taken to inhibit the spread of the pest, at least in those areas, as required by Article 16(1) of Directive 2000/29/EC.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the control measures for Tecia solanivora address the source of the pest and not solely the place of detection, in order to eradicate, or if that is not possible, to inhibit the further spread of the harmful organism, as required by Article 16(1) of Directive 2000/29/EC. and

citations.text: The control measures taken following a finding of T. solanivora focus on infected tubers or the field or store in which the trap on which the moths were caught was placed, which is not necessarily their source. This means that the measures are unlikely to result in the eradication of the pest from the infected area, however they should at least inhibit its spread in line with Article 16(1) of Directive 2000/29/EC. 5.6.2 Control measures for Tecia solanivora in Asturias
The objective of the control measures for T. solanivora in both Galicia and Asturias, is its eradication, however the measures, as applied, are unlikely to achieve this.

recommendations.text: Ensure that in the event of a new presence of PWN in an existing demarcated area or elsewhere in the Spanish territory, control measures are implemented in an appropriate and timely manner in line with Articles 5 and 6 of Decision 2012/535/EU. In particular: The clear-cut and associated sampling and alternative measures to reduce its size, should be appropriately implemented; Control measures taken should be based on an evaluation of risks of infestations and be implemented in a timely manner to mitigate any risks of further spread of PWN; This should be reflected in the Action Plan for the demarcated area Ensure that surveys in the demarcated area are implemented in line with Article 6 and point 6 of Annex I to Decision 2012/535/EU. In particular: 4. 5. The intensity of survey around the tree found infested in 2010 should be increased in line with point 6 of Annex I and this should be reflected in the Action Plan for the demarcated area; Survey activities should be implemented in an effective and timely manner taking into account the risk of latency and vector activity. Ensure that PWN control measures in demarcated areas are systematically implemented in an effective way in line with point 7 Decision 2012/535/EU. In particular: Dead and declining trees are identified and sampled in a timely manner so as to be felled and removed early enough to mitigate risks of PWN spreading; Dead and declining trees identified in a demarcated area from 1 November to 31 March are eliminated before 31 March each year; Dead and declining trees identified in a demarcated area from 1 April to 31 October are immediately eliminated Ensure that felled declining trees in which PWN has not already been found to be present, are sampled and tested for the presence of PWN, according to a sampling scheme able to confirm with 99% reliability that the level of presence of PWN in those plants is below 0,1% as required by point 7 of

citations.text: However, despite of the fact that the demarcated area had been in place since the end of 2010, the regional service had not set up a system ensuring the timely implementation of PWN control measures as required in Decision 2012/535/EU, the Regional legislation and the Action plan for the demarcated area. In particular, In 2016, the resources allocated to the surveys, identification of dead trees or trees in decline and sampling activities were insufficient for the work to be completed in the whole demarcated area at the frequency and within the required deadlines; (see also section 5.4.1) In 2015 and 2016, the work of felling and removal of identified dead or declining trees in the demarcated area did not start before May 2015 and mid-July 2016 despite the requirements of point 7 of Annex I to Decision 2012/535/EU to have the work completed before the start of the flight season of the vector (1 April each year) and to be done immediately from 1 April until 31 October. The delays in felling and removing the infested tree entail a further risk of spread of PWN (see also section 5.4.2). 5.1.2 National and regional provisions 5.1.2.1 National Contingency Plan

The audit team noted that the sample taken from the symptomatic tree in Salvaterra do Mino on 18 February 2016 was confirmed to be infested with PWN by the regional laboratory on 2 May 2016 i.e. 2,5 months after the sample was taken. Although the symptomatic tree was in a demarcated area where there was a requirement to fell and remove identified dead or declining trees before the 1 April, the tree was not felled until the diagnostic was confirmed. Although the confirmation by the National Laboratory is a prerequisite for taking official measures, the handing of the infested wood sample by the Regional laboratory was not done so as to minimise the delays in getting the results confirmed: the first testing took six weeks instead of the three weeks normally required and the Regional laboratory then retested the sample before requesting a confirmation by the National Reference Laboratory. 5.1.4 Communication to the Commission and other Member States

There is a clear organisation of the controls related to PWN and there is a good cooperation and communication between the entities involved. However, in Galicia, this organisation did not ensure the timely and appropriate implementation of surveys, testing of samples and control measures in the demarcated area of As Neves.

The current Action plan for the demarcated area of As Neves is not fully in line with Decision 2012/535/EU as it limits the intensive survey to the surroundings of the new finding although such an intensive survey was still required around the initial outbreak.

The audit team noted that the surveys of trees in the 20 km zone along the border with Portugal and the demarcated area are performed by the same two people from Tragsatec. The map above shows that the work is conducted starting from the border with Portugal and progressing Northward in accordance with the regional service's assessment of the highest risk for PWN infestation. The results of the intensive surveys conducted in this 20 km zone along Portugal since 2010 have demonstrated that PWN is not present outside the existing demarcated area of As Neves. This is confirmed by the preliminary results of the surveys conducted in 2016. Conclusions on annual surveys of the territory outside demarcated areas

The audit team noted that Tragsatec staff involved in these felling and sampling activities did not check for the presence of signs of vectors' activity either in the infested tree or in the dead or declining trees and branches surrounding it. There was no assessment of the risk of further spread from this site before the felling and removal of the susceptible trees. Based on the interviews held by the audit teams, staff involved in these activities and in their supervision had a limited knowledge of the biology of the vector and ways of spreading PWN and could not explain the signs of vector activity.

The audit team noted that there was no investigation of the possible origin of the PWN infestation. The regional service considered that this new finding was a new incursion from Portugal, either by dispersal flight of the vector or human assisted dispersal. However, they had not identified any particular risk in the surroundings or any evidence for two such incursions at short distance despite intensive surveys showing that the 20 km zone along the border with Portugal is free from PWN (see section 5.2). The audit team noted that while there was no evidence of a new incursion from Portugal, the following facts points towards an extension of the outbreak detected in 2010: The two infested trees were three km apart; Significant shortcomings were identified during the three previous DG Health and Food Safety audits which questioned the effectiveness of measures implemented; Based on data provided by the regional service, the level of sampling of dead or declining trees in the demarcated area of As Neves were every year was below 17% in each year from 2011 to 2014 and reached only 38% in 2015. This is not in line with point 7 of Annex I to Decision 2012/535/EU. It cannot therefore be excluded that infested trees were eliminated without being detected; Samples are generally taken at chest height which reduces the probability of finding PWN in trees which died or declined for reasons other than PWN and were infested by oviposition; The possibility of latent PWN infestations in Galicia (see also section 4.1) which could explain that infested trees show wilting symptoms a few years after the first infestation. 5.3.2 Establishment of a demarcated area

The action plan dated May 2016 further specifies the different zones comprising the Buffer Zone and control measures to be implemented in each of these: Zone A: clear-cut zone of 100 m radius around the new infested tree; Zone B: a 100 m to 3 km zone around the new infested tree where intensified surveys of susceptible trees and vectors are conducted; Zone C: the remaining part of the buffer zone also referred to as 3-20 km zone.

The audit team noted that the order delegating the work of felling and removing trees to Tragsa was signed mid-July i.e. at the end of the period given to private owners to organise their sales of wood. Consequently the clear-cut zone was implemented from end-July to September, which is after most of the vectors would already have emerged from trees and branches. These measures were therefore implemented too late to be effective in preventing PWN spread and are therefore not in line with point 2 of Annex I to Decision 2012/535/EU.

According to the regional service, 1,282 susceptible trees were felled in the clear-cut zone. A total of 17 samples were taken from symptomatic trees which were sampled. Only one sample was taken from asymptomatic trees without this being justified based on the risk of spread of PWN which is not in line with point 2 of Annex I. This requires that a number of asymptomatic trees be sampled selected based on the risk of spreading of PWN. All samples tested negative for PWN.

The audit team visited the infested site and the clear-cut zone and noted that the stump of the infested tree was marked with a red ring and was located in an uneven and rocky terrain on a steep slope. The representative of the regional service who had supervised the work stated that after the felling and removal of trees, the branches and cutting remains had been crushed on-site by a tractor and that the result had been judged satisfactory given the characteristics of the area. The audit team noted that on such terrain the method implemented could not be effective and indeed spotted the presence of some branches big enough to contain pupae of the vector. This is not in line with point 2 of Annex I to Decision 2012/535/EU. 11 Conclusions on measures taken following the suspicion of the new detection of PWN

Control measures have been taken to address the new detection of PWN based on the assumption that this is a new outbreak linked to a new incursion from Portugal. However, this is not based on evidence and the extension of the outbreak of 2010 cannot be excluded. This risk is not addressed by control measures taken so far.

The delays in felling and removing the infested symptomatic tree and the absence of preventative measures resulted in a risk of further spread of PWN. These risks would have been significantly less if control measures had been implemented in accordance with Point 7 of Annex I to Decision 2012/535/EU. The inadequate implementation of the clear-cut following the finding of PWN further adds to this risk.

The competent authority reported that at the time of the audit, the survey was completed in zone B while work was still on-going in zone C, as shown in table 1. The audit team noted that the level of samples taken from asymptomatic trees in zone B in 2016 is not consistent with requirements laid down in point 4(a) of Annex I. The regional service confirmed that the asymptomatic trees sampled were those present at the grid points surveyed (see also 5.3.3). recommendations.text: To ensure that a full, comprehensive and up-to-date register of producers, collective warehouses and operating dispatching centers of potatoes has been established in all autonomous communities of Spain in line with Commission Directive 93/50/EEC.

citations.text: All RCAs consulted use the CAP register as a basis for their respective official records of professional potato producers. Typically this is further supplemented with industry information on an on-going basis. However, the team noted that in certain ACs registration is incomplete.

The Valencian RCA stated that registration of pack houses only started there in 2015. So far 19 premises have been registered, but the total number remains unknown. There is no single register. This also applies in the case of growers. In Andalucía, the previous audit reported 91 ware potato wholesalers/packing stations and 195 seed potato wholesalers. The Andalucía RCA reported there are now 280 registered ware potato wholesalers. However, despite the progress observed regarding increased registration of ware potato wholesalers in Andalucía, recent interceptions of potato consignments from this autonomous community in two Member States and follow up investigation during this audit (see also paragraph 69), indicates compliance with the registration requirements requires further improvements.

All RCAs acknowledged difficulties in dealing with the generic issue of small private growers. As there are no legal requirements, small non-professional growers are not registered, and normally produce for private consumption within the immediate locality of production. RCA inspections are largely conducted at random or guided by local knowledge. 5.2.2 Surveillance strategy

Variability in the comprehensiveness of registration of both producers and pack houses exists between the various RCAs visited/consulted. Registration is particularly incomplete in two ACs where considerable surface areas of ware potatoes are grown but the growers are not registered or known to the relevant RCAs. This undermines fundamentally the overall effectiveness and reliability of surveillance efforts and ultimately any control measures in place.

citations.text: At the time of the audit, the regional resolution necessary to deal with this new situation was still in draft format. Consequently, a precautionary approach, based on prohibition orders on the harvest and movement of infested potato crops, was adopted. However, this approach did not include demarcation, or the associated risk management obligations, as required by Decision 2012/270/EU.

The four closely located DAs, of the eight DAs originally established under Decision 2012/270/EU had not been merged within the scope of Annex II section 1 point (2). The RCA of Andalucía does not consider that the distance of approximately 2 km from one another is sufficiently close to merit such action. These four DAs have been merged under a parallel regional "vigilance zone" concept, which is identical to the requirements of a DA as outlined in Annex II Section1, with the exception that potatoes can be moved without washing or brushing. On a visit to one such original DA (now part of this "vigilance zone"), which was claimed to have been intensively surveyed by the RCA, the audit team noted mature and flowering plants of Solanum nigrum (a major weed host) were easily found, reflecting concerns regarding the efficacy of intensive surveillance and monitoring, particularly at this location.

In Andalucía, the recognition of E. papa as the causal organism has led to the emergence of a parallel risk management approach. Management of existing DAs established under Decision 2012/270/EU are only partially compliant with the Decision, whilst new outbreak sites, notified under Article 16.2 were, at the time of the audit, neither demarcated, nor, in the absence of the anticipated regional 17 Resolution, subject to any further measures. Orders prohibiting harvest and movement of two potato fields from the eight new outbreak sites in the province of Seville had been violated.

Merging of geographically close DAs, in line with Annex II section 1 (2) of Decision 2012/270/EU, has not taken place (see section 5.4) with risk(s) as regards the further spread remaining as movement of potatoes from the area between them is not restricted.

citations.text: In the national registration database of producers of seed and nursery plants there are currently 11,655 entries of registered potato operators. A substantial increase from 280 in 2016 to 398 in 2017 was observed in potato operators registered in Andalucía. Similarly the registered potato operators have been increased in Comunidad Valenciana from 19 in 2016 to 25 in 2017. Additional information provided by the single authority indicated that eight potato operators have been registered in Islas Baleares and one operator in Madrid. During 2016, operators in Extremadura and Castilla la Mancha moved ca. 9,300 t of ware potatoes to other EU Member States. However, at the time of the audit registration of certain potato operators had not been completed. Despite substantial professional potato production and trade taking place from these regions to Spain and to other EU Member States certain potato producers still remain without having been registered. citations.text: The audit team visited one field found infested during 2016 within a recently demarcated area in the province of Cadiz and two fields within the buffer zones of areas already demarcated since 2015 in the province of Seville prior to the latest amendment of Decision 2012/270/EU and noted that: the demarcation of the infested zone was limited only to the surface where there is a crop (or "plantación") of potatoes or other E. papa hosts. This could be considered to be in line with the Spanish language version of Decision 2012/270/EU, where the term "plantación" is used, but is not in line with the English1 version, which uses the term "field", i.e. a plot of land with defined boundaries according to ISPM No.5; 1This text was initially drafted in English and then later translated into other languages. 11 the same also applies for fields within the outer border of the 500 m width buffer zone. Demarcation is not carried out in line with Annex II section 1(1b) of the same Decision because only the part of the fields within the 500 radius is included and not the entire fields. The RCA stated that, in the notification letters sent to producers, they require that any potatoes grown in parcels located the outer limits of the buffer zones to be considered, treated and handled as produce grown within the demarcated area.

The audit team also noted that a 500 m width buffer zone beyond the edge of the infested fields is only applied to new outbreak sites; areas which have already been demarcated prior to the adoption of the provisions of Decision EU 2016/1359 remain with a buffer zone of 100 m beyond the infested area; infested zones are not reviewed and buffer zones are not expanded.

As already stated in the previous audit report, merging of four geographically close demarcated areas in a larger demarcated area in the province of Seville did not take place. Instead, an "intensive surveillance zone" composed of the demarcated areas and the areas between them had been established. The RCA stated that possible expansion and further merge of the demarcated areas in line with Article 6 of Decision 2012/270/EC, is not considered to be necessary as monitoring carried out within the demarcated areas had not revealed the actual presence of E. papa but only cases of tubers with signs of Epitrix sp. infestation.

The entire autonomous community of Asturias has now been demarcated whilst in Andalucía the infested area continues to increase. Andalucía has implemented precautionary measures to prevent the further spread of the pest. However, area demarcation is not carried out in line with the provisions of Decision 2012/270/EU, which may reduce the effectiveness of the control measures in place. 13

recommendations.text: Ensure that surveys for Xylella fastidiosa outside the demarcated area are based on sound technical principles and take into account the presence of specified plants with regard to the possibility to detect the pathogen, as required by Article 3 of Decision 2015/789/EU, in particular concerning host plants of high economic interest.

citations.text: The plan includes survey, diagnostic and eradication protocols. The survey protocol takes into account the 2015 Commission guidelines for Xf surveys. It defines the following areas, which are considered as national priorities during the surveys: Nurseries and garden centres in general; Areas (fruit, horticultural plantations, forests, parks, gardens, public roads etc.) established 2-4 years ago with plants from DAs and from non-EU countries, where Xf is present; Nurseries and garden centres on transport routes from DAs; The Valencia coastline; Agricultural crops of particular economic importance for Spain with the following minimum annual inspection rates: olives, citrus, almonds, plums and cherries - 1 per 10,000 ha; vines, apricots, peaches, nectarines - 1 per 15,000 ha and oaks 1 - per 5 50,000 ha with at least one sample per inspection. However, the audit team is not convinced that these minimum annual inspection rates are sufficient for the detection of a possible infection, taking into account the presence of these crops in different parts of Spain; Vector insects collected from the main agricultural crops. Sweeping and direct catch is recommended but not the use of sticky traps. The survey protocol also describes the main symptoms, defines the method and timing of the visual inspections and sampling of symptomatic and asymptomatic plants.

The legislative tools, the national and regional contingency and action plans provide an appropriate framework for the implementation of the control measures. Nevertheless these plans need to be reviewed in the light of the latest information about the presence of Xf and in particular concerning the intensity of surveys in agricultural crops of particular economic importance.

The audit team reviewed the details of Xf surveys in Andalusia and Valencia and noted that: The vast majority of the surveys were carried out in the period of late spring/early autumn, which is suitable for the observation of symptoms and sampling. Nurseries and garden centres were checked during the annual plant passport inspections; Both ACCAs generally followed the priorities of the national contingency plan and adjusted these according to the specificities of the region; There were significant differences in survey intensity of the crops of specific economic interest; Valencia largely implemented the national priorities and especially in the main agricultural crops the survey density was higher that it was recommended nationally. However, even this intensity might be not be high enough for detecting possible outbreaks; Andalusia implemented generally also the national priorities. However, the survey density of olives groves in that AC was only the half of that, which is recommended nationally (one inspection per year per 20,000ha). As Andalusia is the main olive production region, the audit team considers that this survey intensity is not sufficient for the early detection of a possible outbreak and it is not in line with the requirements of Article 3 of the Decision; In Andalusia, the majority of the surveys were carried out by the plant health service and the forestry authorities, while Valencia successfully attempted to involve other organisations, including producer groups into the surveillance and to combine the Xf checks with other plant health activities; Valencia considered that large scale trapping and analysis of insect vectors for the presence of Xf is an effective way of surveying the pathogen. Therefore checks for the presence of Xf were carried out with thousands of sticky yellow traps placed in crops and other areas for monitoring other harmful insects. 5.2.2 Surveys in the Buffer Zone

Xf surveys outside the DA are generally risk based and follow the national guidelines. However, the intensity of these surveys, especially in olive trees in Andalusia, is not high enough to comply with requirements of Article 3 of the Decision.

recommendations.text: Ensure that monitoring of Xylella fastidiosa in the infected zones and in the buffer zone is implemented in line with Articles 6(3) and 6(7) of Decision 2015/789/EU in particular that surveys in the buffer zone are based on a grid split into 100m x 100m squares.

citations.text: Directly after the presence of Xf was confirmed in a nursery in Mallorca the ACCA the ACCA established a BZ of 10km radius and commenced surveying it, based on a 100m x 100m grid as required by the Decision. As this survey quickly resulted in numerous positive findings the CA decided to extend the BZ to the entire territory of the Balearic Islands (see chapter 5.3.1). Due to the available limited human resources and laboratory capacities, it was then decided to carry out surveys in the BZ, based on a 1km x 1km grid. The work started in parallel on each of the four islands. The main aim was to swiftly obtain comprehensive information about the outbreak situation.

The audit team observed inspections carried out by inspectors of the Plant Health Service and by employees of a public company specialised in providing emergency services in agriculture, rural development and nature conservation (TRAGSA) in the DA and noted that the survey teams: Identified the position of the 1km x 1km grid square to be checked with the help of GPS data and with a specific application on their computer tablets, which used satellite pictures indicating the already inspected squares; 13 Attempted to check visually at least 50% of the surface of the square. In order to achieve this goal they drove along all available roads in the square and walked into the fields where possible. However, checking the majority of the area visually was not always possible, due to the lack of roads, accessibility of some parts of the square, including natural areas, abandoned agricultural land and private properties. The survey teams did not report any problems with accessing private properties, as until now they could obtain the consent of the proprietor practically in each case; Checked visually the host and specified plants in the square and tried to identify symptoms, possibly caused by Xf. numerous host plants, especially wild and cultivated olives and almonds, showed some symptoms of a certain decay in the form of dried or scorched leaves and twigs. However, as the region had been suffering from drought for a period it was not obvious which of the symptoms could have been caused by Xf. Due to the limited laboratory capacities only those host plants, which showed severe and typical symptoms, were sampled. Practically no samples were taken from asymptomatic hosts; The sampling for laboratory analysis was carried out according to the method described in the regional action plan and was in line with provisions of the Commission guidelines and the EPPO laboratory protocol; In the case of olive and fruit trees, incremental samples were taken from the different parts of the canopy. The laboratory sample represented a single plant, no composite samples were prepared. The sampled plant was clearly marked for possible follow-up; The results of the survey, including the proper GPS coordinates of the sampled plants were duly recorded on a computer tablet and the data were later uploaded to a regional database.

The ACCA informed the audit team that, at the time of the audit overall 62% of the squares had been surveyed; the coverage was higher in Mallorca and Ibiza. Samples for laboratory analysis were taken from only 15% of the inspected squares (see table III.). Table III. The audit team noted that the intensity and territorial coverage of the surveys in the BZ is not in line with provisions of Article 6(7) of the Decision and consequently cannot provide a comprehensive picture about the territorial spread and extent of the Xf infection. The number of positives and their territorial distribution (see figure I in chapter 4.2) already indicate that Xf is widespread throughout the three islands, in cultivated and abandoned agricultural land, natural and urban areas.
The audit team considers that the current survey results do not provide a comprehensive picture of the host range of Xf in the BZ. 5.2.3 Surveys in the Infected zones

Surveys in the BZ and IZs are not in line with the provisions of the Decision and do not provide a comprehensive picture of the territorial spread and extent of the infection and of the host range. This seriously compromises the eradication measures and has a negative impact on the implementation of other measures, required by the Decision.

citations.text: After numerous positives were identified in the Balearic Islands in the period December 2016 ­ January 2017, Spain decided not to eradicate the outbreaks fully in line with the provisions of Article 6(2) of the Decision. In the vast majority of the IZs only the host plants, which were tested positive, were removed or intended to be removed. All host plants in the 100m radius of the positive plants, regardless of their health status and other specified plants, showing symptoms were not considered subject to eradication measures. At the time of the audit, about half of the positive plants had been removed. Felling orders were issued in general two-to-three weeks after the final laboratory result was available. None of the proprietors has appealed against the official decision. 18 Thereafter, it usually took two-to-three weeks to complete the felling. Nevertheless, there were significant delays in certain cases due to difficulties in identifying the owner (e.g. holiday homes, abandoned land). (see table VI).

The audit team visited IZs in Mallorca and Ibiza, where positive plants had been removed and noted that: In the 100m area of the removed plants, there were numerous host plants, which were not removed (olives, almonds etc.). Many of them showed symptoms of decay to varying degrees. Only some of them had been sampled and found negative; In the IZs, an inventory was not made to identify the (non-host) specified plants and no samples were taken from those plants present; The IZs were not revisited to remove newly identified host plants.

The audit team considers that the current measures are not in line with the Decision regarding eradication, as some of the plants tested positive were removed with delay and the host plants regardless to their health status and other plants showing symptoms were not removed in the IZs. The CAs did not express a clear position about their future intention regarding the removal of host plants other than those tested positive in the IZs. 5.3.3 Agricultural practices

The currently applied measures do not ensure the eradication of the pathogen. Given that Xf is widespread on three of the Balearic Islands on a wide range of host plants and different subspecies of the pathogen are present in the infected area, eradication will be very difficult to achieve.

recommendations.text: Ensure that no specified plants which have been grown for at least part of their life in the demarcated area are moved out from that area, as required by Article 9(1) of Decision 2015/789/EU, in particular with implementing appropriate controls at seaports.

citations.text: The audit team visited nurseries, both producers and traders with outlets in the BZs and noted that: The majority of the establishments are wholesalers or retailers of plants for planting imported from mainland Spain or from other MS. There are some producing nurseries who propagate a narrow range of specified plants; The main professional clients are other nurseries on the island and companies dealing with landscaping or gardening; Each nursery visited stated to the audit team that they do not market specified plants outside the island where they are located. They are fully aware of the measures implemented after the outbreak and they duly inform their professional and private customers about the existing ban; In each nursery, posters and flyers clearly displayed the movement restrictions in force and the list of specified plants; The nurseries keep detailed records on production, incoming stock and sales to professional clients of specified plants; They do not keep records on sales to private clients, however they do inform them about the export ban of specified plants; The ACCA inspects the nurseries at least once a year in order to authorise them for issuing plant passports. Controls related to Xf always form part of these inspections. Since the first outbreak was detected, the ACCA carried out numerous additional inspections in the nurseries; Plant passport and Xf related inspections in the nurseries and garden centres are carried out according to an annual schedule. Therefore the timing may not be ideal to find possible symptoms of Xf and the stock present at the time of inspection do not always represent the annual trading activity of the establishment; ACCA inspectors take samples from each symptomatic plant and randomly from the asymptomatic plants as well. However, due to limited laboratory capacity, the extent of random sampling is not in line with requirements of ISPM 31 and therefore it could not be representative of the stock of specified plants present in the nursery. 5.4.4 Movement control of specified plants at airports, ports

The resolution of the regional minister, which bans the movement of specified plants out of the territory of the Balearic Islands is implemented through a wide set of measures. There is multichannel awareness raising at airports, ports, in the form of posters, flyers informing both arriving and departing passengers. There are controls at airports and sea ports. The relevant authorities or security services reports any findings to the Civil Guard for enforcement.

The audit team noted that: 22 The Agriculture Department of the Balearic Islands maintains close working relations with the airport and seaport authorities, the security services responsible for controlling the exiting passengers and with the Civil Guard. These organisations are members of the recently established regional steering and coordination group for Xf issues; At the international airports, both in the arrival and departure halls, posters and even electronic displays inform passengers about the restrictions in force. At check-in desk there is information material about the ban including the list of specified plants; The airport security services check the presence of living plants during the scanning of cabin bags and check-in luggage. Any plant detected is confiscated and stored in a separate container until it is destroyed. The Civil Guard is informed about each case, however no further enforcement measures are applied. In April-May 2017 the ACCA received reports of 17 cases from Ibiza airport and 11 cases from Mallorca airport concerning plants in personal luggage. Usually lavender, rosemary, rose and geranium plants were detected; Representatives of the port authorities and security services confirmed that they provide information about the existing restrictions to ferry operators and passengers and to staff and passengers of other vessels leaving the islands; At the ferry ports there are practically no exit controls on trucks neither in the traffic between the islands nor to the mainland. There are occasional checks on exiting cars, but there are no controls on the luggage of passengers leaving the islands by ferries or by other type of vessels. 5.4.5 Road controls

The controls in the nurseries provide a level of guarantees that specified plants are not leaving the demarcated area and also that a possible outbreak is quickly detected. However, despite the wide-ranging information campaign it cannot be excluded that tourists or other individuals intend to export specified plants bought in the nurseries. Therefore there is a pronounced plant health risk related to the possible transport of specified plants in the luggage of private persons leaving the islands.

The current measures implemented at the airports provide for a reasonable level of guarantee for containing the infection on the territories of the Balearic Islands. However, at the sea ports the same level of guarantees is not ensured. 23

citations.text: The audit team noted that the laboratory: Was able to cope quickly with the challenges resulting from the outbreak and gained experience in routine real-time PCR testing; Efficiently uses the relatively limited facilities at its disposal; Maintains close working relations with the NRL and with the laboratory responsible for subspecies identification; Participated in an international proficiency test for Xf detection, which had recently been organised within the framework of an EU research project, and was assessed as highly proficient; Applies a serial DNA extract dilution in order to control PCR inhibition caused by substances present in some host plants. However, these inhibition control steps are not elaborated and validated for each host plant, therefore, there is a chance of false- negative results due to the inhibition of DNA amplification; Sends only a proportion of the positive and undetermined samples for confirmatory tests to the NRL (at the time of the audit only in the case of positives from a new area or from a new plant species) (see chapter 5.2.2). LOSVIB usually sends both the plant and DNA extract for confirmation. None of the negatives are re-tested for quality control purpose by a different laboratory. The audit team considers that although it is not a requirement, re-testing would provide additional assurance.
The current system of confirmatory testing on samples originally tested by the LOSVIB laboratory could undermine the effectiveness of the implementation of the control measures.

recommendations.text: Consider organising proficiency tests at regular intervals with participation of each laboratory which tests official samples taken in Spain for the presence of Xylella fastidiosa, in order to provide additional guarantees as to the reliability of the tests.

citations.text: The audit team noted that: Although the staff of these laboratories had experience in detection of pathogenic bacteria in plant samples, only some had participated in any specific training for Xf analysis organised by the NRL; Except the Official Plant Health Laboratory of the Balearic Islands (LOSVIB) the AC laboratories did not have the opportunity to participate in a proficiency test on Xf analysis with molecular or serological methods, organised in the framework of an EU research project. The NRL has not organised any proficiency test for them. The satisfactory performance in the proficiency tests could provide additional assurance and could mitigate the risk of false test results; The NRL advised AC laboratories to use two different real-time PCRs for Xf detection. However, the audit team could not receive confirmation from the CA that this was actually the case in each laboratory. Some laboratories use enzyme linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) tests, which is not recommended by the EPPO protocol PM 7/24(2) for testing samples from pest-free areas. 8

Due to the lack of regular proficiency tests on Xf analysis for the ACCA laboratories sufficient assurance cannot be provided that the official test results reflect entirely the infection status of the samples.

citations.text: Considering the high incidence of CLs, several of the non-sampled 19 places of production in Valderredible are likely to be infected. The ACCA declared that it did not have the resources to take samples at all places. Lacking the evidence of the presence of CLs, the ACCA did not impose measures on those producers. However, given the epidemiological situation there is reason to impose similar measures on producers with an, as of yet, unknown status. Moreover, since potato stocks would be eliminated by the start of the new growing season, the sampling opportunity was lost.

Given the fact that the ACCA of Castilla y León had not been aware of the presence of an infected plot on their territory, it had not been in the position to take measures to address the situation. 5.2.4 Surveillance

The MAPAMA and the ACCAs have not substantiated that the surveys planned and those already carried out in some of the ACs, are representative for the concerned ACs, together representative for Spain, and designed and executed in a way to provide an adequate statistical confidence necessary for the results to be meaningful for regulatory purposes, as advised by ISPM9. 5.2.5 Communication with stakeholders

Whilst the ACCAs are responsible for the control of CLs within their territories, whose activities mainly focus on surveillance, the audit team did not observe a coordinated research effort concerning above questions which are pertinent to ISPM 9 section 2.4.1and 3.2.3. Conclusions on pest control

The initial investigation of the finding of zebra chip symptoms in potatoes in Cantabria has been effective in identifying infected places of production and potato lots. Measures have been taken to contain the infection at those places of production. However, potentially infected farms have not been investigated and communication of important findings has on occasion been delayed due to staff shortages. Current surveillance plans have not been fully elaborated and are insufficient for obtaining essential information concerning the pathology, epidemiology and potential economic impact. Altogether this can undermine the decision making on subsequent control measures and the overall effectiveness of the pest control.

The risk of the disease spreading to other EU Member States is small considering the structure of the production and supply chain of potatoes in the infected area and the current knowledge about the disease. Although containment measures provide additional assurances, these can only be fully effective if applied on all places of production likely to be infected.

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls are capable of verifying that feed business operators meet the requirements on hazard analysis and critical control points (HACCP) in accordance with Articles 6 and 7 of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005, and that the effectiveness of such controls is guaranteed, as required by Article 4(2(a)) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

citations.text: In every establishment visited, the audit team checked the feed inspectors' assessment of the operators' hazard analysis and critical control points (HACCP) plans. In many cases, the inspectors' assessment was sufficient. However, in 6 out of 11 establishments visited, the audit team noted shortcomings in relation to the adequacy of the risk assessment for some ingredients used for the production of feed additives (predominantly contaminants of chemical origin, e.g., heavy metals, dioxins/polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), etc.). The failure of the operators to identify relevant hazards, as required by Article 6(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 183/2005, was neither spotted by the inspectors met during the audit nor had these issues been identified in any of the previous inspection reports.

The system of planning of inspections is based on appropriate risk-related factors and thus ensures that the official controls are carried out regularly, on a risk-basis and with appropriate frequency. The effectiveness of the inspections is weakened by deficient assessment of the operators' HACCP-plans, and incomplete verification of completeness of the operators' record-keeping and of appropriateness of the retained samples. Infrequent verification of the correctness of labelling reduces the competent authorities' possibility to adequately verify that labelling requirements have been met by FeBOs. 5.2.2 Sampling 5.2.2.1 PLANNING OF OFFICIAL SAMPLING

The audit team examined two RASFF notifications (one originated from Spain and one sent to Spain due to the distribution of the affected product) and actions taken by relevant competent authorities. While the immediate actions taken to ensure withdrawal of the products affected from the market were sufficient and timely, the audit team noted that no specific actions were taken to ensure that the FeBOs revised their HACCP-plans with the aim to make sure that the same situation did not occur again. In both cases, the operators' own checks were not designed to identify the deficiencies which had eventually triggered the RASFF notifications. The situation thus cannot be considered as completely remedied as required by Article 54(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls are capable of verifying feed business operators' fulfilment of obligations on traceability, especially in terms of completeness of the operators' record-keeping and appropriateness of the samples taken, as required by Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002, Article 10(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and sections on "Record-keeping" and "Quality control" of Annex II to 12 Regulation (EC) No 183/2005.

citations.text: In general, the feed inspectors met demonstrated good knowledge of the relevant legislative provisions laid down by Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 178/2002 and in the section "Record-keeping" in Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. 6 Nonetheless, in 2 of the 11 establishments visited, traceability was undermined by deficient record-keeping by the operators (namely absence of the batch number of the incoming materials used for production of feed additives/premixtures). This is not in line with the requirements laid down in the section on "Record-keeping" (1 and 2(b)) in Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. These shortcomings were not spotted by the inspectors met during the visits of the two establishments, nor had they been reflected in the previous inspection reports.

As for the operators' obligation to take samples of ingredients and of each batch of products manufactured and placed on the market, or of each specific portion of production (in the case of continuous production) in sufficient quantities using a procedure pre-established by the manufacturer (hereinafter: retained samples), the audit team checked several samples in all of the establishments visited and noted that in many cases they could not be considered as adequate due to the absence of a pre-established written procedure (on taking of retained samples) by the operators, absence of sealing, and/or insufficient quantity. The audit team noted that samples of ingredients are rarely taken in the majority of the FeBOs visited. This is not in line with the requirements laid down in the section "Quality control"(4) of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 183/2005. The audit team noted that this issue was not identified as a non-compliance in the available inspection reports. 5.2.1.4 LABELLING

The system of planning of inspections is based on appropriate risk-related factors and thus ensures that the official controls are carried out regularly, on a risk-basis and with appropriate frequency. The effectiveness of the inspections is weakened by deficient assessment of the operators' HACCP-plans, and incomplete verification of completeness of the operators' record-keeping and of appropriateness of the retained samples. Infrequent verification of the correctness of labelling reduces the competent authorities' possibility to adequately verify that labelling requirements have been met by FeBOs. 5.2.2 Sampling 5.2.2.1 PLANNING OF OFFICIAL SAMPLING

citations.text: The audit team noted that the majority of the inspectors met possessed good knowledge of the relevant labelling requirements. However, only in a few cases did they consult the relevant authorisation acts to identify any additional labelling requirements.

For the vast majority of the labels examined by the audit team, the inspectors interviewed could identify the numerous deficiencies present (primarily absence of the name of the functional group, the directions for use and/or safety recommendations, the identification number (including one of the International Union of Biochemistry for enzymes), the batch reference number and/or the date of manufacture, the correct classification of the product, the active substance concentration/inclusion rate, the name of other substance(s) contained in the preparation, etc.). Notwithstanding their capability to identify such shortcomings, labelling shortcomings were only clearly noted as a non- compliance in one of the previous inspection reports seen.

The audit team noted three labels where the products checked were incorrectly labelled as "complementary feed" due to levels of feed additives being higher than 100 times the relevant fixed maximum content in complete feed. This contradicts the requirements laid down by Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 767/2009 and was not spotted by the inspectors met. Conclusion on the planning and implementation of inspections

The system of planning of inspections is based on appropriate risk-related factors and thus ensures that the official controls are carried out regularly, on a risk-basis and with appropriate frequency. The effectiveness of the inspections is weakened by deficient assessment of the operators' HACCP-plans, and incomplete verification of completeness of the operators' record-keeping and of appropriateness of the retained samples. recommendations.text: To ensure that staff carrying out official sampling follow the sampling requirements laid down by Article 1 and Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009.

citations.text: In the autonomous communities visited, the feed inspectors interviewed could in general demonstrate good knowledge and implementation of the respective requirements laid down by Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. However, in four out of eight cases observed by the audit team, the samplers could not correctly identify the minimum number of incremental samples to be taken due to erroneous identification of the size of the sampled portion, which resulted in fewer incremental samples than required by part 5 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009.

The audit team noted that only in two cases out of eight the correct size of the sampled portion was documented in the sampling record, which is a mandatory parameter according to part 10 of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009.

A systemic shortcoming was noted by the audit team in terms of the preparation of final samples from the aggregate ones for control of substances where non-uniform 9 distribution is presumed. The inspectors would normally use simple manual mixing to ensure the appropriate homogenisation rather than special equipment (mechanical or automatic dividers) required by part 9(4) of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 152/2009. For substances with non-uniform distribution, simple manual mixing cannot ensure complete homogenisation of the aggregate sample. In one autonomous community visited, the respective ACCA informed the audit team that dividers had been purchased and were planned to be put to use in 2019 after relevant training. Conclusion on the planning and implementation of official sampling

The system in place for planning of official sampling is effective and risk-based. However, the effectiveness of the sampling is weakened by the fact that the representativeness of the sampling, and thus the samples' legal and analytical validity, is not ensured for control of substances with non-uniform distribution. 5.2.3 Actions taken on non-compliances

recommendations.text: To ensure that rejected consignments are re-dispatched to the third country of origin or another third country within 60 days in line with Article 21(2) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and Article 17 of Directive 97/78/EC.

citations.text: The audit team noted the following shortcomings: In several cases of transit of fishery products for human consumption from one BIP destined directly to a ship the net and gross weight declared in both CVED and veterinary certificate issued in accordance with Article 1(3) of Commission Decision 2000/571/EC was the same. The competent authority stated that they had noticed this noncompliance during documentary checks. It had (in the opinion of the audit team, incorrectly) decided not to take any further action considering that there was no risk. In one case of direct transit of fishery products for human consumption where the consignment was loaded in two containers, the competent authority acknowledged that whilst the first container was correctly checked at the entry BIP (Cartagena) and exit BIP (Valencia), the second container was not checked at either the entry or exit BIPs. In a case of import of animal by-products (ABP) category 3 destined for the production of pet food, the operator had incorrectly declared the ABP as raw pet food in Part I of CVED (raw pet food). This error had not been identified by the competent authority during the documentary check, which had implications for the way in which the consignment was handled (see finding 66). In another case an operator had tried to import buffalo horns from India as decorative items. The competent authority correctly rejected the consignment 10 due to a mismatch between the health certificate and other documents, and the fact that the operator did not respond to the request of the competent authority to provide supporting documents. The operator tried to re-import the same product three weeks later in the same container with the same certificate number and the same date of signature as the first certificate. According to Customs' information the container had left Spain (with both these certificates). The local competent authority acknowledged that the lack of identity check undermined the identification of this commodity. No evidence was provided to the audit team to confirm that the consignment was re-dispatched to the third country of origin within the period of 60 days as required by Article 21(2) of Regulation (EC) No.882/2004 or even beyond this period (see finding 72). 5.2.3.3 Implementation of controls on food and feed of non-animal origin

The audit team noted several non-compliances in relation to the confirmation of re- dispatch of rejected consignments (see finding 72). 5.2.4 Safeguard measures, re-enforced checks regime, reduced checks regime and procedures for channelled and re-imported consignments

The audit team checked some files where the documentary, identity or physical checks had resulted in the consignments being rejected. Evidence was available that rejected consignments had been adequately destroyed or re-dispatched to the country of origin in line with Articles 19 and 21 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and Article 17 of Directive 97/78/EC with the following exceptions identified by the audit team in two out of three BIPs/DPEs visited: In the cases of correctly rejected consignments of washed wool, game trophies (see finding 59), fishery products and peanuts and capsicum (pepper) destined for human consumption, there was no evidence that the consignments in question had been re-dispatched to the third countries of origin as required by Article 21 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004; At all BIPs visited, samples (that were no longer intended for human consumption for commercial reasons and classified as category 3 ABP) taken from products of animal origin or foodstuffs containing products of animal origin were disposed as part of general waste if the sampling results were satisfactory and as category 1 or 2 ABP only if the results were unsatisfactory. This practice does not ensure that the provisions of Article 14 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 are adhered to. 12

Official controls on imports of live animals and feed and food of both animal and non- animal origin were, for the most part, carried out properly by the competent authority. The national monitoring plan for imports of products of animal origin did not reach all of the planned sampling targets, undermining the objective of the monitoring plan. In the cases where the confirmation of re-dispatch of rejected products was absent or inconclusive there is a risk that these products may not have left the EU territory. Furthermore, the absence of confirmation that temporarily admitted horses had left the EU territory does not comply with EU requirements. Some minor shortcomings were found in relation to the implementation of documentary checks but these were not considered by the audit team to have a negative impact on public or animal health.

recommendations.text: To ensure the fulfilment of the national monitoring plan for imported products of animal origin as stipulated in Article 1.2 and Annex II to Commission Regulation (EC) No 136/2004.

citations.text: The sampling programmes of MSCBS comprised two phases covering different parameters. The targets of the 2016 sampling plan of phase I (heavy metals and sulphur dioxide), histamine, biotoxins and pathogenic micro-organisms) were not reached (64.6% of the planned samples were taken (824 samples taken/1276 samples planned). The sampling level was particularly low for Listeria (7.5% of the planned samples were taken (80 samples allocated of which only 6 were taken)). The targets of phase II (antibiotic and pesticide residues and aflatoxins) were not reached (73,2% of the planned samples were taken (109 samples taken/149 samples planned)). Likewise not all targets of the 2017 sampling and monitoring programme were reached. The 2017 results are reported in a different format: compliance percentage/parameter/BIP, which makes the comparison between the two years impossible. The competent authorities were aware of 9 this and stated it was due to a compatibility problem with the computer database they had used. The competent authorities stated that the discrepancy between the sampling targets at BIPs and the sampling level reached was partly due to lack of staff and partly due to low number of consignments received.

Official controls on imports of live animals and feed and food of both animal and non- animal origin were, for the most part, carried out properly by the competent authority. The national monitoring plan for imports of products of animal origin did not reach all of the planned sampling targets, undermining the objective of the monitoring plan. In the cases where the confirmation of re-dispatch of rejected products was absent or inconclusive there is a risk that these products may not have left the EU territory. Furthermore, the absence of confirmation that temporarily admitted horses had left the EU territory does not comply with EU requirements. Some minor shortcomings were found in relation to the implementation of documentary checks but these were not considered by the audit team to have a negative impact on public or animal health.

recommendations.text: To ensure that BIP staff complete part III of the Common Veterinary Entry Document for live animals (CVEDA) when temporarily admitted registered equidae leave the EU territory as required by Annex I to Commission Regulation No (EC) 282/2004.

citations.text: The audit team checked in total 11 files related to import of live animals (horses, circus animals such as lions, pumas, tigers and reptiles) and noted that the documentary checks had been performed correctly. However, in all five cases of horses temporarily admitted and checked by the audit team, there was no evidence indicating that these animals had left the EU territory (see finding 73). The competent authority declared that since there is no legal obligation requiring the owner of the temporarily admitted horses to notify the competent authority and the customs of the arrival of the horses at the exit BIP it makes it difficult for the BIP staff to confirm whether the horses have left the EU territory.

At one exit BIP which is approved for live animals in several cases of temporarily admitted live equidae from Morocco no evidence was provided to the audit team confirming that the horses had left the EU territory in the period of time (90 days) required in Annex II(E) to Commission Decision 92/260/EEC. Conclusions on implementation of official controls on imported goods

Official controls on imports of live animals and feed and food of both animal and non- animal origin were, for the most part, carried out properly by the competent authority. The national monitoring plan for imports of products of animal origin did not reach all of the planned sampling targets, undermining the objective of the monitoring plan. In the cases where the confirmation of re-dispatch of rejected products was absent or inconclusive there is a risk that these products may not have left the EU territory. Furthermore, the absence of confirmation that temporarily admitted horses had left the EU territory does not comply with EU requirements. Some minor shortcomings were found in relation to the implementation of documentary checks but these were not considered by the audit team to have a negative impact on public or animal health.
