recommendations.text: Ensure that, as part of the controls carried out at the port for the purposes of Article 21 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005: checks are made to verify that the sea leg of the journey is to be carried out by an approved transporter, as required by Article 6(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005; copies of tachographs are collected, as required by Article 21(2) of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005, to enable verification of travelling and resting times. checks are made to verify that journeys are planned until the final place of destination in the non-EU country with a responsible person identified, including the sea leg of the journey, as required by Articles 14(1) and 5(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005;

citations.text: The large majority of consignments arriving at the port are accompanied by a national movement document instead of a journey log (see also finding 18). This movement document is not nationally harmonised. In the different versions seen by the audit team, the declaration of fitness for transport was always signed by either the transporter or the farmer at the place of departure.

For the few trucks that arrived after long road journeys, the official checks do not detect the absence of a transporter for the sea journey on the journey log (which should have been indicated in box 6.4 of Section 1). Copies of tachographs are not collected, as required by Article 21(2) of the Regulation, to verify journey times from the place of departure to the port.

The competent authorities follow the instructions of the national protocol and do not request journey logs for animals travelling short road journeys before reaching the port. This is not in line with the Zuchtvieh judgement4, which indicates that these should also be considered as long journeys since it takes more than 8 hours to reach the destination in the non-EU country. In 2015 the Spanish authorities asked the Commission in writing about this issue and they proposed means of addressing it (see also finding 22); they have received no reply to date.

The fact that the authorities do not request journey logs for most consignments, as these start mostly in Spain, prevents them from ensuring that journeys are realistic and have been planned in line with the requirements, in particular to avoid unnecessary waiting times at the port and the identification of a person or entity responsible for the sea leg of the journey.

recommendations.text: Ensure that official controls performed at ports functioning as exit points, in particular checks on the animals' fitness to continue the journey and inspections of livestock vessels prior to loading, required by Article 20 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005: are supported by documented procedures, as required by Article 8(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, that address all the relevant requirements of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005 thereby removing existing gaps; are carried out on every consignment and properly recorded, as required by Article 9 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004; are effective by putting in place the necessary verification procedure, as 12 required by Article 8(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

citations.text: The national protocol: Does not indicate the need to identify a transporter for the sea leg of the journey, required by Article 6(1) of the Regulation, nor their responsibilities (see also findings 17 and 35); Indicates that a journey log is only required if the time taken to reach the exit point is more than 8 hours.

The national protocol also includes sections indicating legal requirements and additional instructions. They both go into more detail than that the Regulation for both the approval of livestock vessels and their inspection prior to loading. It also includes relevant checklists. The pre-loading inspection checklist (Annex 5D) is incomplete, e.g. it does not include checks that the equipment listed in Chapter IV of Annex I of the Regulation is in good working order.

The competent authority indicated that the above-mentioned national protocol has not yet been fully implemented. Namely, the central competent authority has not yet verified how the measures prescribed in the protocol translate into practice, and how they are being applied. Article 4(2)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 requires the competent authority to ensure the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls.

During the audit, the competent authorities at the two ports exporting animals could not provide annual data on the number of animals for which they had refused loading due to the animals being unfit or having arrived dead at the ports.
The new documented procedures could ensure ­ when fully implemented ­ that in general, animals are spared unnecessary suffering during the journey.

The lack of appropriate facilities at ports for checking the animals in the trucks and of no permanent veterinary presence during loading of the livestock vessels, combined with the absence of an official veterinarian at the place of departure to certify fitness for transport5 create a risk of unfit animals being transported. The system is further weakened by the lack of registers at the ports about the animals' fitness for transport.

The national protocol procedures are in general sufficient for inspections to livestock vessels, but have not yet been fully implemented. These procedures include many of the criteria contained in the Network Document on livestock vessels agreed by the National Contact Points' network, and were well-known by the personnel met by the audit team.

The competent authority provided the information in the table below. This shows the total number and outcome of livestock vessel inspections at the time of loading (Article 20 of the Regulation) between January 2015 and June 2018. The type of deficiencies detected included: non-operational drinkers, presence of rust, lack of identified "hospital/isolation pens", dirty or poorly maintained feeders, no first-aid kits/supplies for the animals, lack of alarms at the wheelhouse for the systems for ventilation, light and water production, and lack of stunning equipment. The competent authority informed the audit team that all deficiencies could be corrected prior to loading and there was no need to cancel any livestock vessel loading during this time period. Year Total number of Complied with With inspections Regulation 1/2005 deficiencies 2015 158 2016 150 143 15 2017 143 7 2018 (until June) 187 182 5 79 76 3 A livestock vessel which was seen during a DG Health and Food Safety audit in another Member State at the end of April 2018 had loaded animals at one of the Spanish ports in March and April 2018 (see also finding 34). This vessel, which was seen during the audit at the end of April, had long standing deficiencies, was in a poor state of repair and lacked several essential systems. Nevertheless it had been allowed to load animals in the Spanish port twice in 2018. It was deficient regarding Points 2(a), 4, 5, 6 and 7 of Section 1 of Chapter IV of Annex I to the Regulation, i.e.: ventilation, the fresh water system, drainage, lighting, no alarms for these systems and no fire alarms in the decks accommodating animals. 9
The competent authorities at both ports are not using the pre-loading checklist that is included in the national protocol.

During the audit, the officials described and demonstrated pre-loading animal welfare controls of livestock vessels carried out at the port visited. They were correct and well- performed. Regarding documentation: Records indicate that controls are carried out on ventilation (Point 2 Section 1 Chapter IV Annex I of the Regulation), cleaning and disinfection, watering equipment (Point 4 Section 1 Chapter IV Annex I of the Regulation) and ramps; Records also indicate that calculation is made to evaluate the stocking density (Chapter VII Annex I of the Regulation) and the amount of water and feed necessary for the animals (Section 2 Chapter IV Annex I of the Regulation); There are no records indicating that the other requirements of Section 1 Chapter IV Annex I of the Regulation had been checked, in particular that drainage, lighting and fire-fighting systems and the monitoring and alarm systems remain in good working order.

The available documentation of those controls in the port which was not visited was very poor, indicating only that a control according to Article 20 of the Regulation had been carried out but without giving details on what had been checked.

The official veterinarians seen carrying out pre-loading inspections of livestock vessels were competent in this task and this provides a good level of assurance that livestock vessels inspected in this way are suitable to prevent unnecessary animal welfare problems notwithstanding the poor quality of records kept. However, the poor conditions on a livestock vessel which was allowed to load at one of the Spanish ports earlier in 2018 indicates that some pre-loading inspections are insufficient and do not ensure that essential systems for animal welfare are in place.

recommendations.text: Ensure that arrangements are in place to safeguard animal welfare when the loading or sailing of a livestock vessel cannot occur and can be promptly implemented if and when needed, as required by Articles 22(2) and 23 of Regulation (EC) No 1/2005.

citations.text: Both ports lack appropriate facilities to rest, feed and water the animals outside the means of transport. This would not allow the authorities to fulfil the requirements in Annex I, Chapter III, Point 1.2(a) of the Regulation in the case, for instance, where unloading and loading of the animals from each truck requires more than four hours. The competent authorities require organisers to plan the arrival of trucks at the port in a way that avoids unnecessary waiting.

In one port there are no plans to add such facilities. In the other, there is a project to build a facility, with an estimated capacity for 600 cattle and a covered area with a capacity to park 40 trucks in the shade. The authorities will discuss this project for its approval in November 2018.

The competent authorities require organisers to submit contingency plans for each shipment, which must include providing for a situation where the loading of animals is not authorised. At the port visited, the operator, as part of its contingency plan, has an agreement with a holding, located 60 km from the port, to use it for unloading the animals in case of need. According to the operator, the holding has capacity for 5600 cattle or 15000 sheep. The competent authorities have not visited this holding to confirm whether it would be feasible to use it at short notice, and its suitability.
The other port has not identified nearby facilities in which to unload the animals in case of need. Conclusions on welfare of the animals arriving at the port

The absence of facilities to unload the animals at the port might lead to welfare problems, particularly if a delay occurs with the loading of the animals. Although this is 5 In their response to the draft report the Competent Authority noted that at the place of departure there is an official veterinarian who issues health attestations, although these do not always include an attestation of fitness for transport. 8 mitigated by provisions in the contingency plans, the feasibility and suitability of the arrangements have not been fully verified by the relevant authorities.

citations.text: Both the Balearic Islands and Valencia have produced their own Regional Contingency and Action Plans. recommendations.text: To ensure that food controls, are implemented in Spain consistently and include sampling, as required by Article 16(3) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and Article 9(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1830/2003.

recommendations.text: To ensure that for food, feed and seed samples the analytical scope is extended, either within the individual laboratories or through cooperation between laboratories, to enable screening and identification of authorised and unauthorised GMOs as required by Article 11(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and by Regulations (EC) Nos 1829/2003 and 1830/2003.

citations.text: Central CAs and CAs of ACs generally have access to appropriate analytical capacity. In certain cases, the scope of laboratory analysis is limited and does not cover all pending and known unauthorised GMOs (see also section 5.3.7 below). Otherwise, the audit team did not identify any cases where facilities or equipment necessary for official controls were inadequate. Conclusions on resources for performance controls

The CA stated that these types of samples ("prospective samples") are sent for analysis to the regional laboratory in another AC for screening of two elements (p35S and 14 tNOS). According to their workflow, in the case of a positive screening, they would repeat sampling and would take an official sample, in three repetitions and send these for analysis to an accredited GMO laboratory. So far, they have not used that option for additional sampling.

The audit team noted that the scope of accreditation for some of the regional official laboratories is very narrow. For example, the public laboratory in Cantabria, authorised for GMO analysis of food and feed samples, is accredited only for two screening elements, p35S and tNOS and for three event-specific qualitative methods; and in Aragon only two screening elements, p35S and tNOS were used which means that only certain relevant GM events can be detected (e.g. in soya bean some 50 % of events cannot be detected).

Furthermore, in cases of positive screening results, a limited number of EU validated event-specific detection methods were applied to identify GM events which were potentially present. For example, one food sample (snack) tested positive for both p35S and tNOS and tested negative for Roundup Ready soya bean, maize Bt11 and MON810. No further testing was carried out to identify the GM event present. The laboratory explained the result was due to traces of soya bean in the product. In another case, a conventional maize seed sample tested positive for p35S and negative for tNOS. To identify the GM events, only five common GM events were tested and MON810 tested positive below 0.1%. No further tests were conducted to exclude other events which might be present in the sample (result was explained by MON810 presence only).

The limited analytical screening scope, particularly at official laboratories designated by competent authorities of ACs, means that analytical methods used for official controls do not comply with relevant EU rules. This is not in line with Article 11(1) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 which requires that sampling and analytical methods used in the context of official controls shall comply with relevant Community rules. 18 Furthermore, Article 9(1) of Regulation (EC) No 1830/2003 requires that member states implement control measures including testing to ensure compliance with placing on the market GM products. NRL

At the central level, the CAs have access to a broad scope of accredited analytical capability for GM events. However, the limited analytical scope at regional level is not compliant with the EU rules and poses a risk that some GM events which might be present in food, feed and seed are not detected and thus placed on the market. 19 5.3.8 Enforcement measures Legal requirements Articles 4(5) and 33 of Directive 2001/18/EC. audits.title: Processed animal proteins, including exports, imports and intra-union trade

recommendations.text: To ensure that transporters eligible to transport animal by-products to establishments producing processed animal protein for feed of aquaculture animals fulfil the requirements of Section D, Chapter IV, Annex IV to Regulation (EC) No 999/2001.

citations.text: In the two Regions visited some transporters transported ABP to processing plants authorised for the production of PAP for feeding aquaculture animals. These transporters were registered for transport of Category 3 ABP from all kind of species including ruminant and non-ruminant animals. In accordance with point (b) Section D, Chapter IV, Annex IV of Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 the animal by-products of non- ruminant origin intended for production of PAP for feeding aquaculture animals should not be transported in vehicles and containers used for the transport of ABP of ruminant origin unless these vehicles and containers have been cleaned beforehand in order to avoid cross-contamination in accordance with a documented procedure which has been given prior authorisation by the competent authority. Whenever such a cleaning procedure is used, a documented trace of its use should be kept available to the competent authority for a period of at least two years. At the transporters visited, no evidence was available that the vehicles and containers were not being used for transport of ABP of ruminant origin. In addition, the two regional competent authorities visited had never given prior authorisation for a cleaning procedure that would allow derogating from the ban on the use of the same containers and vehicles for the transport of ruminant and non-ruminant ABP. Verification of compliance with point (b) Section D, Chapter IV, Annex IV of Regulation (EC) No 999/2001 is not specifically indicated in the checklists used by inspectors during the official inspections. The auditor was informed of a case of ruminant cross-contamination in one processing plant visited authorised for 1 After the audit the competent authority carried out a comprehensive official investigation. Based on this investigation they excluded that the source of the ruminant contamination was Category 1 or 2 ABP. 11 the production of PAP for aquaculture animals whose likely source was an ABP transporter (see finding 35).

However, problems identified regarding the official inspection of commercial documents, limited controls of transporters transporting ABP for the production of PAP for aquaculture, and the authorisation of validation of processing method 7 weaken the effectiveness of these official inspections.

recommendations.text: To ensure that demonstration of microbiological sampling during official authorisation of the 30 day validation of processing method 7 is in line with the requirements of point G, Chapter III, Annex IV to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.

citations.text: Two processing plants visited were using processing method 7, which had been authorised by the competent authority. In one processing plant, during the 30 day validation period microbiological samples had been taken (Salmonella, Enterobacteriaceae, Clostridium perfringens) by the operator. The local inspector was not present during this sampling. The operator could not demonstrate that there was a sampling procedure in place at the time of the validation and the operator also could not demonstrate the place of the sampling. The operator sent these samples to a laboratory which was not accredited for testing Clostridium perfringens. The operator stated that the sampling protocol did not accompany the samples. This is not in line with the requirements of point G, Chapter III of Annex IV to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. The local inspector collected official samples once (see finding 24) during the validation period; the samples were sent to an official laboratory and the results were compliant for all microbiological criteria. However, official laboratory results for Clostridium perfringens were communicated as 'less than 10/g', not as 'absent/g'. This is not in line with the requirements of point G(c)(i) of Chapter III of Annex IV to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. The competent authority authorised the validation of processing method 7.

In the other processing plant the whole validation procedure was well documented, and the microbiological results were adequate. The official inspector was not present when the samples were taken. The operator had a written sampling procedure in the HACCP plan following the legal instructions. When the operator explained to the auditor his sampling procedure during validation, he stated that the samples were taken at the border of the end of the processing line and the place of storage. The samples for Salmonella and Enterobacteriaceae were taken only 3-4 hours later than the end of the production. This very short time after a relatively high temperature (80 C) heat treatment does not give sufficient time for aerobic microbes which survived to start growing. This sampling practice significantly reduces the chance of finding potential Salmonella and/or Enterobacteriaceae contamination in the produced PAP whose shelf-life is one year. Based on the laboratory results these samples were sent for analysis only when all 30 samples had been taken, thus approximately half of the samples were sent to the laboratory one month later than the date of the collection. Since the validation procedure had been authorised, the operator took samples for microbiological control from each produced batch using the same method. Salmonella and/or Enterobacteriaceae 10 contamination had thus never been identified. Official controls did not identify this shortcoming in the HACCP plan.

However, problems identified regarding the official inspection of commercial documents, limited controls of transporters transporting ABP for the production of PAP for aquaculture, and the authorisation of validation of processing method 7 weaken the effectiveness of these official inspections.

recommendations.text: To ensure that commercial documents accompanying trade of animal by-products destined for feed contain all information required by Chapter III, Annex VIII to Regulation (EU) No 142/2011.

citations.text: Checks on commercial documents accompanying consignments of raw ABP and derived products is part of the routine official inspections and these checks should be recorded in the relevant checklists. The auditor identified a significant number of commercial documents at processing plants, transporters, and storage plants visited that did not contain information on the sub-category of ABP, contrary to the requirement of Article 10 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009, and/or without information on the species despite the fact that these consignments of ABP were sent for the production of feed. Several commercial documents of intra-EU trade of Category 3 ABP originating from Spain did not contain information on "commodities certified for" and also on the requirement of Article 10 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009 despite the fact that the destination of these 12 consignments was a pet food producer. These practices are not in line with the requirements of Chapter III, Annex VIII of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. These non- compliances were not noted in official control reports.

In some cases local inspectors stated that they orally communicated non-compliances relating to commercial documents to the operators or they sent emails informing the operators on these non-compliances, however these were not recorded in official inspection reports. This is not in line with the requirements of Article 9 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2204. The auditor saw evidence of email notifications. A similar problem was identified by an internal audit in 2016 (see finding 8).

However, problems identified regarding the official inspection of commercial documents, limited controls of transporters transporting ABP for the production of PAP for aquaculture, and the authorisation of validation of processing method 7 weaken the effectiveness of these official inspections.

recommendations.text: To ensure that on the arrival of each consignment of processed animal protein, information is sent back to the Member State of origin, by means of TRACES, as required by Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009.

citations.text: The central competent authority has prepared a procedure for the notification of intra- EU trade of PAP and MBM in the Trade Control and Expert System (TRACES). Point 3 of this procedure describes the obligation of the Spanish competent authorities to inform the competent authority of Member State of origin of the arrival of each consignment. Based on this procedure the Spanish competent authorities have two options of how to inform the competent authority of origin. The first is via TRACES, which is the requirement of Article 48 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009; the second is to send back the fourth copy of the commercial document from the receiver business to the producer business based on point 2 of Chapter III, Annex VIII of Regulation (EU) No 142/2011. With the second option the information exchange is carried out between business operators which cannot replace the obligatory information exchange between competent authorities as required by Article 48 of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009.

The auditor noted that the Spanish competent authorities did not systematically inform via TRACES the competent authorities of the Member State of origin of the arrival of consignments of PAP, contrary to Article 48(3) of Regulation (EC) No 1069/2009. In 2017 and 2018, no information was sent to the Member State of origin in relation to around 80% of such arrivals. The auditor also noted that most of the operators visited used the second option of the procedure described in finding 23.

Inadequate implementation of requirements concerning information to be transmitted back to the competent authority of the Member State of origin via TRACES relating to intra-EU trade of PAP negatively affect the reliability of the flow of information on the intra-EU trade of such products. 14

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls in establishments producing RTE food are organised in such a way as to adequately cover FBOs compliance with the relevant EU legislation and the risks associated with production of RTE food, in line with Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. In addition, to strengthen and where needed put in place, CAs assessments of good hygiene practices and HACCP-based procedures required by Article 10.2(d) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004 and audits required by Article 4(3)(a) of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004, in particular when assessing compliance with Articles 4 and 5 of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. d, 53-56, 59, 60, 65 and 66

citations.text: The CAs met reported certain human resources challenges over recent years, which in some cases - together with organisational changes, information technology (IT) systems changes and resources allocation - were highlighted by the CAs met as the cause for reduced implementation of certain controls (e.g. on FBOs HACCP based procedures in Navarra, and supervisory controls in both regions visited).

However, some recommendations dating from 2015 such as putting in place audits of FBOs and an internal (CA) verification/supervisory system had not been closed to date. This is not in line with Article 4, Paragraph 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The ACCA took some actions to address them, though limited for the RTE sector. The CA cited IT - and staffing issues (see paragraph 14), but indicated that these recommendations would be addressed this year.

Challenges were identified in particular in relation to aspects of training, efficient cooperation and coordination in practice, and the verification of effectiveness of controls. These challenges, together with delays in effectively addressing audit findings, may and sometimes do impact on the controls over the production of RTE foods.

In Navarra, the risk-based criteria are used for establishing the frequency for general hygiene controls for new FBOs and new activities. For other cases, the frequency is every five years. The risk- based criteria are not used for establishing the frequency of controls over FBOs own controls including HACCP- based procedures, nor for controls on specific sector requirements (e.g. raw milk criteria). In Cataluña, the frequency of all types of controls is established on a risk basis.

In Navarra, CAs are required to carry out controls over FBOs HACCP-based procedures at approval, for expansion of activity, and in the case of alerts. Individual inspectors decide when to carry out controls on specific sector requirements. In the dairy establishment visited in Navarra the last control for specific requirements was carried out in 2014. In the same establishment, the last control related to FBOs HACCP- based procedures took place at the time of approval (in 2007) despite expansion works and changes in production.

The CA prioritisation of the controls for an FBO with multiple-activities and more establishments with the same approval (in Cataluña) did not allow an adequate focus on the risk areas. Consequently, the high-risk area visited by the audit team was not subject to recent controls. This prevented the CA from detecting several non-compliances noted during the audit team's visit, some of them long-standing. 4.4.1.2 Procedures for official controls

Each CA has procedures and instructions for staff performing official controls that apply to RTE food production. To the extent assessed by the audit team, these procedures are facilitating the official controls and are in general known and used by the staff met during this audit. The inspectors met considered them as supportive to their work. The procedures cover inspections and sampling, and in Cataluña also audits. Navarra does not have procedures for audits of FBOs' practices and procedures as required by Article 4, Paragraph 3 of Regulation (EC) No 854/2004.

In Navarra the procedures are under review to ensure that a frequency for certain controls (e.g. on routine controls for FBOs HACCP based procedures and on sector 13 specific requirements) and for the use of related checklists is defined. Certain aspects (e.g. some provisions of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005, the use of identification marks) that are mandatory for official controls, were not included in the checklists. This led to a lack of related controls. The regional CA undertook to include them during the revision of the checklists.

The CAs produce reports on the official controls carried out. In line with Article 9 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, these reports include a description of the purpose of official controls, the methods applied, the results obtained and action to be taken by the FBO concerned. The FBOs receive a copy of the report. The audit team noted, in some of the reports in both AC, limited evidence that all aspects included in the scope of the control were covered, as required in the ACCAs control procedures. 4.4.1.3 Scope/coverage of official controls

Official controls are performed in Programmes that are grouped together in blocks. The following Programmes, particularly relevant for the scope of this audit, and the related implementation data provided by the CCA are summarised below: a. Programme 1 - general control of food establishments - include hygiene inspections. The MANCP data indicate that this Programme is applied yearly in all ACs and that the ACCAs implemented approximately 85% of the 435 809 scheduled controls under this Programme for the country in 2017 and detected non-compliances in 26 % of these controls. b. In establishments (excluding retail) in the meat, dairy, fishery and composite products/prepared dishes sectors - i.e. those most likely to produce RTE food, Programme 1 controls took place with a national average of just under two of such controls per establishment in 2017. The variations are between controls in 42% of the establishments in Islas Baleares up to 12 controls per establishment in Castilla la Mancha on average, in 2017. c. Programme 2 covers FBO's own controls, including HACCP based procedures and FBO's compliance with the provisions of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. Overall, the ACCAs implemented approximately of 85% of the 96 136 scheduled controls under this Programme for the country in 2017. CA detected non- compliances in 15.8 % of these controls (highest in the dairy sector). d. In establishments (excluding retail) in the meat, dairy, fishery and composite products/prepared dishes sectors - i.e. those most likely to produce RTE food, Programme 2 controls took place in 32% of the establishments in the country in 2017. The variations noted are between 2% of the establishments in Navarra to 121% of the establishments in Comunidad Valenciana. The frequency of controls, according to these figures, varied considerably between other AC, e.g. 3% in Cataluña, 5% in Galicia, 10% in Castilla la Mancha, 11% Pais Vasco, 14% in Andalucia). e. Programme 5 covers official controls over FBOs compliance with the legislation on food labelling and food contact materials (see paragraph 65). 14 f. Programme 11 covers official sampling and testing for microbiological criteria (see chapter 4.4.1.4). g. Programme 12 covers official controls over FBOs controls for Anisakis (see paragraph 64).

Both CAs have put in place a system of routine risk-based official controls over production of RTE foods, supported by procedures and a comprehensive network of accredited laboratories under national coordination. Inspections, official sampling and in the Cataluña also audits cover relevant aspects of the legislation. The procedures for organisation of controls are currently under review in Navarra for further fine-tuning the risk determination for the RTE sector, for deciding the frequency for controls over FBOs HACCP based procedures, currently limited, and specific sector requirements and for starting to implement audits of FBOs' procedures and practices.

The controls cover satisfactorily a range of aspects of the "Hygiene Package", although there is scope for improvement in the controls over FBO's measures for prevention of cross-contamination and verification within the HACCP-based procedures, including the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 and of the EURL guidelines. The CAs' ability to detect relevant non-compliances and require adequate corrective actions is hindered by the fact that the control focus does not or not necessarily target (all) the areas relevant for food safety, whether by design or at the time of their implementation, and by some gaps in the knowledge of control staff.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the official control staff receive the necessary additional training and support, in line with the provisions of Article 6(b) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, for carrying out their control duties in establishments producing RTE food in relation to the different applicable areas of the legislation, taking account of their individual needs. e, f, g, 75-79, 81-83

citations.text: While an overall good number of inspectors receive yearly relevant training, there are differences between the AC in the array of training topics offered to their staff, and in the percentage of inspectors participating to training. Limited training was offered for controls over microbiological criteria in some AC.

The official control staff met was in general trained and knowledgeable for some parts of their work within the scope of this audit. The audit team identified training needs, mainly in relation to: a. the approval of establishments in Cataluña (see paragraphs 31-35). A new training session on this topic was ongoing at the time of the audit; 7 b. the focus and depth of the controls, and the assessment of the flexibility options and HACCP-based procedures implemented by FBOs, including compliance with Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 in both AC visited (see paragraphs 53-62, 66, 88.e, f and g); c. the evaluation of the gravity of certain non-compliances in both AC and taking the required actions in case of non-compliance (see paragraphs 75-79, 81-83).

The findings above suggest that while a wide range of training is offered to staff, the systems in place for identifying and addressing training needs do not adequately capture the individual needs that arise, in particular considering the wide area of official controls over production of RTE food, in order to ensure that staff is kept up-to date in their area of competence as required by Article 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

Challenges were identified in particular in relation to aspects of training, efficient cooperation and coordination in practice, and the verification of effectiveness of controls. These challenges, together with delays in effectively addressing audit findings, may and sometimes do impact on the controls over the production of RTE foods.

The procedure for adding new approved activities in Cataluña emphasised that the official controls should not verify FBOs HACCP based procedures, but focus on infrastructure. The ACCA explained that this approach was intended for particular situations. However, its wording led to some confusion amongst control staff on the requirements in the case reviewed by the audit team. The ACCA swiftly modified this procedure during the audit and provided examples of reports of approval visits demonstrating that the approval visits check FBOs' compliance with all relevant requirements of the applicable legislation.

These reports indicated delays of days or months for the approval visits in five out of eight cases (e.g. nine months conditional approval; five months between the first and second approval visit). The district team carrying out controls in the newly approved 10 establishment visited during the audit considered that six months between the first and second approval visit complies with the rules in place. These examples are contrary to the provisions of Article 31, paragraph 2(d) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, and of the regional procedures.

In the case of a recent approval assessed by the audit team, the district CA evaluated FBOs HACCP-based procedure solely during the visit for full approval contrary to the regional procedures. The duration of the full approval visit did not allow a thorough check of FBOs HACCP-based procedures. Consequently, the inspector had not evaluated certain elements thereof, like its validation and verification, as required by the regional procedures.

The CA acknowledged that the extent to which FBO's own procedures are evaluated depends on the background of the inspectors, and some aspects may be overlooked. The inspectors met had not received training in relation to the approval of establishments. A new training session on this topic was ongoing at the time of the audit.

The audit team noted during another visit that more establishments of the same group, located over a few km radius, with public roads between them, have the same approval number. The CCA clarified this is not in line with the legislation. The ACCA indicated this as a particular case due to historical reasons and that work was ongoing to address it. The ACCA started an investigation during the audit to confirm that this was not the case with other establishments in the AC.

The inspectors were in general able to detect non-compliances during the visits carried out as part of the current audit, in particular as regards the general hygiene requirements. While several aspects were adequately covered by the official controls, some aspects were missed and/or not addressed: a. In three establishments (two dairies and a fishery) CA challenges concerning the implementation of flexibility measures led to acceptance of cross-flows in the absence of adequate mitigating measures, as well as to under-detection of some unhygienic practices (e.g. in relation to unpacking, cleaning during production) with potential for cross contamination; b. In one of these establishments (in Cataluña), long standing maintenance and design issues as well as some operational hygiene non-compliances detected during the visit by the inspector were not noticed in the report of the previous recent official control (see paragraph 81.e). c. In another multi-activities establishment, the CA did not detect the potential for contamination coming from the practice of handling raw materials and packed final products in the same room where condensation was noted on the ceiling, followed by unpacking in a way that involved product touching of outer packaging prior to slicing.

The CAs met required the FBOs to take corrective action once they understood the potential impact on the safety of the product and provided the audit team with official control reports of swift follow-up controls. In an establishment producing RTE fishery involved in several alerts in another AC, not visited by the audit team, the official control report immediately prior to the alert suggested a fully compliant FBO. The control reports related to the alerts indicate several non-compliances including structural, hygiene, temperature controls and shelf-life studies. The ACCA reported to have replaced the inspector in the meantime (see paragraph 80).

The approach to controls over FBOs HACCP-based procedures differs between the ACCAs. In Navarra, these controls are comprehensive at the time of approval (except for validation and verification of HACCP based procedures), but they are limited afterwards (see paragraphs 49 and 51d). In Cataluña these controls are part of the routine controls carried out within the risk-based frequency, but limited as regards certain elements of FBOs' HACCP-based procedures. In particular: 15 a. in a multi-activity establishment, FBOs' practical implementation of the critical control point cooking validation and the reprocessing activity had not been part of CA controls for one of the production lines considered as "high risk" by both FBO and CA; b. in a dairy establishment, the critical limit used by the FBO differed from the values in different documents of the HACCP-based procedures, although previous controls had detected this non-compliance and reported it as having been addressed by the FBO. In addition, the controls did not check whether the alternative methods used by the dairy FBOs for alkaline phosphatase testing are validated against the ISO method in Regulation (EC) No 2074/2005, as the CA was not aware of the requirement.

The official controls over FBOs' compliance with Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 are part of Programmes 1 and 2. In Cataluña, these controls are part of the routine risk-based controls. In Navarra, these controls check if the FBOs implement the sampling plans described in their HACCP based procedures (evaluated before starting operation). Nonetheless, FBOs further changed the procedures after approval, as noted in the establishments visited, and the CA did not evaluate if the changes ensure continued compliance with the above Regulation.

In the cases assessed by the audit team, the CAs checked whether FBOs implement their sampling and testing plans for food safety criteria. In one case, the CA accepted the limit of 100cfu/g Listeria monocytogenes at the end of production for RTE sushi with a shelf- life of five days, in the absence of adequate FBO demonstration that this value would not be exceeded throughout the shelf-life of the product. This is not in line with Chapter 1, Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. The CA acknowledged challenges with the controls over FBOs' compliance with this Regulation and the lack of related training.

As regards process hygiene criteria, the controls had not been satisfactory in one of the three cases evaluated by the audit team. The CA considered the process hygiene criteria in Chapter 2, Annex II of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 as a FBO's choice and did not require the FBO to include in their procedures the compliance limits for these criteria and the action to be taken in case of non-compliance, as required by Article 7 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005.

The controls as regards the number of sampling units were in most cases satisfactory. In the relatively recently approved establishment visited, the CA accepted the FBO's reduction of sampling units from five to one in the absence of historical documentation proving effective HACCP-based procedures, contrary to the requirements of Article 5.3 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. FBOs' testing methods had not been subject to official controls in the cases assessed. This is not required by the procedures in Navarra.

FBOs' shelf-life studies for RTE food able to support the growth of Listeria are required to be verified by the CAs routinely in Cataluña, but not in Navarra. The cases assessed by the audit team, both in Cataluña and in Comunidad Valenciana, revealed that in 16 general the CA asks for FBO shelf-life studies for Listeria monocytogenes or checks them thoroughly at the time of alerts, but not beforehand or routinely otherwise.

The provisions of the EURL Guidance on sampling the food processing area and equipment for the detection of Listeria monocytogenes and of the EURL Technical Guidance Document for conducting shelf-life studies on Listeria monocytogenes in RTE foods were in general not known, and not taken into account by CAs met which had not dealt with Listeria alerts.

Consequently, CA accepted that FBOs sampling only after cleaning and disinfection, which makes the detection of the pathogen difficult leading to a false sense of security. In one case where the CA evaluated the FBOs studies as satisfactory, the studies did not demonstrate that the food safety criteria applicable throughout the shelf-life of the products can be met under reasonably foreseeable conditions of distribution, storage and use as required by Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. Also, the CA did not detect the lack of shelf-life studies for some product classes. In other cases, the CA accepted shelf-life studies based solely on organoleptic properties.

The CAs met during the audit highlighted different challenges in the organisation and performance of controls over the production of RTE food: a. assessing FBOs decisions to classify different types of food as RTE or not considering production product characteristics, heating/cooking instructions, national or regional consumption habits; assessing FBOs shelf-life studies and the limit applied for Listeria monocytogenes, in the absence of more specific guidance and reference persons/experts; b. limited knowledge of some FBOs producing high risk RTE food, especially small ones challenge CAs in their work with these FBOs, in particular in relation to the implementation of own controls including HACCP based procedures; c. resources limitations in some districts (e.g. insufficient number of calibrated thermometers for official controls; sometimes lack of clear indication of the date where re-calibration would be due as well; inspectors' excessive workload); some of these operators are remotely located adding an additional travel burden to CAs for swift follow-up visits; certain district inspectors need to travel for training was mentioned also a challenge; d. the multitude of tasks for individual CAs not supporting the thoroughness of the controls-the same official control staff carries out controls in different types of establishments and sectors and has responsibilities for checking FBOs' compliance with several parts of the legislation, not only food hygiene; CAs in Navarra highlighted inspectors' difficulty to adapt to different types of establishments. e. in the districts and provinces where the inspection tasks are distributed per geographical area, some inspectors carry out controls in a limited number of establishments of one sector (e.g. one fishery establishment in the area). In one of the cases assessed during the audit, the limited practical experience and the lack of specialised training in the specific sector undermined the inspector' confidence in challenging FBOs in their decisions; f. the inspectors met mentioned the need for specialised training mainly on food technologies/production process including for new foods and new production technologies, technical requirements for high risk areas, equipment measurement uncertainty, controlling hazards in RTE foods, the provisions of Regulation (EC) No. 2073/2005, weighing non-compliances and deadlines to implement corrective actions, administrative procedures and legal and technical content of the reports; 23 g. The practical implementation of certain requirements, for example in relation to flexibility in small establishments as well as in the implementation of the information received during training for example for the evaluation of FBOs' shelf-life studies; h. The lack of a clear definition for high risk food as regards other dangers than Listeria. Some outdated procedures or rather large procedures for which one of the inspectors met welcomed the possibility to highlight the most relevant parts for inspectors. 4.4.4 Suggestions and measures put in place to address the identified challenges aiming to facilitate compliance with the EU food hygiene requirements in this area and reducing food borne outbreaks related to RTE foods

The audit team noted difficulties with ensuring that approvals are kept updated in relation to activities no longer carried out by FBOs. In Navarra, one of the 11 establishments visited had approval for an activity not performed in ten years. In Pais Vasco, a dairy FBO informed the CA that the production ceased and the business was intended to be sold or rented. This type of information does not trigger temporary suspension of activity. The CA became aware that production restarted with a new owner due to an alert caused by detection of 100 000cfu/g Listeria monocytogenes in a RTE food produced in the establishment. The CA's visit on-the-spot identified serious non-compliances and the establishment had been closed since. Conclusions on registration and approval of food business operators

The ACCAs have systems in place for registration and approval of establishments producing RTE foods which for several aspects are supportive of achieving compliance. The ACCAs visited in general apply the related procedures, to a larger extent in Navarra. However, the procedure in Navarra and the implementation of the procedure in Cataluña, connected with training needs, do not ensure full and consistent compliance with the provisions of establishments' approval as provided for in Article 31 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

recommendations.text: To ensure official controls over FBOs' sampling and testing are carried out as required by Article 1 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 and Article 6a of Regulation (EC) No 2074/2005, and that these controls are adequate as regards the provisions of Articles 3, 5 and 7 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 and Chapter II, Annex VIa to Regulation (EC) No 2074/2005.

citations.text: The regional guidelines for dairy production in Cataluña do not require FBOs to ensure the alternative methods used for alkaline phosphatase testing to verify the effectiveness of the pasteurisation process, are validated against the ISO method provided in Regulation (EC) No 2074/2005. As the guidance is used by both FBOs and CA staff, this aspect was not checked by FBO and not subject to official controls in the case assessed by the audit team. Conclusions on national measures

The national measures in place support both FBOs in addressing the microbiological hazards and control the production process of RTE foods, as well as CAs in performing the related official controls. Advice for consumers aiming to prevent food borne outbreaks is also available. There is scope for reviewing the regional measures to support a harmonised and correct implementation by the dairy industry of the measures for verifying the effectiveness of pasteurisation and related official controls.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the CA classifies non-compliances taking into account of the specific risks related to RTE products and take the required action to ensure the operator remedies the situation, as required by Article 54 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004.

citations.text: The actions taken in the cases of alerts related to RTE food assessed by the audit team showed a mixed picture. In Navarra, the CA carried out a swift visit on-the-spot and had verified and documented, in subsequent visits, a rapid tracing back, recall and destruction of the merchandise. Contrary to the national procedure for alerts, an official control to ascertain that the measures put in place by the FBO adequately address the cause(s) and prevent its(their) reoccurrence, does not take place. In Cataluña, the CAs carried out on-site visit and investigated the possible causes of RASFF alerts in the cases assessed by the audit team. 19

In Cataluña, the CA releases the detained product involved in a RASFF alert following detection of Salmonella by a molecular method in an outbreak investigation in the absence of apparent causes at establishment level, according to the official control reports carried out at the time and with negative official test results, Subsequently, the confirmation for Salmonella presence using the ISO method and information that the same strain had been involved in an outbreak was received via the RASFF network.

The new information received resulted in the CA questioning the FBO's food safety management system, called for more thorough official controls and CA requests for adequate shelf-life studies. Nonetheless, the CA had accepted that the FBO uses Salmonella-positive ingredients, in the absence of an indication of the level of contamination, provided 15 samples of the final products were negative. According to the FBO demonstration made available to the CA, the respective production process ensures one log reduction.

The ACCA stated the approach taken by the district CA in managing the RASFF alert above is not the routine one. In addition, following the audit team's visit, the CA requested the FBO to review their HACCP based procedures and to demonstrate that the processing is eliminating the hazard in question as required by Article 7 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005.

The action taken by the CA in Comunidad Valenciana in relation to several alerts concerning the same establishment producing RTE fishery products revealed also difficulties in ensuring that the contaminated foods are traced and recalled in a timely fashion, and that the actions put in place by the FBOs prevent recurrence. a. Some of the CA on-the-spot visits took place with one and two weeks delay that could not be justified. The control reports indicate delays in tracing back the product until the product had expired and a recall was not needed, and delays in addressing the root cause (sanctioned with 1000 penalty). b. Seven months after the first alert of these series, based on the outcome the shelf- life study, the shelf-life of the RTE products had been significantly shortened, for some RTE category by half. For non-compliances related to hygiene and lost traceability, the report indicate repeated request for immediate action in three consecutive reports, the third one with a 30 days deadline.

The ACCAs stated to have realised that the case could have been handled better, and to have taken action to address the control weaknesses. As a result, and for the year following this series of alerts, the monitoring system for on-the-spot visits following food incidents indicated a rapid response (see paragraph 54).

When the inspectors do not consider the non-compliances to be serious, the measures taken do not ensure that these are corrected routinely and in a timely fashion. In most of such cases seen by the audit team, the potential for product contamination was not adequately assessed, and CAs in general did not request action in relation to exposed products: 20 a. the CAs had given the same importance and same deadline (e.g. between seven days and 3 months) to maintenance non-compliances like peeling rust and peeling paint, irrespective of whether they could impact on exposed product or not (e.g. in the establishments producing composite products in Navarra, and in the fishery establishments in Cataluña). b. For action in relation to equipment in contact with food (inadequate cleaning of the slicer in a dairy establishment, peeling slicer in a composite products establishment), the CA in Navarra had given the same deadline as for addressing holes in the floor, while the FBO continued to use the former in production. c. In two of the three establishments visited where condensation was noted above exposed ingredients or intermediate products, the CA did not require FBO action in relation to the products or otherwise (Navarra). One of these was an establishment where Listeria had previously been detected in final products. In another establishment, CA accepted inadequate mitigating measures, considering that condensation was difficult to manage in the relevant area. d. In a third establishment, in Cataluña, the control reports documented repeated findings, including of ceiling condensation. Non-compliances considered minor had in general not been followed-up. At the time of the audit, the detection of ceiling condensation in the vicinity of exposed ingredients led to inadequate FBO action suggesting that the food safety management system in place was not able to effectively address this repeated failure. This did not trigger stronger enforcement action. e. In Cataluña, in an establishment producing different high risk RTE fishery products, the CA had not recorded in previous controls several and extended long standing maintenance and design issues as well as some operational hygiene ones noted by the same inspector during the audit. The inspector considered as minor non-compliance all maintenance issues, including when present above or in contact with exposed product, and stated to be reluctant to challenge the FBO whom he considered to have greater expertise. f. In the absence of adequate supervisory controls, the head of the district team did not detect the above mentioned situation. The report of a new reinforced district CA control in the same establishment identifying numerous shortcomings with short deadlines for remedy was submitted to the audit team at a later stage. g. Nonetheless, the approach to consider all maintenance issues minor, regardless of the potential for contaminating the product was in general shared by the control staff met in the ACs visited. This impacted on the corrective actions required by the CA and their effective follow-up. 21

In Cataluña, the CAs met by the audit team explained that they are not required to give a deadline for the FBO to rectify minor non-compliances. The CA is required to request action from FBO only in case of serious non-compliances5. This resulted in either non- compliances repeatedly recorded in control reports (e.g. meat establishment) without adequate action (this was the case also for the fishery establishment Comunidad Valenciana) or lack of recording of non-compliances considered to be of minor nature (e.g. fishery establishment).

In those cases where the potential risk associated with non-compliances considered as "minor" is not adequately assessed, this impacts on both the necessary requests for corrective action, as well as on the timeliness of their implementation. The action in case of non-compliance differs between the regions visited and the action in relation to the products is in general limited to instances of confirmed non-compliant official test results. 5 In their comments to the draft report the CA noted that under the procedures corrective measures must always be taken in case of non-compliance, whether minor, serious or very serious. The procedures do not set deadlines for the corrective measures to be implemented in the event of non-compliance; rather they establish, on the basis of the severity of the non-compliance, whether the corrective measure should be immediate or a timetable be set for their implementation. Hence, in Catalonia, non-compliances of this nature detected in the control reports can be attributed to incorrect application of the established procedures. 22

citations.text: The measures targeting a specific pathogen are more developed as regards Listeria monocytogenes. National or regional measures aiming to support FBOs and CAs in addressing the main cause of outbreaks, human cases and hospitalised persons 5 (Staphylococcus in dairy products) according to the national data (see chapter 3) have to date not been adopted.

Cataluña was implementing an initiative to address the main cause of food alerts due to pathogenic microorganisms (Salmonella detection in meat products) at the time of the audit. This initiative includes relevant guidance for official control staff, based on expert advice. Relevant information of this initiative, from which the control staff in other AC might benefit, has not been shared between ACs.

National guidelines to support FBOs in implementing HACCP based procedures and good hygiene practices are available for the production of RTE milk, egg products and fruit juices. Each AC may have other guidelines in place. In Cataluña such guidance documents are available as regards Listeria control in the food industry, and concerning hygiene requirements for raw milk cheese production. The production of increasingly popular types of foods considered as potentially presenting a higher risk, like raw products or composite RTE food, does not benefit yet from industry guides.

The regional guidelines for dairy production in Cataluña do not require FBOs to ensure the alternative methods used for alkaline phosphatase testing to verify the effectiveness of the pasteurisation process, are validated against the ISO method provided in Regulation (EC) No 2074/2005. As the guidance is used by both FBOs and CA staff, this aspect was not checked by FBO and not subject to official controls in the case assessed by the audit team. Conclusions on national measures

The national measures in place support both FBOs in addressing the microbiological hazards and control the production process of RTE foods, as well as CAs in performing the related official controls. Advice for consumers aiming to prevent food borne outbreaks is also available. There is scope for reviewing the regional measures to support a harmonised and correct implementation by the dairy industry of the measures for verifying the effectiveness of pasteurisation and related official controls.

There is scope for further exploring in the national or regional measures the options to address the hazards stemming from the highest number of outbreaks, human cases and hospitalised persons following consumption of RTE food in recent years, according to the national data, and for sharing relevant regional measures where available.

Coordination and cooperation mechanisms within and between the ACCAs and by AESAN are in place (e.g. inter-territorial and inter-sectoral coordination bodies, including a permanent working group for applying Hygiene Regulations, in tools for sharing good practices and problems). Examples of coordination and cooperation relevant for the RTE sector were presented to the audit team. While, in all cases assessed, the CA acted upon receipt of notification or request, the audit team noted that these actions are not necessarily swift: a. In the example of inter-AC coordination provided by the audit team (a complaint from a consumer with medical symptoms upon consumption of RTE food produced in a different AC), the local CA carried out the investigation two weeks after receiving the notification. The regional CA submitted the feedback to the other AC within one month from the initial communication as the suspicion had not been confirmed. b. AESAN informed the audit team that for production of unpasteurised dairy products, a coordination system is in place to ensure that CA carrying out controls in such establishments are informed when the animal health status of the herd providing the milk, changes. The deadline provided by the national legislation for communicating this information is maximum seven days. c. In the example provided to the audit team (i.e. the detection of tuberculosis at farm level), and while the public health CA received the notification from the animal health team promptly, an on­the-spot visit was organised four months after receiving the information. During this visit the official controls found raw milk cheese production using the milk from the herd where TB was detected.

Challenges were identified in particular in relation to aspects of training, efficient cooperation and coordination in practice, and the verification of effectiveness of controls. These challenges, together with delays in effectively addressing audit findings, may and sometimes do impact on the controls over the production of RTE foods.

The ACs visited have different procedures in place for approval of establishments. Some elements thereof support compliance with the provisions of Article 31, paragraph 2 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. a. In Navarra, an ACCA group of experts carries out an "in depth" initial evaluation of the written HACCP-based procedures before the FBO may start production. When the outcomes of this evaluation and of the on-site visit by the district CA are satisfactory, the ACCA grants the approval. The audit team received examples demonstrating the correct implementation of the regional procedure. b. In Cataluña, the district CAs issue conditional approval for three months when the outcome of the on-site visit, carried out upon receipt of an application for approval and before FBO starts operations, is satisfactory. Before issuing a full approval, another on-site visit within three months is required to establish compliance with the EU law while the establishment is in operation. The same procedure requires district CA to evaluate FBOs' compliance with infrastructures and own controls during these visits.

Different approaches are in place between ACs. Whether the product is RTE or not, and the risk data identified by the CA (see chapter 3) -for example, manipulation potentially introducing a hazard (e.g. slicing), lack of pasteurisation, the history of non-compliance- impact differently on the attributed the risk category, depending on the AC. The same RTE meat products are considered as medium risk by some ACs, but as low risk by others, while raw meat is considered high risk. In Navarra, the procedure allocates more points (i.e. a higher risk category) if FBOs do not have own controls/procedures than if 12 these controls/procedures are not implemented.

The data on the control frequency for RTE producing establishments (e.g. dairy, meat, fishery, composite products) assessed by the audit team indicate that the minimum frequency of controls in establishments of the same sector varies between once per year to four times per year, depending on the AC. Some AC did not provide information on their minimum frequency of controls. Certain controls are limited (see paragraph 51).

In Navarra, the risk-based criteria are used for establishing the frequency for general hygiene controls for new FBOs and new activities. For other cases, the frequency is every five years. The risk- based criteria are not used for establishing the frequency of controls over FBOs own controls including HACCP- based procedures, nor for controls on specific sector requirements (e.g. raw milk criteria). In Cataluña, the frequency of all types of controls is established on a risk basis.

Official controls are performed in Programmes that are grouped together in blocks. The following Programmes, particularly relevant for the scope of this audit, and the related implementation data provided by the CCA are summarised below: a. Programme 1 - general control of food establishments - include hygiene inspections. The MANCP data indicate that this Programme is applied yearly in all ACs and that the ACCAs implemented approximately 85% of the 435 809 scheduled controls under this Programme for the country in 2017 and detected non-compliances in 26 % of these controls. b. In establishments (excluding retail) in the meat, dairy, fishery and composite products/prepared dishes sectors - i.e. those most likely to produce RTE food, Programme 1 controls took place with a national average of just under two of such controls per establishment in 2017. The variations are between controls in 42% of the establishments in Islas Baleares up to 12 controls per establishment in Castilla la Mancha on average, in 2017. c. Programme 2 covers FBO's own controls, including HACCP based procedures and FBO's compliance with the provisions of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. Overall, the ACCAs implemented approximately of 85% of the 96 136 scheduled controls under this Programme for the country in 2017. CA detected non- compliances in 15.8 % of these controls (highest in the dairy sector). d. In establishments (excluding retail) in the meat, dairy, fishery and composite products/prepared dishes sectors - i.e. those most likely to produce RTE food, Programme 2 controls took place in 32% of the establishments in the country in 2017. The variations noted are between 2% of the establishments in Navarra to 121% of the establishments in Comunidad Valenciana. The frequency of controls, according to these figures, varied considerably between other AC, e.g. 3% in Cataluña, 5% in Galicia, 10% in Castilla la Mancha, 11% Pais Vasco, 14% in Andalucia). e. Programme 5 covers official controls over FBOs compliance with the legislation on food labelling and food contact materials (see paragraph 65). 14 f. Programme 11 covers official sampling and testing for microbiological criteria (see chapter 4.4.1.4). g. Programme 12 covers official controls over FBOs controls for Anisakis (see paragraph 64).

The differences in the approach between ACCAs towards various aspects of the organisation and implementation of the controls suggest a missed opportunity for sharing good practices and exploiting synergies between ACCAs with a view to providing comparable support for staff carrying out controls in establishments with similar risks, further strengthening the control systems and their consistency, as well as ensuring a uniform control approach towards all FBOs. 4.4.3 Challenges encountered by the CA in the organisation and performance of controls over the production of RTE foods

citations.text: However, some recommendations dating from 2015 such as putting in place audits of FBOs and an internal (CA) verification/supervisory system had not been closed to date. This is not in line with Article 4, Paragraph 6 of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004. The ACCA took some actions to address them, though limited for the RTE sector. The CA cited IT - and staffing issues (see paragraph 14), but indicated that these recommendations would be addressed this year.

In 2016 the supervisory system's objective was changed aiming for the yearly supervision of all inspectors. This objective was not met in 2016. Between 2016 and 2018 the system required documental supervision, including the possibility of on-site verification at the monitoring team's request. The later was used to a limited extent, mainly in relation to exports. The ACCA highlighted that from 2019 onwards each inspector has to be supervised on-the-spot.. In the absence of adequate verification of effectiveness of the controls, required by Article 8, Paragraph 3, point (b) of Regulation (EC) No 882/2004, the training needs affecting the performance of the controls had not been identified. The actions taken in the cases of alerts related to RTE food assessed by the audit team showed a mixed picture. In Navarra, the CA carried out a swift visit on-the-spot and had verified and documented, in subsequent visits, a rapid tracing back, recall and destruction of the merchandise. Contrary to the national procedure for alerts, an official control to ascertain that the measures put in place by the FBO adequately address the cause(s) and prevent its(their) reoccurrence, does not take place. In Cataluña, the CAs carried out on-site visit and investigated the possible causes of RASFF alerts in the cases assessed by the audit team. 19

In Cataluña, the CA releases the detained product involved in a RASFF alert following detection of Salmonella by a molecular method in an outbreak investigation in the absence of apparent causes at establishment level, according to the official control reports carried out at the time and with negative official test results, Subsequently, the confirmation for Salmonella presence using the ISO method and information that the same strain had been involved in an outbreak was received via the RASFF network.

The new information received resulted in the CA questioning the FBO's food safety management system, called for more thorough official controls and CA requests for adequate shelf-life studies. Nonetheless, the CA had accepted that the FBO uses Salmonella-positive ingredients, in the absence of an indication of the level of contamination, provided 15 samples of the final products were negative. According to the FBO demonstration made available to the CA, the respective production process ensures one log reduction.

The ACCA stated the approach taken by the district CA in managing the RASFF alert above is not the routine one. In addition, following the audit team's visit, the CA requested the FBO to review their HACCP based procedures and to demonstrate that the processing is eliminating the hazard in question as required by Article 7 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005.

The action taken by the CA in Comunidad Valenciana in relation to several alerts concerning the same establishment producing RTE fishery products revealed also difficulties in ensuring that the contaminated foods are traced and recalled in a timely fashion, and that the actions put in place by the FBOs prevent recurrence. a. Some of the CA on-the-spot visits took place with one and two weeks delay that could not be justified. The control reports indicate delays in tracing back the product until the product had expired and a recall was not needed, and delays in addressing the root cause (sanctioned with 1000 penalty). b. Seven months after the first alert of these series, based on the outcome the shelf- life study, the shelf-life of the RTE products had been significantly shortened, for some RTE category by half. For non-compliances related to hygiene and lost traceability, the report indicate repeated request for immediate action in three consecutive reports, the third one with a 30 days deadline.

The ACCAs stated to have realised that the case could have been handled better, and to have taken action to address the control weaknesses. As a result, and for the year following this series of alerts, the monitoring system for on-the-spot visits following food incidents indicated a rapid response (see paragraph 54).

When the inspectors do not consider the non-compliances to be serious, the measures taken do not ensure that these are corrected routinely and in a timely fashion. In most of such cases seen by the audit team, the potential for product contamination was not adequately assessed, and CAs in general did not request action in relation to exposed products: 20 a. the CAs had given the same importance and same deadline (e.g. between seven days and 3 months) to maintenance non-compliances like peeling rust and peeling paint, irrespective of whether they could impact on exposed product or not (e.g. in the establishments producing composite products in Navarra, and in the fishery establishments in Cataluña). b. For action in relation to equipment in contact with food (inadequate cleaning of the slicer in a dairy establishment, peeling slicer in a composite products establishment), the CA in Navarra had given the same deadline as for addressing holes in the floor, while the FBO continued to use the former in production. c. In two of the three establishments visited where condensation was noted above exposed ingredients or intermediate products, the CA did not require FBO action in relation to the products or otherwise (Navarra). One of these was an establishment where Listeria had previously been detected in final products. This did not trigger stronger enforcement action. e. The inspector considered as minor non-compliance all maintenance issues, including when present above or in contact with exposed product, and stated to be reluctant to challenge the FBO whom he considered to have greater expertise. f. The report of a new reinforced district CA control in the same establishment identifying numerous shortcomings with short deadlines for remedy was submitted to the audit team at a later stage. g. Nonetheless, the approach to consider all maintenance issues minor, regardless of the potential for contaminating the product was in general shared by the control staff met in the ACs visited. This impacted on the corrective actions required by the CA and their effective follow-up. 21

In Cataluña, the CAs met by the audit team explained that they are not required to give a deadline for the FBO to rectify minor non-compliances. The CA is required to request action from FBO only in case of serious non-compliances5. This resulted in either non- compliances repeatedly recorded in control reports (e.g. meat establishment) without adequate action (this was the case also for the fishery establishment Comunidad Valenciana) or lack of recording of non-compliances considered to be of minor nature (e.g. fishery establishment).

recommendations.text: To ensure that, in order to support detection of non-compliance, the CAs use adequate tools such as the provisions of the EURL "Guidelines on sampling the food processing area and equipment for the detection of Listeria monocytogenes" and of the "EURL Technical Guidance Document for conducting shelf-life studies on Listeria monocytogenes in ready-to-eat foods", for the official controls over FBOs' sampling procedures and shelf-life studies on Listeria monocytogenes in ready-to-eat foods.

citations.text: The provisions of the EURL Guidance on sampling the food processing area and equipment for the detection of Listeria monocytogenes and of the EURL Technical Guidance Document for conducting shelf-life studies on Listeria monocytogenes in RTE foods were in general not known, and not taken into account by CAs met which had not dealt with Listeria alerts.

Consequently, CA accepted that FBOs sampling only after cleaning and disinfection, which makes the detection of the pathogen difficult leading to a false sense of security. In one case where the CA evaluated the FBOs studies as satisfactory, the studies did not demonstrate that the food safety criteria applicable throughout the shelf-life of the products can be met under reasonably foreseeable conditions of distribution, storage and use as required by Article 3 of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. Also, the CA did not detect the lack of shelf-life studies for some product classes. In other cases, the CA accepted shelf-life studies based solely on organoleptic properties.

The controls cover satisfactorily a range of aspects of the "Hygiene Package", although there is scope for improvement in the controls over FBO's measures for prevention of cross-contamination and verification within the HACCP-based procedures, including the requirements of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005 and of the EURL guidelines. The CAs' ability to detect relevant non-compliances and require adequate corrective actions is hindered by the fact that the control focus does not or not necessarily target (all) the areas relevant for food safety, whether by design or at the time of their implementation, and by some gaps in the knowledge of control staff.
