citations.text: MAPA and the ACPHS for Galicia confirmed that no further notifications had been provided since 2016, although the T. erytreae had since continued to spread in Galicia, including into the Province of Lugo. The distribution of T. erytreae in Galicia is illustrated in Figure 1 below, which also indicates the year in which the pest was first found in each municipality. Figure 1: Distribution of T. erytreae in Galicia in 2019 10

The data in Figure 1 above indicates that T. erytreae was found in a number of new areas only in 2019 or 2018, in particular in the Province of Lugo and eastern parts of the Province of A Coruña. Neither the new information concerning the spread of the pest into a new area, nor the change of control strategy for T. erytreae detailed in section 5.3 below, were notified to the Commission and other Member States, as required by Article 2(5) of Decision 2014/917/EU.

The initial outbreaks of T. erytreae were notified to the European Commission and other Member States, however, the pests' continued spread into new areas of Galicia was not notified, which hinders the ability of other areas of Spain and the other Member States, in adapting their official controls as necessary.

recommendations.text: To ensure that host plants of Trioza erytreae are moved only if they satisfy the conditions established for the production and movements of such plants, by item 10.1 of Annex IV Part A Section II to Directive 2000/29/EC. and

citations.text: As noted in section 5.2.2 above, the ACPHS has not legally revised the demarcated areas for T. erytreae since 2016. Instead, the ACPHS stated that it implements a 'flexible demarcation' in the event that T. erytreae is found in a new area. In practice, this means that the movement of host plants from nurseries in areas, or even places, where T. erytreae has been found is not prohibited. The infested plants identified in the places must either be destroyed or heavily pruned and treated with a plant protection product, but other (un-infested) host plants on the site may be moved within the demarcated area. The audit team noted that the flexibly demarcated areas are not recorded, and the ACPHS inspectors performing checks did not appear to be aware, or concerned, whether a nursery or retailer of host plants was situated in such a flexibly demarcated area or not.

However, such an approach is not in line with EU requirements for the production and movement of host plants in item 10.1 of Annex IV Part A Section II to Directive 2000/29/EC, nor is in line with the national or regional legislation for the pest, which undermines confidence in the guarantees, and pest free status of host plants, that are intended to be provided by that legislation. Conclusion on control measures for T. erytreae, D. citri and HLB

The control measures have also not been fully applied in Galicia, in particular in those areas in which T. erytreae occurs, but that have not been demarcated, as required. That undermines confidence in the guarantees, and pest-free status of host plants, which are intended to be provided by the national and regional legislation and EU legislation, and poses a risk for the further spread of the pest in trade.

responses.response: Como ya se indicó durante la auditoría, en Galicia, la presencia de plantas hospedantes de Trioza erytreae es muy dispersa pués está fundamentalmente localizada en pequeños huertos y jardines de propietarios particulares. ismo, no hay producción de planta y, en general, la disponible en viveros procede de zonas de fuera de Galicia que están libres de la plaga. Los viveros de zonas libres que venden planta, restringen su comercialización a su entorno local por lo que los movimientos son muy reducidos. Nuestra experiencia parece indicar que la infección no se produce por el movimiento de planta, sino por la dispersión de la plaga de una zona infestada a otra próxima debido al vuelo de los adultos. En cualquier caso, está previsto publicar breve una resolución que actualice las zonas infectadas por Trioza eritreae. Así mismo se notificará, a todos los viveros y comercializadores de cítricos, las restricciones existentes en el movimiento de plantas hospedantes. Los interesados también podrán consultar las zonas infestadas, y las medidas a aplicar para evitar la extensión de la plaga a través de una página WEB. Page: 1 /02/2020 eport ref. recommendations.text: To ensure that the control measures, including national contingency plans for Trioza erytreae, Diaphorina citri and Huanglongbing, are reviewed in light of experience gained and the restricted availability and effectiveness of plant protection products, which form a key element of the current control strategies, in order to ensure their effectiveness, as provided for by point 12 of EPPO Standard PM9/10(1), and that all measures necessary to inhibit the further spread of T. erytreae are being taken, as required by Article 16(1) of Directive 2000/29/EC. and

citations.text: The National Contingency Plans establish the means for implementing the measures required by the Royal Decree. MAPA confirmed that there have been no changes to those plans since the previous audit, and the plans have not been reviewed or tested through test-exercises.

MAPA and the ACPHS of the Canary Islands and Galicia provided details of their experience with the use of plant protection products as part of their control measures for the eradication or containment of T. erytreae, which were initiated following the first findings of the pest in those Autonomous Communities. The report of the previous audit provides a detailed description of the area-wide pesticide applications by TRAGSA in Galicia at that time, which were based on the initial experience in the Canary Islands. Although the treatments had proved effective at protecting individual host plants, the ACPHS stated that they had proved ineffective at preventing the spread of the pest or even in suppressing it, in infested areas.

MAPA highlighted the continued withdrawal of authorisation of a number of the plant protection products since the previous audit, including for neonicotinoides14. MAPA stated that they would not grant emergency authorisation under Article 53(1) of Regulation (EU) No 1107/2009, for the use of such plant protection products.

MAPA and the ACPHS also highlighted the problem with false-positives in the initial laboratory screening tests for HLB. That can lead to a significant number of results, which must subsequently be confirmed, or refuted by further laboratory analysis. MAPA stated that the additional tests may take a long period of time and are resource intensive and that this complicates the surveys and means that it is legally difficult for the authorities to take action, based on a possibly false preliminary positive result for HLB.

There were no requirements for the establishment or review of contingency plans in the EU legislation applicable at the time of the audit. MAPA informed the audit team that National Contingency Plans had not been reviewed or evaluated in light of experience, as recommended by point 12 of EPPO Standard PM9/10(1).

However, the legislation and contingency plans have not been reviewed in light of experience, in particular the proven ineffectiveness of plant protection products, which play a key role in the control measures, which undermines confidence in the ability of the proposed control measures to ensure the prompt and effective eradication of new outbreaks of those pests.

citations.text: The demarcated area of As Neves was established following the first finding of PWN in the area in 2010. The situation up until November 2016 was evaluated in detail by the previous audit. The demarcation was revised following the seven new findings in the demarcated area in August 2018 after a significant delay, by the Resolution of 28 December 2018 of the Directorate-General of Livestock, Agriculture and Agri-Food Industries (14). The revised demarcated area is illustrated in Figure 1 below (Annex IV of the Resolution), and is in line with the provisions of Article 5(2) of Decision 2012/535/EU.

The ACPHS indicated that there were no particular reasons why the demarcated area was not revised `without delay' as required by Article 5(3) of Decision 2012/535/EU. The audit team noted during visits to wood processing industry and heat-treatment facility in Galicia, that susceptible material continued to move from the area, pending its demarcation. Figure 1: Situation of PWN in Galicia ­ As Neves demarcated area

The significant delay in establishing a new demarcated area following the finding of seven new infested trees in As Neves, did not hinder the felling and removal of those trees. However, it did delay the application of controls on the movement of susceptible material from the area, necessary to limit the potential of the pest to spread through such movements. 13

responses.response: The identification of the new outbreaks in 2018 meant the e immediate elimination of the affected trees and their destruction, following the protocol established in the national contingency plan for the Pine Wood Nematode and the Galicia Action Plan. recommendations.text: Ensure that each laboratory, involved in the analysis of official samples for the presence of Tomato brown rugose fruit virus, carries out the test with methods listed in the Annex of Regulation (EU) 2020/1191 and the proficiency of the tests is confirmed by the National Reference Laboratory as required by Article 101(c) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. to 21.

citations.text: The National Reference Laboratory (NRL) for the viruses of non-woody plants is the Laboratory for Virology of the Polytechnic University of Valencia. Their activity is based on an agreement with the MAPA. The laboratory is responsible for the confirmatory tests of the positive and undefined results on ToBRFV obtained by the ACCA laboratories. Until the time of the audit, this practically meant the confirmation of tests results carried out with enzyme linked immunosorbent assay method (ELISA) and with real-time polymerase chain reaction method (RT-PCR). In the case the ACCA laboratory tested the sample with a molecular method the same RNA extract was used for the confirmation. The laboratory stated that since 1 October they carry out ToBRFV tests with RT-PCR methods, listed in the Annex of Regulation (EU) 2020/1191.

An appropriate laboratory network assists the implementation of the official controls. However, the lack of effective and coordinated proficiency tests on the use of the RT- PCR method for the detection of ToBRFV by the numerous ACCA laboratories could influence negatively the effectiveness of the controls. The staff of certain official laboratories have experience in testing with molecular methods; however, this experience is not evident for the detection of ToBRFV using the method described by Regulation (EU) 2020/1191. Therefore, proficiency tests are necessary to assess the performance of the ACCA laboratories.

audits.title: Food of animal origin - bovine meat, including traceability

recommendations.text: To ensure that there is an effective and timely mechanism to provide feedback to OVs that had reported animal welfare non-compliances to give them information about the results of their actions as required by Article 4(2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The procedures of communication regarding animal welfare issues between the Health and Agriculture departments in one of the ACs were not satisfactory, resulting in a lack of feedback from Agriculture of the impact of the actions taken by the OVs working for the Health department at slaughterhouse level. This does not allow the OVs to understand how effective their work is or, potentially, to learn from mistakes. 5.2.2 Impartiality, freedom from conflict of interest,

The cooperation and coordination arrangements between and within the CA(s) are satisfactory for the performance of official controls and enforcement, apart from the provision of feedback information to slaughterhouse OVs that report welfare-related 10 issues to the department dealing with farms and primary production, and which in one of the ACs was not in place.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the CAs have a suitable system to train and support those veterinarians that deliver official controls only occasionally, as required by Article 5(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: Neither of the two CAs have a specific and structured training procedure for those veterinarians that work for them occasionally, covering absences of permanent OVs. The audit found evidence of some problems related to PMI in two out of six establishments, in both ACs, where the resident OV was not present and a locum one was in charge.

Equally, private veterinarians doing AMI on farm for ES are not included in these training activities. As mentioned in paragraph 15, one of the CAs has already taken steps to resolve this. 9 5.2.5 Supervision and audits
The two ACs have a system of internal audits and checks to monitor the performance of their OVs and ensure they deliver official controls adequately.

Both CAs have procedures to train, support and control the OVs delivering official controls on a regular basis, but neither have a specific and structured procedure for those veterinarians that work for them occasionally.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the system of review of approval verifies that the establishments maintain the approval for only those activities that are relevant and that the official controls on newly approved establishments are performed with the appropriate frequency, as required by Articles 148 (5) and 9(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: In one of the ACs, for establishments other than slaughterhouses, there is no set procedure to regulate when the first inspection or audit of the establishment has to take place after approval and once the activity has started. As a result, the CA might not inspect a new establishment for a long period of time and cannot assess compliance with legislation and FBO's own checks.

Both CAs have procedures to review the approval status of the establishments in their territory on a regular basis, in order to ensure that it reflects the activities that the FBO carries out. However, one of the slaughterhouses reviewed by the audit team was still approved to slaughter a species that had not been processed for the last five years. The controls did not review if this slaughterhouse still met the conditions for this species. Conclusions on approval of establishments

In one of the ACs, there are no arrangements to ensure that, following the approval process, a suitably short period of time for newly approved establishments other than slaughterhouses is established in which to carry out an FBO's audit or an operational inspection.

The system for review of approvals does not currently ensure, in one of the ACs, that the establishments maintain the approval for only those activities that are relevant or that the approval conditions for activities not carried out, continue to be met.

recommendations.text: To ensure that post mortem inspection of bovine carcases and offal is carried out in accordance with Article 19 to Regulation (EU) 2019/627 at all times. 6. 7. 8. To clarify the instructions in the relevant procedures regarding a) the role of FBO staff in respect of PMI tasks in red meat slaughterhouses, and b) about the actions to be taken regarding animals in the lairage with serious injuries, in order to ensure compliance with Article 18(3) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and point 1.11 in Annex III to Council Regulation (EC) No 1099/2009, respectively. To ensure that only official veterinarians carry out the ante mortem inspection of bovines subject to emergency slaughter on farm, that they issue a certificate with the complete information and details as required by Article 4 of Regulation (EU) 2019/624 and that there is a system to supervise or audit the performance of those veterinarians involved in the process. To ensure that the reason for on-farm emergency slaughter of bovine animals is clearly stated in the required certificate, to allow a decision on the fitness for human consumption or otherwise to be taken in compliance with Chapter VI of Section I of Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004. To ensure that there is a system in place to verify that only slaughtermen with the required level of competence perform on-farm emergency slaughtering as required by Article 7(1) of Regulation (EC) 1099/2009.

citations.text: According to the OVs' explanations and descriptions of the activities, in two of the six slaughterhouses audited (one in each AC), the PMI was not carried out in accordance with the legislation.

In one of them, the OV stated to have passed as fit for human consumption the carcase of an ES bovine without having inspected the lungs and green offal, as the FBO staff did not present them for inspection.

In the other slaughterhouse, where only one veterinarian is normally present, the OV explained that they would not be able to inspect the green offal (which would go directly to the gut room) of the carcases processed during the time they would spend in the lairage for AMI reasons as the slaughtering line would not stop. Nevertheless, those carcases would be health marked and passed as fit for human consumption. This is not in line with Article 19 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627.
In both cases, the OVs explained that, if any doubt, the slaughterhouse staff know what is fit and unfit for human consumption and would save for them any offal with signs of being unfit.

It has to be noted that, in the second AC and in order to address the fact that the PMI was not carried out in accordance with the EU requirements, management at central level took immediate action and arranged for a second and more experienced OV to be deployed to the slaughterhouse as a support mechanism.

Also in two of the six slaughterhouses, the FBO staff carried out the removal of the spinal cord, which is classed as a specified risk material, after the carcases had been inspected and health marked as fit for human consumption. This is not in line with Article 45 (q) to Regulation (EU) 2019/627. Procedures for poultry
The implementation of the official controls does not ensure that PMI of all carcases and offal takes place in accordance with Article 19 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627.

To ensure that laboratories involved in official controls for biotoxins provide timely results, as required by Article 34(d) of Regulation 2017/625, so that competent authorities can act promptly to impose closures when needed, as required by Article 65(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627.

citations.text: The monitoring programme indicates that biotoxins monitoring results that exceed the limits established in in Annex III, Section VII, Chapter V Point 2 to Regulation (EC) No 853/2004, trigger an immediate closure of production areas and, in one autonomous community, an increased sampling of water and bivalve molluscs in the adjacent production areas. Only one of the autonomous communities had a closure in the last two years due to exceedance of biotoxins. Closure of the production area, and withdrawal and recall of bivalve molluscs already placed on the market, was correctly implemented but there was a significant delay (7 days from the date of sampling) in the availability of test results (see also paragraph 60).

Significant delays in obtaining laboratory test results for some biotoxins lower the effectiveness of weekly monitoring, delays area closures and can increase the risk of placing unsafe product on the market.

The audit team noted significant delays in the issuing of laboratory test results to both autonomous communities, requiring often four to six days for ASP and lipophilic toxins and seven to ten working days in the case of PSP, instead of the three days commonly needed. The legally required, Art. 37(4)(d) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, timely delivery of test results is not achieved. Conclusions on laboratories

recommendations.text: To ensure designation of national reference laboratories for biotoxins and E.coli, as required by Article 100 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, covering primary production and that this designation includes the tasks and responsibilities of Article 101 of that same Regulatio

citations.text: The competent authority has not designated National Reference Laboratories either for E. coli or for biotoxins testing of live bivalve molluscs sampled at primary production level for the monitoring of production areas, contrary to the requirements of Article 100(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

Due to the above currently there is no coordination of activities of the official laboratories involved in testing of live bivalve molluscs sampled at primary production level. Nor organisation of proficiency testing and respective follow up for those laboratories or of any of the other tasks under the responsibility of a national reference laboratory, contrary to the required by Article 101 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

The absence of national reference laboratories for biotoxins and E.coli at primary production, with the consequent gap on their tasks and responsibilities, is an important shortcoming in a control system for which laboratory performance has high impact.

responses.response: To ensure designation of national reference laboratories for biotoxins and E.coli, as required by Article 100 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, covering primary production and that this designation includes the tasks and responsibilities of Article 101 of that same Regulation. Recommendation based on conclusion No 61. Associated findings Nos 44 and 45.

recommendations.text: To ensure that laboratories carrying out testing on samples for official controls are: all designated, in line with the requirements of Article 37 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625; designated with a detailed description of arrangements to ensure efficient and effective coordination and collaboration with the competent authority. Including, in particular, timely delivery of all test results, provisions for competent authority access and supervision to verify respect of the obligations of official laboratories, as required by Articles 37(3), (4) and 39(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625; and subject to audits organised by the competent authorities, and/or the accreditation assessment from the accreditation body promptly provided to the competent authorities, to allow the competent authority to act immediately as required by Article 39(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: Both autonomous communities started designating official control laboratories, as required by Article 37(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, in 2021. Not all involved laboratories are designated yet, namely for one autonomous community in relation to chemical contaminants (see also paragraph 52).

Nevertheless, in both autonomous communities the official designations and/or contractual obligations do not include sufficient details to fulfil the requirement in Article 37(3)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 (and in the MAPA procedure) for `arrangements necessary to ensure efficient and effective coordination between the laboratory and the competent authorities'. For example none of those designations include: a maximum response time for any of the different analysis performed, failing to address the requirement in Article 37(4)(d) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 to deliver results in a timely manner (see also paragraph 60); an indication of any supervisory activities (beyond maintaining accreditation) and right of access by the competent authority, as required by Article 5(1)(g) and (h) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

With regard to supervision of the designated laboratories, both autonomous communities decided that audits by the national accreditation body (Entidad Nacional de Acreditación, ENAC) address all the supervisory needs for that designation. However: accreditation audits cover exclusively accreditation requirements from EN ISO/IEC 17025 or from the accredited testing methodology. Official designation requirements (Article 38 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625) or contractual obligations, such as a defined maximum response time and official access to documents would not be covered; the competent authorities plan to verify the accreditation status of the designated laboratories but not to obtain the accreditation assessments produced by ENAC, contrary to the required in Article 39(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625; in one autonomous community the internal audits programme can include laboratories but the criteria indicated for such audits would not address the points above. These gaps can result in the inability of the competent authorities to detect failures from the designated laboratories and immediately withdraw that designation, completely or partially, contrary to the required by Article 39(2) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. 5.2.1 Laboratories for microbiology and chemical contaminants

Claiming confidentiality concerns, the laboratory that analyses monitoring samples for PSP, and part of the samples for ASP and lipophilic toxins, refused to provide several documents to the audit team (such as standard operating procedures) even after receiving 13 precise legal details of the confidentiality obligations of the audit team. This raises doubts on the competent authorities legal powers, and procedures, to perform official controls and have access to documents, required by Article 5(1)(g) and (h) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The analyses are performed using the EU reference methods, established in Article 60 of Regulation (EU) 2019/627, and are all accredited by ENAC, as required in Article 37(5)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The laboratory has in principle appropriate equipment for the analyses performed. The laboratory has validated the analytical methods. The audit team assessed the validation process of one of these methods and noted that the laboratory concluded to a successful validation even for the non-complying criteria. It analyses all the legislated compounds, but the very limited number of documents that the laboratory agreed to provide had insufficient information to allow the audit team to assess the performance of the method. The assessment of the documents provided generated certain doubts that the procedures followed produce accurate results. This laboratory participates in proficiency testing once every five years for each group of marine biotoxin (most recently for lipophilic toxins in 2016 and for PSP and ASP in 2018). Results seem in general to be satisfactory for lipophilic toxins and ASP. However, for PSP there is a significant number of questionable results, for which a repetition was carried out but not an investigation that led to a conclusive explanation of these results, which raise doubts on the accuracy, and therefore reliability of PSP testing results.

The designation of official control laboratories does not yet include all relevant laboratories, and is lacking in details to ensure timely provision of results, and efficient and effective coordination and supervision. As a consequence laboratory underperformance or failures may be detected with delay, or go undetected, negatively impacting on the quality of official controls.

One of the laboratories for biotoxins could be evaluated and was determined to be providing reliable results for the ASP and lipophilic toxins testing it performs. The other laboratory could not be fully evaluated and the data received causes doubts on PSP method validation and accuracy, and on PSP proficiency testing. Therefore, quality and reliability of the testing it performs is doubtful.

recommendations.text: To ensure that laboratories performing E.coli testing do so in a way that provides results with the precision required by Articles 54(3) and 55(2) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627, so as to allow the competent authority to decide on re-classification or closure of production areas in line with Article 62(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627.

citations.text: Sample collection and handling, and E. coli testing procedures as described in the laboratory procedures are generally satisfactory (see also paragraph 50). However, the number of dilutions made during the analyses of samples is not enough to provide an exact E.coli most probable number when results are > 18 000 per 100 g of flesh and intravalvular liquid. Therefore, in the limited cases this happened it was not possible to determine if these areas exceeded the limit of 46 000 per 100 g of flesh and intravalvular liquid established in Articles 54(3) and 55(2) of Regulation (EU) 2019/627 for class B and C areas (although there were no class C production areas in the autonomous communities visited). Therefore, decisions made in these cases about reclassification and/or closure of production areas were not adequately informed. b) For the presence of toxin-producing plankton in water

The few cases where the results of the microbiological monitoring of class B production areas do not provide an exact result (number) pose a challenge to the decisions for reclassification and/or closure of these production areas.

Both laboratories involved in microbiological testing met during the audit provided documentation showing that the testing methods used for: E. coli and Salmonella are the required EU reference methods (respectively, EN/ISO 16649-3 and EN ISO 6579-1), and are accredited and their correct performance is supported by participation in proficiency testing with satisfactory results; the standard operating procedures for E. coli testing are in line with requirements but the number of dilutions made during the analyses is not enough to provide an exact 12 number when results are > 18 000 per 100 g of flesh and intravalvular liquid (see also paragraph 12); one of the laboratories has two E. coli testing acceptance criteria that are not in line with those of ISO 16649-3 (namely, sample temperature > 10ºC and start of testing beyond 24h from time of sampling). Nevertheless, it has also performed the required validation studies that satisfactorily demonstrate this divergence in acceptance criteria has no negative impact on test results.

Laboratories for microbiology and for chemical contaminants perform the required methods and provide timely results. However, in a few cases, E.coli testing provides insufficient detail to allow the competent authorities to decide correctly if a production area requires a downgrade of classification, or even closure, to prevent unsafe product from entering the market.

citations.text: The National Contingency Plan for Xf (see section 5.3) includes the survey protocol. It describes in detail the procedures for risk based surveys, including the survey period, sampling priorities and practice, laboratory tests and communication of the results. The protocol is based on the guidance provided by the Xf Survey Card of the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA), which are adapted to the specific Spanish conditions. The following priorities are set for inspections and sampling: · Nurseries and garden centres in general; · Areas surrounding nurseries, garden centres and DAs, routes from DAs; · Valencia coastline; · A minimum number of samples from Citrus, Vitis, Olea, Prunus and Quercus sp. plantations in relation to their total surface area in the region; · Plantations which were established recently (2-4 years) with material originating from areas considered as risky; · Places/areas with favourable climate for Xf; · Collection sites for vectors.

The survey protocol of the National Contingency Plan provides comprehensive guidance for the ACs for Xf surveys outside the DAs. However, no mechanism exists to verify whether the surveys are risk based and whether they are implemented consistently and effectively.

recommendations.text: Ensure that the Spanish contingency plan for Xylella fastidiosa deals with all the provisions required by Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2020/1201, in particular concerning the procedures for making additional resources available as necessary to deal with possible outbreaks.

citations.text: The regional autonomy established in the Spanish Constitution means that the National Contingency Plan cannot specify the minimum resources for controls that each AC shall make available, including procedures for making additional resources available as necessary. Similarly, it cannot specify rules detailing how to identify the owners of plants subject to measures or how to notify the order of removal and powers to access private properties. These are specifically required by Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2020/1201. These issues may be dealt at AC level and annexed to the national contingency plan. However, in the absence of appropriate regional measures, compliance with EU rules may not be ensured.

The National Contingency Plan was prepared and updated according to the provisions of the EU legislation and provides a general framework for the implementation of the necessary actions in the case of an outbreak. However, it does not contain specific provisions required by the EU legislation, which are within the competency of the 12 ACCAs. The absence of information on how these provisions are addressed by the regions calls into question the ability of ACs to control any future outbreaks.

recommendations.text: Ensure that all plants, listed in Article 7(1) of Regulation (EU) 2020/1201, are immediately removed in each infected zone of the demarcated area in Alicante. In particular, ensure that measures are taken addressing any complications that prevent, hinder or delay eradication, including laboratory capacities, administrative procedures and accessibility of the locations, as requested by Article 11 of that Regulation. to 51.

citations.text: The audit team noted that the laboratories of the ACs Balearic Islands and Madrid have sufficient capacity to test all official plant and insect samples collected in the AC. Although the capacity of the official laboratory of AC Valencia has increased since the last audit, it is still not sufficient for testing all official samples within the timeframe technically necessary. In particular, in 2020, there were substantial delays during testing plant samples from the DA. The ACCAs stated that requirements for personal distancing in the laboratory during the COVID-19 pandemic and a shortage of PCR reagents contributed to the delay. For 2021 the delays decreased, however the laboratory still needed on average 18 days to complete the tests. The ACCAs, met by the audit team did not have defined testing deadlines or arrangement to prioritise high-risk samples. In 8 particular, in AC Valencia these issues contributed to the long delays between sampling and the removal of plants (see section 5.5.2) Conclusions on the organisational aspects of the plant health controls

The ACCA stated that in the DA Alicante : · Since 2017, 4,694 plants were tested positive. After the establishment of a new IZ, the first priority is the removal of the positive tested plant as it is the proven source of any further spread by the vector. Until the time of the audit, 97.7% of the positives (4,588 plants) have been removed. In 2021, the average time elapsed between the test result and the removal of plants was 89 days. · For the removal of plants listed in Article 7(1)(a)to(e) of Regulation (EU) 2020/1201 (i.e. specified plants other than the positive), priorities are applied. The DA, where numerous overlapping IZs are surrounded by a common BZ of 2.5 km radius, was divided into priority zones (see figure VI). To achieve the best level of protection against the spread of the disease out of the DA with the resources allocated to the ACCA; · The 2.5 km "outer" part is drawn around the IZs, which are located closest to the border of the DA (green stripe ­ see figure VI), has the highest priority. If any positive is found there, a new IZ is established, and the eradication measures are completed as soon as technically possible; · The rest of the BZ is divided into sections of 5 km (red, orange and yellow stripes). The further the zone is from the border of the DA, the lower priority it has, and consequently the longer delays in the completion of the plant removal. In 2021, the average time needed for the plant removal was 94 days for the priority 1 IZs, 120 days for the priority 2 and 150 days for the priority 3. These figures relate only to IZs where the removal of plants was completed by the time the audit (see table III); · The removal of specified plants was completed in 43.7% of the territory of the IZs, established since 2017, covering an area of 1,150 ha. Even in the highest priority area 77% of the plants to be felled had been removed at the time of the audit, while it was only 18% in the lowest priority parts of the DA. Although in the IZs established in 2020 in the highest priority area the level of completion is satisfactory, the non- completion of the work in the IZs established earlier significantly reduces the impact of those efforts (see table III). In the areas of second and third priority the works were completed in a low or very low percentage of the IZs and in the vast majority of the cases with significant delays; · At least 771 IZs were revisited, in order to identify and remove the plants, which were qualified as specified plant for Xf subspecies multiplex after the plant removals in those IZs was completed. 18 Figure VI. In the IZs of the DA Alicante, only a part of the specified plants were removed and in the vast majority of the cases with substantial delays. The delayed completion of the works and the system of prioritisation of the removals are not in line with the EU legislation. The applied measures do not sufficiently control the spread of the disease and cannot result in eradication. There is a pronounced risk that the bacterium continues to spread within the DA and a there is a risk of further natural spread from the DA into the neighbouring areas. 21

audits.title: Official controls on animals and goods entering the European Union and verification of compliance of border control posts with European Union requirements

recommendations.text: To ensure that documented control procedures are updated as appropriate. Legal basis: Article 12(3)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 To ensure that designated border control posts comply with the minimum requirements for border control posts appropriate for the categories of animals and goods for which the border control posts have been designated, including the commercial storage facilities which may be used for identity and physical checks on products of non-animal origin, and that those BCP facilities are maintained and cleaned appropriately.

citations.text: The two exceptions concerned the MS protocol for performing physical checks on food of animal origin and the protocol for sampling on food of animal origin for laboratory testing, which were issued in 2011 and 2015 respectively, which had not been updated in line with Article 12(2) of the OCR.

The audit team also noted that the guidance for the selection of items or packages provided in those two protocols was not in line with the percentage of items or packages in a consignment of products of animal origin and the maximum number of items or packages specified in point 4 (b) of Annex II to Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/2130. Similarly, the guidance for the selection of items or packages for the performance of identity checks of products of animal origin, was not in line with Article 3(3) of the same Regulation (See also finding 64).

However, the lack of updated documented procedures for performing physical checks and sampling of consignments of goods of animal origin, internal audits and lack of deadlines for completion of corrective actions have an adverse impact on the overall effectiveness of the organisation of official controls on animals and goods entering the EU, and its compliance with Union legislation.

The audit team observed official controls of consignments of food of animal origin during their visits to the BCPs of Madrid Airport and Bilbao Port and noted that the documentary checks were carried out in line with Article 2 of Regulation 2019/2130. The selection of the items or packages for identity checks and the samples for examination was based on the documented procedures detailed in section 5.1.4 above. One percent of the number of items of a consignment was selected for checks, however the selected number of items or packages was less than the minimum specified by Article 3(3) and point 4 (b) of Annex II to Regulation 2019/2130. 5.2.4.3 Checks on consignments of goods of non-animal origin

recommendations.text: Legal basis: Article 64(3) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and Articles 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014 Recommendation based on conclusions: 89 and 90 Associated findings:77, 79, 80, 82, 83, 85, 87 and 88 To ensure that the Common Health Entry Document is duly completed by the competent authorities, to record the outcome of official controls performed and any decisions taken on that basis.
recommendations.legal_basis: Article 64(3) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 and Articles 3, 4, 5, 6 and 8 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014

citations.text: The MS informed the audit team that certain BCPs, which that had been designated and listed for categories of goods referred to in Article 47(1), (d), (e) or (f), had been designated for the performance of documentary checks only. At such BCPs, consignments are subsequently transferred to a designated control point when identity and physical checks are required. The seven BCPs and 10 inspection centres concerned, which are indicated in the published list (18) do not have the required minimum facilities for the performance of identity checks and physical checks, including sampling of the categories of goods for which they have been designated, which is not in line with Article 64(3) of the OCR and Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. As indicated in the above table, BCP A Coruña is one such BCP.

The audit team noted during their initial assessment of the BCP Bilbao port, and confirmed during the visit to the BCP, that the cold storage facilities for food of non- animal origin were restricted to a single room for both frozen and chilled goods, which is not in line with Article 3(1)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014.

The audit team also found during the visit to the BCP Bilbao port that the unloading rooms and storage rooms were not fitted with the walls and floors that are easy to clean and disinfected, and that the unloading room did not have adequate drainage, which is not in line with Article 3(2) of that Regulation. Some storage rooms, and part of the (18) See: https://www.sanidad.gob.es/profesionales/saludPublica/sanidadExterior/controlesSanitarios/instaAlmacen/ home.htm [in Spanish] 17 unloading area, were not clean, with presence of dust, mould, spider webs and dirt. In addition, during a period of heavy rainfall, rainwater flooded into one part of the unloading area. The competent authorities' verification control reports had identified the poor maintenance of the facilities, however a deadline for corrective actions to address those issues had not been provided. The reports had also not identified the lack of cleaning and disinfection of the facilities.

The audit team noted that at the BCP Madrid airport, there are no storage facilities for chilled and frozen categories of products of non-animal origin for which it is designated, which is not in line with Article 3(1)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014. In addition, the competent authorities informed the audit team that, in exceptional cases, it permits physical checks on consignments of products of non-animal origin to be carried out at commercial storage facilities. However, the audit team noted that those facilities did not have the required inspection rooms or areas, which is not in line with Article 3(11) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014.

The audit team visited the facilities at the inspection centre Iberia as part of the BCP Madrid airport, and noted a number of shortcomings that were similar to findings identified by MAPA and the MS as a result of their audits and verification checks, detailed in section 5.1.6 above, and which therefore, had not been appropriately addressed by the operator. Those shortcomings concerned: a. the cross-flow of movements of animals and goods due to the unloading area being shared for certain categories of animals and goods, and the facilities for products of animal origin, category POA-NHC listed in 6(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014 not forming one integrated and whole working unit, which is not in line with Articles 5(3), 5(5) and 6(2) of that Regulation, nor Article 64(3)(h) of the OCR; b. the housing of consignments of live insects transported at chilled temperatures in the storage rooms for chilled products of animal origin, category POA-NHC; which is not in line with Article 64(3)(b) of the OCR; c. the use of storage rooms dedicated for products of animal origin not intended for human consumption for the storage of other goods and animals including live insects intended for export, Union origin goods and medical devices and medicines, which is not in line with Article 6(3) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014; and d. the poor maintenance and cleaning of the facilities throughout the inspection centre, which is not in line with Article 4(4) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014 and Article 64(3)(i) of the OCR. 18

The MS informed the audit team that an action plan was received following their supervision check of the inspection centre Iberia carried out in June 2021, which had identified shortcomings in the facilities for products of animal origin for human consumption, including the flooring of the inspection rooms and refrigerated storage room. The MS confirmed that their assessment of the plan was sent to the inspection centre on 14 June 2022, requiring that the planned action be completed within one month.

The audit team assessed the facilities at the inspection centre Progeco as part of the BCP Vigo port based on the completed assessment table and supporting documents provided by the MS and noted that the although the inspection centre is designated for products of non-animal origin intended for human consumption with three temperature regimes (ambient, chilled and frozen), it has only storage rooms for chilled and frozen products respectively, which is not in line with Article 64(3)(b) of the OCR nor Article 3(1)(c) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1014.

During the audit, the MS provided an updated assessment table and supporting documents, indicating that an additional temperature-controlled container would be installed on-site, with a deadline for completion by October 2022. 19 Conclusions on the compliance of border control posts with minimum requirements

The majority of the BCPs and inspection centres thereof evaluated during the audit were not fully compliant with the minimum requirements for BCPs, for one or more of the categories of animals and goods for which they had been designated. The lack of minimum facilities for controls on consignments of food of non-animal origin is a systemic deficiency in certain BCPs.

The competent authorities have taken immediate action to address deficiencies identified at certain BCPs and inspection centres, however in the remaining BCPs, the competent authorities cannot guarantee the appropriate handling of animals and goods, the proper verification of compliance of those animals and goods and the prevention of the risk of cross-contamination.

citations.text: The 2019 and 2020 national residue monitoring plans included relevant species and commodities except for farmed game and crustaceans. They covered all of the substance groups required and complied with the sampling levels and frequencies laid down in EU law (13). The number of samples planned to be taken in each of the 17 Autonomous Communities is largely based on their respective production volumes for all commodities and animal species, which is in line with EU requirements (14), with the exception of farmed game where only five samples were planned for in 2019 and 2020, respectively, and none in 2021 and 2022. In addition, for farmed crustaceans, no samples were planned to be taken during those years, which is contrary to EU law (15) (16).

With regards to farmed game, there is no clear overview at national level on the number of farms producing farmed game and what the production volumes per species may be in order to guide the planning of the residue monitoring plan for this commodity. The audit team identified several farms in Spain where farmed game, as (8) Programa nacional de control de investigación de residuos de medicamentos veterinarios y otras sustancias (PNIR) en producción primaria. The animals (deer) on these farms are kept in large enclosures, are individually identified, fed, treated with veterinary medicinal products, such as vaccines or anthelmintics, and are sent for slaughter to commercial slaughterhouses or are slaughtered in on-farm slaughter facilities. The audit team also identified two farms keeping ostriches, batches of which are sent regularly to a slaughterhouse. The competent authority stated during the audit that they intend to include farmed game in the 2023 residue monitoring plan (see finding 21).

With regard to farmed crustaceans, the audit team found that several species are being produced for human consumption, albeit with small production volumes: common ditch shrimp (Palaemon varians) ­ estimated production 240 tonnes in 2018 and 180 tonnes in 2019), white leg shrimp (Penaeus vannamei) ­ estimated production 7 tonnes in 2018 and 2019), tiger shrimp (Penaeus japonicas) and freshwater shrimp (Macrobrachium carcinus).

For aquaculture finfish, both the national annual residue monitoring plan (18) and the residue monitoring plan sampling instructions of the multi-annual control plan (8) stipulated that samples which are to be analysed for Group A substances, should not be taken from juvenile fish (alevines). This is not in line with the EU requirements (19), as samples for Group A substances should be taken at all stages of farming. The MAPA representatives sent during the audit an e-mail to all Autonomous Communities a message to the effect that aquaculture samples, to be tested for Group A substances, shall be collected at all stages of farming and that this change should be implemented as soon as possible. Existing instructions in Catalonia provided the option to collect samples for the analysis of substances from Group A at different stages of the animal production cycle. Equally evidence was received that the Autonomous Communities of Galicia and Valencia plan to implement this change already in 2022 and the Autonomous Communities of Navarra and Aragón in 2023.

With the exception of farmed game, aquacultured crustaceans and Group A substances in aquaculture, the planning of residue monitoring is comprehensive, timely and takes relevant risk factors into account, thus contributing to the effectiveness of controls on residues. recommendations.text: To update the contingency plan(s) to ensure high levels of preparedness and the ability to launch a rapid response, and that regularly validate it and test it (e.g., simulation exercises, recent epidemics, etc) in line with the analysis of data from the epizootic in 2022 and the gaps identified as a result, to allow: - The quick identification, contact details and responsibilities of the services (including delegated bodies) which would be involved during an emergency. - The performance of complete epidemiological investigations, including the identification and investigation of epidemiological contacts, the timely veterinary visits and sampling. - The adequate and timely depopulation and disposal of infected birds. Article 29 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625; Articles 3(1)(a), 13, 43, 45, 54, 57, 61(1)(b), 62, 65(1)(a) and (b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429; and Articles12(1)(a) and (b),15, 17, 18, 19, 25, 26 and points A and B of Annex IV of the Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687. Recommendation based on main conclusions No. 36, 77 and

citations.text: For certain information not included in these three documents and in the national coordinated plan for alerts on animal health, MAPA requires the authorities of the regions to elaborate any necessary instructions reflecting their regional information and needs in case of an emergency (i.e., regional communication protocols in case of crisis, human resources available and their deployment in case of a crisis, protocol for the slaughter of birds of establishments in the restricted zones, resolutions on burial, exceptional movements, restocking procedures and compensations). It also requires the national disease crisis centre to approve the regional contingency plans. Six Autonomous Communities out of 17 hold such a document.

The audit team noticed some examples of missing information in the contingency plans at Autonomous Community level: a. Contact emergency telephone numbers for the general public and operators to notify any suspicion (including holidays and weekends). b. Framework of cooperative communications with veterinary services at regional level, designated bodies or natural persons, relevant stakeholders, and local designated laboratories. c. Human resources and specific roles of all animal health professionals who should be involved in the implementation of the control and eradication measures. d. Location of local disease crisis centres, list of facilities and equipment required in case of an emergency. Responsibilities for keeping this equipment up to date. 6 Arrangements for the deployment of equipment and personnel from other provinces or Autonomous Communities. e. Specific depopulation and disposal arrangements in each Autonomous Community. f. Emergency funds at Autonomous Community level. Due to the unavailability of contingency plans or their incompleteness at regional level, in most cases there were no records of some of the necessary information to ensure a high level of disease awareness and preparedness and the ability to launch a rapid response to an emergency of HPAI. This is not in line with Article 43 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429.

Since 2019, the authorities conducted several simulation exercises concerning responses to epizootic outbreaks. No simulation exercises specifically relating to HPAI have been carried out. Some of the Autonomous Communities most affected by the last HPAI epidemic in 2022, did not have a written contingency plan with the regional information necessary for rapid response in case of emergency. The audit team did not see any evidence that this last epidemic led to any updates on their contingency plans' procedures. The competent authorities do not sufficiently ensure that simulation exercises concerning the contingency plans are carried out regularly or at appropriate intervals to verify their functionality. All this is not in line with Article 45 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429. Early detection

In the event of suspicion of HPAI in poultry, the competent authority set restrictions on the suspected establishments without delay. However, the initial veterinary investigation and sampling was delayed in several cases. Although in most cases, informal communications with the national disease crisis centre occurred immediately, there were delays in the regional authorities conducting the required investigation to confirm or rule out the presence of HPAI. This is not in line with Article 54 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429.

Epidemiological investigations were generally done at the time of sampling. They were regularly incomplete. In most cases, the official veterinarians did not include in the investigation report the likely time that the infection was already present in the establishment, the likely origin of the infection or the full list of direct and indirect contacts. This is not in line with Art 54(1)(g) and 57(1) Regulation (EU) 2016/429.

Identification of epidemiological contacts (tracings back and forth) were regularly delegated to the private sector. However, the audit team rarely saw any evidence that the authorities followed up on those tracings and applied control measures on possible contact establishments. This is not in line with Articles 57(1) and 62 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 and Articles 17, 18 and 19 of the Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687.

The standard procedure does not include, within the minimum information required during the preparation process, the need to plan such depopulation in such a way as to avoid any risk of spreading the relevant category A disease agent during and after killing. The audit team saw strong evidence that some of the secondary cases, could be due to airborne transmission of virus during depopulation of the nearby primary case. The dates on which the secondary case could have been infected, coincided with the dates when the depopulation of the primary case was carried out.5 This is not in line with Article 12(1)(a) and (b) of Delegated regulation (EU) 2020/687.

The authorities ordered the depopulation of suspect cases during the epidemic, sometimes without waiting for their confirmation. The competent authority had already identified that they had an important shortage of resources and personnel during the epidemic to timely implement the depopulation of cases. Nine of the 38 outbreaks (24%) did not need depopulations measures because all birds were already dead due to the disease by the time the depopulation could be implemented6 (Table C). This is not in line with Articles 13(1)(a) and 61(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429. Table C Days from suspicion to depopulation (source- ADIS) Days Number of outbreaks (%) <5 12 (32) 5-7 9 (24) >7 8 (21) No depopulation 9 (24) 5 In its response to the draft report, the competent authority stated that "use of additional slaughter techniques that prevent or reduce that dispersion route has been studied and is being assessed, in particular gas killing within production houses." 6 In its response to the draft report, the competent authority stated that this "was due to the high mortality rate among the species present on the farm given the strain circulating. 14 Total 38 (100)

The authorities identified logistics as the main difficulties for the disposal of dead birds and products, due to the concentration -in a short period of time- of outbreaks with a high number of birds. The authorities encountered lack of processing plant capacity, shortage of trucks for the transfer of manure and dead birds and big difficulties for establishing dedicated burial sites for mass disposal of birds (lack of machinery and sometimes rain). This is not in line with Articles 3(1)(a) and 61(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429.

The audit team noted significant delays between depopulation or disposal of infected birds and products and the subsequent implementation of preliminary cleaning and disinfection measures. In 38% (14) of the outbreaks, the preliminary cleaning and disinfection was carried out 10 to 47 days after the disposal of dead birds. This is not in line with 62(1) and 65 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429 and Article 15 and points A and B of Annex IV of the Delegated regulation (EU) 2020/687 2020/687.

The EU reference laboratory provided the authorities with a phylogenetic analysis that helped understand from which areas in Europe the virus was introduced. The competent authority did not provide any evidence to the audit team of other epidemiological analysis that has been carried out on the 2022 epidemic to identify possible risk factors that contributed to the introduction and the spread of diseases and thus, to develop and implement better informed policies on prevention and early detection accordingly. The authorities have not identified and addressed their gaps in the response to the HPAI epidemic in 2022 and thus they have not used the lessons learnt during the epizootic, to improve the national and regional contingency plans. This is not in line with Article 43 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429.

responses.response: To ensure that each Autonomous Community has a contingency plan adapted to its reality, services and needs, which is regularly validated and tested (e.g., simulation exercises, recent epidemics, etc) and allows: - The quick identification, contact details and responsibilities of the services (including delegated bodies) which would be involved during an emergency. - The performance of complete epidemiological investigations, including the identification and investigation of epidemiological contacts, the timely veterinary visits and sampling. - The adequate and timely depopulation and disposal of infected birds. Article 29 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625; Articles 3(1)(a), 13, 43, 45, 54, 57, 61(1)(b), 62, 65(1)(a) and (b) of Regulation (EU) 2016/429; and Articles12(1)(a) and (b),15, 17, 18, 19, 25, 26 and points A and B of Annex IV of the Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687. Recommendation based on main conclusions No. 36, and 80 and associated findings No. 16,17, 18, 48, 50, 51, 52, 53, 54, 57,59, 64, 65, 69 and 70.

recommendations.text: To improve the early detection system for HPAI and the authorities' abilities to stop the spread of the disease from wild birds to poultry by implementing measures aimed at: - Ensuring regular testing of dead and sick poultry in high-risk areas when the risk has increased due to cases detected at national or European level of either poultry and/or wild birds in high-risk areas - Reducing the delays in getting laboratory results for the samples taken from wild birds. Section 3 of Annex II and Section 2, paragraph 2(a)of Annex II of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/689 Recommendation based on main conclusion No. 38 and 18

citations.text: For the early detection in wild birds, the veterinary authorities also worked closely with the environmental departments and conservation agencies and stakeholders. The audit 7 team considered the number and location of samples taken, both for active and passive surveillance of wild birds adequate and in line with high-risk areas and high-risk periods of introduction of the infection. In 2021, the NRL in Spain processed 1,225 samples from wild birds, of which two were positive. In 2022, there were 3,040 such samples of which 144 were positives.

There were major delays in confirming the infection (Table A) for the positive samples taken either by active or passive surveillance of wild birds (172 from September 2020 to April 2023). Nearly 99% of all cases were confirmed more than three days after sampling, and 50% of them were confirmed two weeks after sampling. The timescales were due to the involvement of two laboratories in the diagnosis of the disease ­ the Autonomous Community laboratory where the generic Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test is carried out and the national reference laboratory where the virus is subtyped and its pathogenicity determined. The authorities explained that in many of those cases, confirmation was not considered urgent because cases in wild birds had already been confirmed in the same areas. Table A Days from Suspicion to Confirmation of avian influenza in wild birds -Sep 2020 to April 23- source ADIS Days Number of positives (%) 0 to 3 2 (1.2) 4 to 7 26 (15) 8 to 10 24 (14) 11 to 14 32 (19) >15 up to 75 86 (50) no date 1 (0.6) Total 172 (100)

The authorities took samples of dead and sick wild birds reported under passive surveillance in the same areas where the first cases of poultry were confirmed a few days after (January and February 2022). However, the fact that those wild birds' samples were processed and confirmed several days after the poultry cases were detected, prevented the competent authority from implementing the enhanced surveillance in poultry, that should have been triggered after confirmation of the infection in wild birds. This is not in line with Section 2, paragraph 2(a)of Annex II of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2021/689.

During passive and active surveillance, the NRL detected six positives to avian influenza virus other than H5 or H7 in 2020, 43 positives to other than H5 or H7 avian influenza virus in 2021 and, 67 non H5 and no H7 avian influenza virus in 2022. All these were detected in wild birds. Laboratory capacity- Diagnostics used for general early detection.

In the event of suspicion of HPAI in poultry, the competent authority set restrictions on the suspected establishments without delay. However, the initial veterinary investigation and sampling was delayed in several cases. Although in most cases, informal communications with the national disease crisis centre occurred immediately, there were delays in the regional authorities conducting the required investigation to confirm or rule out the presence of HPAI. This is not in line with Article 54 of Regulation (EU) 2016/429.
