recommendations.text: To ensure that adequate risk assessment is carried out and properly documented before granting movement derogations from restricted zones due to cases of HPAI in line with relevant EU requirements. Article 28(1) and 43(1) of Commission Delegated Regulation 2020/687. Recommendation based on main conclusion No. 78 and 19

citations.text: The authorities granted a total of 752 movement derogations from restricted zones to free areas. The great majority (740) were direct movements to slaughter. The remaining 12 movements were granted from hatcheries in the restricted zone to other neighbouring areas outside the restricted zone. 12

These movements were carried out in line with the majority of requirements, e.g., clinical inspections, testing, sealed transports, best available routes to avoid cross contamination, and they were all under official supervision. But the audit team saw evidence that the authorities did not carry out an adequate risk assessment before they authorised those movements considering all relevant EU requirements. There is no protocol or instructions to carry out this risk assessment taking into account relevant legislation. This is not in line with Article 28(1) and 43(1) of the Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687. E.g. during this epidemic in Spain, there was evidence that some neighbouring establishments to a confirmed case, were likely infected during the time of the depopulation and disposal of infected animals. However, one of the movements' derogations to slaughterhouse was from a turkey establishment located near an infected premises (approximately 500m). The authorities allowed this movement to take place just one day after suspicion and three days after depopulation of the close-by infected establishment. This was a high-risk movement, and the authorities did not provide evidence of a risk assessment before granted this movement derogation (see finding 64)4. Laboratory capacity in emergency situations

responses.response: To ensure that an effective risk assessment is carried out before granting movement derogations from restricted zones due to cases of HPAI. Article 28(1) and 43(1) of Commission Delegated Regulation 2020/687. Recommendation based on main conclusion No. 81 and associated finding No. 57.

audits.title: evaluate the authorisation and controls of marketing and use of Plant Protection Products

recommendations.text: To ensure that the results of monitoring activities carried out for the purpose of Article 8 of Directive 2000/60/EC are taken into account when establishing the frequency of risk-based official controls on the marketing and use of PPPs, as required by Article 24(2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: With regard to the risk-based planning criteria the programme requires the regional CAs to choose a number of risk criteria from a list. For agricultural holdings, it contains the following: the result of previous control, whether checks have been carried out in the last 4 years, the size of the holding, the toxicity and the overall quantity of the PPPs used, the reliability of own controls, the type of crops cultivated (from a food safety perspective), the location of the holding (proximity to source of contamination for the crops) and other criteria which may be added by the autonomous communities11. For PPP service provid- ers, the risk criteria are the following: the result of previous control, the toxicity of the PPPs used, the overall quantity of the PPPs used and the size of the treated areas, and oth- er criteria which may be added by the Autonomous communities. The audit team noted that among the afore-mentioned risk criteria, the results of monitoring activities of PPP residues carried out for the purpose of Article 8 of Directive 2000/60/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council12 are not mentioned in the national programme. This is not 10 The Decree establishes and regulates also the Digital Agricultural Farm Notebook 11 In its response to the draft report, the competent authority stated that: `The SIEX database, which includes the REAs of all Autonomous Communities, includes information on the operator, the location of the holdings and the crops, and whether the operator sells directly to consumers or carries out own checks. This application au- tomatically generates a first risk categorisation for each holding, taking into account the risk categorisation of each crop (based on several criteria such as iRASFF alerts, results of controls on hygiene control programmes for agricultural primary production and use of plant protection products, non-compliances detected under AE- SAN's Pesticide Residues Control Programme and other combinations of factors) and the area under cultivation. Operators are required to update information once a year to reflect the crops they have'. 12 Also called the `Water Framework Directive' 14 in line with article 24(2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

In CLM, the regional control programmes for 2022 and 2023 reviewed by the audit team included annual controls of 550 agricultural holdings. In both programmes, they were planned across risk categories in line with the percentages specified in the national pro- gramme. The criteria used to classify agricultural holdings were essentially the crops cul- tivated and the size of the holding, therefore, in line, as well, with the indications provid- ed in the national programme, although not in line with Article 24 (2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 (see paragraph 53).

In VC, the 2022 and 2023 regional control programmes on agricultural holdings set a target of 314 annual controls and the specific number for each province. In both pro- grammes, the controls were planned across risk categories in line with the percentages specified in the national programme. The main criteria to classify agricultural holdings were the crops cultivated, the size of the holding and its location with respect to the risk of nitrate loss, therefore, in line, as well, with the indications provided in the national programme, although not in line with article 24 (2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 (see paragraph 53).

Comprehensive national control programmes on the marketing and use of PPPs are in place and are updated at central level regularly, in agreement with the various autono- mous communities. These control programmes, which include risk-based plans for PPP formulation analyses and are underpinned by advanced IT databases, provide good guid- ance and support for the regional CAs to plan their controls on a risk basis. The autono- mous communities reviewed follow in general these national programmes and plan their controls, prioritising operators with higher risk, and this helps a better functioning of the system of official controls. Nonetheless, the results from the monitoring of PPP residues in water bodies are not taking into account, which is not in line with EU requirements and reduces to an extent the efficacy of the programme. Delegation of certain tasks Findings

recommendations.text: To ensure that samples of PPPs are analysed to determine the presence of unac- ceptable co-formulants set out in Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 and the content of impurities whose maximum content is established in the ap- proval of relevant active substances, as referred to Article 6(b) of the same Regu- lation. Such controls are required by Article 24(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: Samples for PPP formulations are analysed by three accredited laboratories all designed by the relevant CAs. The main one is in Madrid, which is the national reference laborato- ry for PPP formulation. Catalunya and Andalusia avail of their own laboratories. These laboratories carry out analyses of a wide range active substances, more than 240, which are included in the scope of accreditation. However, the audit team noted that neither im- purities nor co-formulants are analysed. Consequently, the CAs are unable to verify the absence of unacceptable co-formulants in PPPs set out in Annex III to Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009 and cannot determine whether certain impurities do not exceed the maxi- mum content permitted in the approval of the relevant active substances as provided in Article 6(b) of Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009. This is also not in line with Article 24(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Representatives from the central CAs stated that this is a general problem in the EU because there are no validated methods at EU level for the de- tection of these substances14. 14 In its response to the draft report, the competent authority stated that: `During the audit process, the Spanish central authorities repeatedly pointed out the need to set up a European reference laboratory and thus to comply with Article 92 of Regulation (EC) No 2017/635 on official controls. The aim of this request when setting up this European laboratory is to respond to the need of the various national laboratories to develop master tech- niques for this subject, as well as the possibility of sending samples for analyses'. 17 Conclusions on laboratories used for formulation analysis of plant protection products as part of official controls

There are designated and accredited laboratories for PPP formulation analyses. This pro- vides solid basis for ensuring reliable results of tests and analyses. Nonetheless, the lack of analyses for unacceptable co-formulants and regulated impurities in the sampling pro- gramme together with the limited controls on the source of active substances (see conclu- sion 81) partly undermines the capability of the system of official control to ensure the safety of the PPPs placed on the market.

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls of active substances used for the manufacturing of PPPs include checks that the producers of such active substances are actually those specified in the relevant PPP authorisation. This is to comply with Article 24(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Recommendation based on conclusion: No 81 Associated finding: No 77

To define conditions and establish criteria for when prior notice to agricultural users would be necessary and duly justified for the official controls to be carried out. This is in order to comply with Article 9 (4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Recommendation based on conclusion: No 96 Associated findings: No 94, 95

audits.title: Evaluation of the implementation of animal health controls in relation to sheep pox and goat pox

recommendations.text: To review the procedures so they prescribe the routine collection of samples for laboratory examination during the immediate investigations of all suspected cases of SPGP to confirm or rule out the presence of disease. Regulation (EU) 2016/426 of the European Parliament and the Council, Article 54, paragraph 2(b), and Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687, Article 6, paragraph 2(b)

citations.text: Disease control measures on suspected cases were generally adequate. However, the lack of routine sampling and testing in suspected cases may have delayed outbreak confirmation, and potentially increased the viral load in the farm, or weakened the basis for ruling out suspected cases.

recommendations.text: To review the procedures to include that, in cases where SPGP have been confirmed, officials will trace animals sent to slaughter and milk dispatched during at least the 21 days prior to the notification of suspicion. That tracing should be part of the epidemiological enquiry and should be recorded, shall extend at least to the first food processing or animal by-product establishments, and shall be followed by risk- mitigating treatment or disposal of such products if they are not listed as safe commodities. Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/687, Article 17, paragraph 1(b) and Article 19, paragraph 2.

citations.text: For confirmed cases, the authorities implemented appropriate control measures, except they fail to trace animal products dispatched from infected farms. Although the oversight is unknown, it could have led to the unintentional spread of sheep pox 4 https://food.ec.europa.eu/horizontal-topics/official-controls-and-enforcement/legislation-official-controls/better- training-safer-food_en. 4 to other farms and regions, presenting inconsistent risk-mitigation measures and hampering the assurance provided by the disease containment measures.

audits.title: Microbial safety of food of non-animal origin

recommendations.text: To ensure that operators placing seeds for sprouting to final consumers in the market are registered as producers of food as required by Article 6(2) of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, and subject to official controls as required by Article 10 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The audit team identified some establishments packing and placing in the market seeds for sprouting for the final consumer which were not found in the existing registers. This type of companies might be registered as operators selling seeds for sowing, but there were not registered as food producers. This is not in line with Article 6(2) of Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. Therefore, these operators are not subject to control by the competent authorities. Approval of sprout-producing establishments

In the case of post-primary production operators, there is a system for registration that covers all type of activities with the exception of operators placing seeds for sprouting to the final consumer. This prevents the CA to conduct the appropriate official controls to verify compliance with the applicable rules in the latter area of controls.

recommendations.text: The competent authorities should ensure that official controls in sprout-producing establishments verify that seeds for sprouting of EU origin have been produced in compliance with Regulation (EC) No 852/2004.

citations.text: However, the inspectors did not properly cover the suitability of the seeds of EU origin to be used for sprouting. In all visited establishments, there were bags of seeds of different species stored which were labelled as seeds for sowing, with no indication of suitability for sprouting, neither in the labels, nor in the associated documentation such as invoices or delivery notes. Inspectors did not require evidence that the seeds were appropriate for producing sprouts, and that had been obtained in compliance with the requirements of Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 852/2004.

The competent authorities carried out official controls to sprout producers with overall an adequate scope. However, the verification of compliance that seeds produced in the EU stored and used in these establishments are suitable for production of sprout has been systematically overlooked during official controls. This undermines the effectiveness of such official controls.

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls verify that the analytical methods used by operators for their own controls are in compliance with the method requirements set out by Commission Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005, and that the competent authority had formally authorised the operator to use alternative methods as required in Article 5(5) of Commission Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005.

citations.text: As part of the official control, inspectors verify the operator's sampling plans (final products and surfaces) and analyses carried out for testing pathogens. Operators visited were using used both non-accredited and accredited laboratories for the analyses of their samples. In general, the analytical methods used were not the reference methods of Commission Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. Inspectors did not verify that the used alternative methods had been validated in accordance with ISO 16140-2 or no evidence was presented that the competent authority had formally authorised the operator to use other analytical methods. This is not in line with Article 5(5) of Commission Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005.

The CAs do verify that operators carry out microbiological testing as set out in Regulation (EC) 2073/2005. However, there is no control of whether the methods used are in line with Article 5(5) of Regulation (EC) No 2073/2005. This lack of assessment to challenge the reliability of the own controls carried out by operators weakens the effectiveness of the official controls.

recommendations.text: To ensure that official controls to establishments producing ready to eat cut fruit and vegetables are effective to verify compliance by the operators with the rules in the area of food safety, as required by Articles 2(1)(a) and 9 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The audit team identified serious deficiencies in the establishment visited in the AC of Madrid. These deficiencies included structural issues, such as the location of crates washing facilities within the production area of high-risk products, the deficient separation of clean and dirty areas, lacking appropriate changing facilities for personnel accessing to "clean" areas and the inadequate crossing flows of raw material, packing material and finish products. These are not in line with the requirements set out in Chapter I, II, V, IX of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 852/2004. In addition, food safety culture was deficient and risk practices were identified which include, among others, peeling and de-rooting onions in the same area than packing ready to eat products (RTE); the placement of a floor brush over the water basin for cleaning tools; use of cutting tools without observing internal colour code to avoid cross contamination with allergens (celery); lacking system to identify clean/dirty crates for raw material and final product. These are not in line with the requirements set out in Chapter XIa on Food Safety Culture of Annex II to Regulation (EC) No 852/2004.

The audit team reviewed previous inspection reports, and some non-compliances had been documented. However, the CA had failed to identify serious structural and operational shortcomings despite inspecting that operator for more than 10 years.

To address the serious deficiencies identified during this audit, the Health Department of Madrid informed the audit team of actions taken: · Regarding the operator, the CA has drafted a comprehensive report indicating all identified shortcomings and activity suspended until deficiencies are corrected. · Regarding the official control system, in the last quarter of 2024 an official control to all establishments in the region producing cut fruits and vegetables. These official controls will be carried out by two inspectors. The responsible for the technical unit of FNAO will carry out one supervision on the performance of the inspector on the spot in that type of establishments. · Changes in the planning of official controls for 2025 programme. The inspection criteria will prioritise establishments producing RTE with higher frequency of controls. The annual programme will be adjusted to consider the workload due to non-programmed activities to ensure that all operators are subject to an annual complete control. The official control procedure has been changed to require that inspections are carried out by a team of two inspectors in the high-risk establishments. A new supervision procedure will be adopted requiring supervision on-site to be carried out in high-risk establishments. · The internal audit unit will include for the 2025 plan, one audit to the programme of official control of FNAO and specifically of RTE operators. 16 Other control systems

The serious structural and food safety culture shortcomings identified in a producer of 17 RTE cut fruit and vegetable calls into question the effectiveness of the official controls associated to this type of high-risk production. Consequently, the deficiencies in the enforcement measures compromises the effectiveness of the system of official controls.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the procedures and/or arrangements to ensure the effectiveness and appropriateness of official controls are effective to identify deficiencies in the performance of official controls as required by Article 5(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: The audit team checked reports of such supervision activities to official controls within the scope of this audit. In some cases, the number of on-site supervision controls were not in compliance with the planned ones. In Murcia, the department of Health indicated that in 2022, where more than 10 500 official controls were carried out in all areas related to food, 8 supervision on-site inspections were conducted. In 2023, out of more than 11 000 official controls, 11 on-site supervision inspections were carried out. The on-site supervision inspections were not related to FNAO. In Madrid, no in-situ supervision inspections were carried out in 2022, 2023 and 2024. As seen in paragraphs 6 66 and 68 below, these supervision arrangements have not been effective to identify deviations or deficiencies in the performance of official controls in the area of FNAO, and therefore has not fulfilled the requirement sets out in Article 5(1)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. Conclusions on competent authorities.
The lack or ineffective supervision activities prevent the competent authority to identify, correct and therefore improve the system of official controls.

The Madrid Health Department informed the audit team that the reorganisation will be accompanied with a change of the supervision system to be implemented from 2025. 15 Before 2021, supervision activities consisted in a documentary revision by the line manager. In 2021, one supervision on site was performed, in a sector different than FNAO, and from 2022 to 2024 no supervision activities were conducted, neither documentary nor on the spot. This is not in line with the guidance agreed between AESAN and the ACs.

The audit team reviewed previous inspection reports, and some non-compliances had been documented. However, the CA had failed to identify serious structural and operational shortcomings despite inspecting that operator for more than 10 years.

recommendations.text: To ensure that the competent authorities · take appropriate action as per Article 138 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 in case of non-compliances with EU legislation on animal welfare, in particular to prevent further occurrences of such non-compliances; · take all measures to implement the rules on penalties as required by Article 139(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 hence penalties for non-compliances with EU legislation on animal welfare can be effectively applied. apply penalties that are effective and dissuasive, as required by Article 139(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. to 64

citations.text: Most operators have the necessary knowledge and motivation to ensure proper animal welfare at slaughter. Improvements in animal welfare at slaughter are driven by that, supported by effective official control activities with adequate follow-up actions from operators. However, administratively burdensome and lengthy sanctioning process reduce the dissuasive effect of enforcement when operators are reluctant to comply. Sanctioning procedures are not dissuasive, risking repeated or prolonged animal suffering.

recommendations.text: To ensure that samples taken in the context of official controls are tested in laboratories which comply with Article 37(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. For this purpose, the definitions for official control and other official activities in national plant health legislation should be aligned with those established in Article 2 of Regulation (EU) 2017/625.

citations.text: All official laboratories designated for the analysis of samples for PWN are exempt from mandatory accreditation under Article 40(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The CA also indicated that all designated laboratories are under the official supervision of the NRL and will participate in proficiency tests for PWN in 2025. Data provided by the CA show that some laboratories have participated in proficiency tests in the past, such as the Centro de Sanidad Forestal Calabazanos in 2010. Additionally, some laboratories have organized inter-laboratory collaborative studies on PWN, including the Laboratorio Agrario y Fitopatológico de Galicia and Centro de Sanidad Forestal Calabazanos in 5 April 2025. The audit team noted that while laboratories designated by the AC authorities for the analysis of PWN samples in the three PWN affected ACs have quality assurance systems in place (either accreditation to EN ISO/IEC 17025 or ISO 9001:2015) as required by Article 40(1)(b)(iv) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625, there is no information available to MAPA regarding the compliance of other designated laboratories with this requirement.

Authorisation is required prior to the movement of specified wood outside the DA in the AC Extremadura. This process also includes official sampling of the wood. In the AC Galicia, official samples for PWN are taken during the annual official control visits to operators authorised to issue plant passports. Additionally, an official sample was taken at a suspended operator to confirm his compliance with requirements to issue the ISPM mark (see details in section 5.8, point 61). Article 2(1) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 defines that official control means activities in order to verify compliance by operators and goods with plant health legislation. Therefore, the samples described above were taken in the context of official controls. The testing of these samples in designated laboratories using methods which are not accredited to ISO 17025 is not in line with Article 37(4) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625. The derogation from mandatory accreditation under Article 40(1)(b) of Regulation (EU) 2017/625 applies only to laboratories conducting analyses in the context of other official activities. 5.1.4 Public awareness campaigns

There is sufficient testing capacity in the network of designated laboratories under supervision of the NRL. Most samples tested are taken for surveys. A small number of samples are taken for official controls, and the testing of these samples in laboratories, which are not accredited to ISO 17025, does not provide the level of quality assurance required by EU legislation.
